So, we take out a factor of $2$ from the entire expression:

$$
2({x}^{2}-2x+\frac{3}{2})
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+\frac{3}{2}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+\frac{3}{2}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${1}^{2}$, writing the constant term $\frac{3}{2}$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}}-{1}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
(x-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-2x+\frac{3}{2}) & =2((x-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2{(x-1)}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =2{(x-1)}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186332892 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11a795cb-9f0e-5939-900e-adafa303f8bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6{\left(x-\frac{1}{6}\right)}^{2}-\frac{1}{9}" :db/id 17592186330103} {:answer/id #uuid "586c59c4-4661-5f6d-8c14-a8719591fc01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6{\left(x-\frac{1}{6}\right)}^{2}-\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186330738} {:answer/id #uuid "72076787-7552-58b8-8ad4-00b516cbaf7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\left(6x-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}+\frac{1}{9}" :db/id 17592186330976} {:answer/id #uuid "98ee28e9-1737-5e3b-81c5-05141104f588" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\left(6x-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186331315} {:answer/id #uuid "f630c36b-13b8-5df3-93c0-7e5b92d1a0cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6{\left(x-\frac{1}{6}\right)}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186332110}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186330738} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d388fcd-2c84-5c86-86ee-03feb01e614c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186332301}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "38a732d9-8b0e-58f3-ab88-f23eff634c61" :question/math-academy-id "q-52537" :question/problem "Rewrite $6{x}^{2}-2x$ by completing the square." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $6$. Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{2}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{4})$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x}\right)}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186332904 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "201bd2a8-775c-5f63-8baf-ac9dc04377cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,b)$ and the radius is $3b$" :db/id 17592186330224} {:answer/id #uuid "3f70825c-f5da-5f48-b74c-bf021c464ed8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(b,2b)$ and the radius is $4b$" :db/id 17592186330513} {:answer/id #uuid "43273b72-7486-5fc8-9bb6-6aed8683a7ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(b,3b)$ and the radius is $3|b|$" :db/id 17592186330552} {:answer/id #uuid "48cc3302-2b74-5f48-9d8a-67f2334f31eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,2b)$ and the radius is $5b$" :db/id 17592186330603} {:answer/id #uuid "c00cbe3e-f562-5e50-a789-640dc927d1e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(b,b)$ and the radius is $5|b|$" :db/id 17592186331654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186330603} :answer-field/id #uuid "0c0ccf6d-0f98-5c63-9d4a-320be7de233a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186332214}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "15c2ddf4-52c0-50dd-8f5f-235054ec7d90" :question/math-academy-id "q-54052" :question/problem "The segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ is the diameter of a circle where the points $A$ and $B$ have coordinates $(3b,6b)$ and $(-3b,-2b)$, respectively, with $b>0.$ Find the coordinates of the center and the radius of the circle." :question/worked-solution "The center of the circle is located at the midpoint of the diameter. So, we can calculate the coordinates of the center using the midpoint formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}(h,k) & =(\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2},\frac{{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{3b+(-3b)}{2},\frac{6b+(-2b)}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{0}{2},\frac{4b}{2}) \\  & =(0,2b).\end{aligned}
$$

The radius can be found by calculating the distance between the center $(0,2b)$ and a point on the circle, such as $A(3b,6b):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{({x}_{1}-{x}_{2})}^{2}+{({y}_{1}-{y}_{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-3b)^{2}+(2b-6b)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3b)^{2}+(-4b)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{b}^{2}+16{b}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{b}^{2}} \\  & =5|b|.\end{aligned}

Finally, since $b>0,$ we have that

r=5|b|=5b.

Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{4}-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2$, as shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{4} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=0$ and $x=2$ is $x=1.$

Since $1\in [0,2]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

Notice that the region for $x\in [0,1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[\frac{1}{5}-1]-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [1,2]$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-x)|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =([\frac{32}{5}-2]-[\frac{1}{5}-1]) \\  & =\frac{26}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}+\frac{26}{5}=\frac{30}{5}=6.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186332945 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0864cdf9-1ffd-56c1-8cec-9c7e3634c2e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The integral is divergent" :db/id 17592186330021} {:answer/id #uuid "757f2c97-4c6e-5a4b-b58e-740ddec39baa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{15}{8}" :db/id 17592186331005} {:answer/id #uuid "c02ca5ed-e5be-530f-b339-6203cf61077f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186331655} {:answer/id #uuid "d82819b4-466e-564f-a4fd-bc1c368333eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{15}{2}" :db/id 17592186331867} {:answer/id #uuid "e39d5946-f20c-5fd9-9c4f-e13376e2ce60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186331960}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186330021} :answer-field/id #uuid "4b6c3b91-0868-5cbe-bd0f-5ddc36c6f516" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186332333}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "06fd8b41-8200-5edd-a18c-2621495e1f13" :question/math-academy-id "q-5964" :question/problem "$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\lim_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{6}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\lim_{a\to -\infty }({\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{x}{6}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\lim_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{a}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\lim_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{a}{6} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot \left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.

$$

$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+\frac{16}{{x}^{2}}+8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{x}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $3\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{6}$ seconds." :question/worked-solution "The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=9\,⟹\,\omega =3.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is $12\operatorname{cos}⁡3t.$ The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3t$ because this is already included in the complimentary function. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is  

$$
{y}_{p}=t(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3t),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined.  

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =0,\beta =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2t\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡3t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+(B+2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡3t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $3\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=3.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=0,\,B=1.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=(1+2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡3t.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{6}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ We get

$$

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨-\frac{0}{\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨0,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{(1-{t}^{2})}^{3/2}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨-\frac{1}{(1-{0}^{2})^{3/2}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨-1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(0)$ and ${r}^{″}(0)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨0,\,1,0⟩\times ⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}}=\frac{1}{(1)^{3}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335763 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a7c30e6-c4fd-5b9f-8b33-63bfdc242a7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186333536} {:answer/id #uuid "47032272-9a8f-5bdd-9811-23fd93f7bd48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186333645} {:answer/id #uuid "4b0ba869-1963-5543-916a-61f21bdfe6e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186333678} {:answer/id #uuid "879c0d1e-5384-5707-b993-66e2366ac32c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186334189} {:answer/id #uuid "fd0f9487-b82f-52b2-9b68-320c61641358" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186335213}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333536} :answer-field/id #uuid "20586bf7-c2fd-57ac-825e-1691e50c888b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335299}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "146a5e9e-6c97-5732-9c84-59f28f9f2729" :question/math-academy-id "q-64925" :question/problem "$\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{4}\right)=$" :question/worked-solution "Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=12\operatorname{ln}⁡x,\,x>0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\underbrace{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{\text{chain rule}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+6y=12t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{2t}+B{e}^{3t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta $ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0-5\alpha +6(\alpha t+\beta )=12t
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
6\alpha t+(-5\alpha +6\beta )=12t.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6\alpha &=12\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ -5\alpha +6\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Hence, $\alpha =2$ and $\beta =\frac{5}{3},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2t+\frac{5}{3}.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335768 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c9a56e0-5972-5209-9d5c-ea16e82e995f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186333100} {:answer/id #uuid "66686a01-21cc-56d7-951a-bacb93258c0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186333921} {:answer/id #uuid "79013707-fe29-522d-ac8d-ac18b46d1880" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186334075} {:answer/id #uuid "989e0c9d-3b24-5671-9e42-b86c26764caf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186334342} {:answer/id #uuid "b3886518-c45d-5987-8dfe-39a52ed04936" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186334564}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333921} :answer-field/id #uuid "6a4e3654-a019-5e30-92b9-ed3bae770d8d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335446}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1f6c71da-f5b0-5c03-871d-e07fb324730c" :question/math-academy-id "q-64968" :question/problem "A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P$ with $y$-coordinate $0$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\sqrt{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+\frac{\pi }{4})$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=0$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =\sqrt{2}(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 0+\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335772 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11b05fec-223c-56bf-846e-c1dd3e529fc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186333147} {:answer/id #uuid "4316fb3b-4ead-50d9-b393-d3a3f73206fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186333614} {:answer/id #uuid "5dafac36-0012-58ad-9ae8-980b43b4e78d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186333848} {:answer/id #uuid "8e74c3fb-c1c2-53e1-980d-f0ad20d22a8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186334261} {:answer/id #uuid "c6b9be1d-865a-5c53-a7cd-250bdaf0a6b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x" :db/id 17592186334716}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333614} :answer-field/id #uuid "c83a3c69-9ddf-5684-bac6-3760d114ab07" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335606}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "afb025b0-c527-5d33-8970-81ceec1a4be4" :question/math-academy-id "q-64998" :question/problem "Given that ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}+9y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation." :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3u\operatorname{cos}⁡3x \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+6{u}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9u\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+6{u}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-9u\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+9u\operatorname{sin}⁡3x & =0 \\ {u}^{″}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+6{u}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x & =0 \\ {u}^{″} & =-6{u}^{′}\operatorname{cot}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=-6w\operatorname{cot}⁡3x.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{\csc }^{2}⁡3x.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{\csc }^{2}⁡3x\,⟹\,u=-\frac{{c}_{1}}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡3x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u\operatorname{sin}⁡3x$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x(-\frac{{c}_{1}}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡3x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-3$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x(\operatorname{cot}⁡3x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335773 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25d95a4e-4af7-5ebb-b4dd-2de74fa3aba4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186333339} {:answer/id #uuid "a706e74c-a1f5-5e97-a835-24d8665d49a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186334453} {:answer/id #uuid "bc11635f-094d-5065-8e13-fceb1d4a4682" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{x}" :db/id 17592186334628} {:answer/id #uuid "be682b4a-c5cd-5b73-82ea-0fbeabc91ce5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{4}" :db/id 17592186334637} {:answer/id #uuid "c770c084-de35-587f-8920-be3df11d6079" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{3}" :db/id 17592186334721}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186334637} :answer-field/id #uuid "1bac7152-54aa-518e-bf1d-cd26c24529c9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335291}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e0e220b1-dde9-5e74-a722-221f7a53c2e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-65000" :question/problem "The function ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{2}$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{2}{y}^{″}-5x{y}^{′}+8y=0$ for $x>0.$ Use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation." :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\cdot {x}^{2}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x){x}^{2}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{x}^{2}+2ux \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{x}^{2}+4{u}^{′}x+2u.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}+4{u}^{′}x+2u)-5x({u}^{′}{x}^{2}+2ux)+8u{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}+4{u}^{′}x+2u-5{u}^{′}x-10u+8u) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{2}-{u}^{′}x) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}({u}^{″}x-{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{3}\ne 0$ for $x>0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}x-{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}x-w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}x.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}x\,⟹\,u=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}{x}^{2}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{x}^{2}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}(\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}{x}^{2}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}={x}^{4}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335780 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "69f8a84a-8b1c-5b4b-ae96-4f1ce54a0d1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6{x}^{3}" :db/id 17592186333958} {:answer/id #uuid "b0086e4c-f2ab-58cc-b400-c55ea3081f1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186334538} {:answer/id #uuid "c9ea28ec-318d-5a44-93ad-fdb3eb4634c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12{x}^{3}" :db/id 17592186334745} {:answer/id #uuid "ce7619f4-8535-50b4-a5ba-ca66a9885dbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24{x}^{3}" :db/id 17592186334788} {:answer/id #uuid "eb8021b3-dcba-55aa-a35f-3cf830aac491" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186335049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333958} :answer-field/id #uuid "f2a7031e-0a46-5707-8cc1-67be04bd5a30" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335661}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "41c56114-5724-5a96-85b7-73980267ba4b" :question/math-academy-id "q-65038" :question/problem "Given that $$
\displaystyle D={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x},
$$ what is $D(y)$ for $y=2{x}^{3}+4?$" :question/worked-solution "The given operator is a second-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{2}={x}^{2},{f}_{1}=-x,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(2{x}^{3}+4) \\  & =({x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x})(2{x}^{3}+4) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(2{x}^{3}+4)-x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}+4) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{2})-x\cdot 6{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot 12x-6{x}^{3} \\  & =12{x}^{3}-6{x}^{3} \\  & =6{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335781 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0dc8479d-39ef-5832-bde9-2f979468cdcf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12{e}^{-2x}" :db/id 17592186333112} {:answer/id #uuid "38110e20-24ec-514c-82eb-c30506c87026" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186333506} {:answer/id #uuid "4be5d3fd-a0e7-52cb-af31-0b85e3903078" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{e}^{-2x}" :db/id 17592186333687} {:answer/id #uuid "ad306801-c548-5532-a9b2-d6d29e133a01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16{e}^{-2x}" :db/id 17592186334515} {:answer/id #uuid "d33cd2ed-cf57-5c03-999e-34d09e84333c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4{e}^{-2x}" :db/id 17592186334840}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333506} :answer-field/id #uuid "854e6369-19da-58fe-880c-9d36a6f10073" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335493}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d6f06f58-bcd8-56e9-88ce-5e51b6beca8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-65055" :question/problem "Given that $$
\displaystyle D=\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+4\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x},
$$ what is $D(y)$ for $y={e}^{-2x}?$" :question/worked-solution "The given operator is a third-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={a}_{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{a}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}_{1}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{a}_{0}y
$$

with constant coefficients ${a}_{3}=1,{a}_{2}=4,{a}_{1}=4,$ and ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =(\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+4\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}){e}^{-2x} \\  & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}({e}^{-2x})+4\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({e}^{-2x})+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(-2{e}^{-2x})+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{e}^{-2x})+4\cdot (-2{e}^{-2x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{e}^{-2x})+4\cdot 4{e}^{-2x}-8{e}^{-2x} \\  & =-8{e}^{-2x}+16{e}^{-2x}-8{e}^{-2x} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335800 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10ef7585-f490-52ce-84d4-c14afbd71f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y(\operatorname{ln}(xy)+2)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x(\operatorname{ln}(xy)+2)\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186333143} {:answer/id #uuid "21b12eb3-67b9-5f76-80f9-150884fc0d5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y(\operatorname{ln}(xy)+1)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x(\operatorname{ln}(xy)+1)\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186333290} {:answer/id #uuid "3ea7c594-0a56-5e0b-a1fd-7fd5413db99e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{i}-y\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186333580} {:answer/id #uuid "f9a4ec80-da82-5689-8ecb-e79e98294b6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+y\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186335176} {:answer/id #uuid "fe69f0a9-435b-5c17-9a63-9c54c8b0d0ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186335228}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333290} :answer-field/id #uuid "c8f1d221-bfab-57b4-bd66-7eea20107505" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335609}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "838d032d-5600-5cb9-9af4-36cc70864ee1" :question/math-academy-id "q-65131" :question/problem "Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}(xy),\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain:

Applying the difference formula for sine with $x=\frac{7\pi }{6}$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{4}$, we obtain

\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the sum formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x),$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ &=1 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =1 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =1 \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\ ϕ & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={1}^{2}+{1}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({\sin }^{2}⁡ϕ+{\cos }^{2}⁡ϕ) & =2 \\ {R}^{2} & =2 \\ R & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x-\frac{\pi }{4})
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335845 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21e5506f-4577-5036-ada5-dc6f9bc99169" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{10}" :db/id 17592186333292} {:answer/id #uuid "366585d6-d0fc-50e1-b496-79591f6c5405" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186333490} {:answer/id #uuid "75f6de9c-83fb-55b9-9419-ef8f92a5ae22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{7}" :db/id 17592186334056} {:answer/id #uuid "e198d2ca-23db-5649-85de-6116093fd7d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186334955} {:answer/id #uuid "ee45bb2e-4cfb-5586-96b6-963f79e9e559" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186335079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333490} :answer-field/id #uuid "10496ff6-7779-5051-aba6-5bba4e7b9c2c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335269}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "baa94592-3dad-5374-a846-3b63aecad625" :question/math-academy-id "q-65571" :question/problem "![](images/2f/2f11d5b11c53f7b826291e0b7e95828f57d6f1242b768baf12c874be229b2935.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{5}+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$" :question/worked-solution "The parameter $C$ represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{5}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{5C}{3}$ indicates that the graph of $$
\displaystyle y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{3}))
$$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{3x}{5}\right).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](images/5e/5e9b6568ec493d95db6fe72a6a19024326c5b920629e9ff44a85db54089aa2a6.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{3x}{5}\right)$ by $\frac{\pi }{3}-0=\frac{\pi }{3}$ units to the right. Therefore:

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine:

- The $y$-value of the point must lie in the range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x,$ which is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$

- First, we consider the point $(0,-2\pi ).$ We note the following:

- The point $(-2\pi ,0)$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\,✓$

- The range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x$ is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and $y=-2\pi $ does **not** lie within this range. $\,\times $

Therefore, the point $(0,-2\pi )$ does **not** lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x.$

- Next, we consider the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\pi }{6}).$ We note the following:

- The point $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{1}{2})$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\,✓$

- The range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x$ is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{6}$ lies within this range. $\,✓$

Therefore, the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\pi }{6})$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x.$

- Finally, we consider the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\pi }{4}).$ We note the following:

- The point $(-\frac{\pi }{4},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\,✓$

- The range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x$ is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and $y=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies within this range. $\,✓$

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2\ge 1+2 \\  & f(x)\ge 3.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2\le -1+2 \\  & f(x)\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$

$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,1]\cup [3,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186335877 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "45a3eba8-c533-5642-9359-8f5adc8b7616" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-\frac{5}{3}]\cup [-\frac{1}{3},\infty )" :db/id 17592186333632} {:answer/id #uuid "4e1fa6ed-4b2a-5d71-826d-be906b534cee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [3,\infty )" :db/id 17592186333709} {:answer/id #uuid "87065fa6-f5a0-550b-80b1-867e887a3b57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-\frac{1}{3}]\cup [0,\infty )" :db/id 17592186334185} {:answer/id #uuid "eba6ed51-4e84-5f9b-ba75-8c440bbe6acc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-3]\cup [-\frac{1}{3},\infty )" :db/id 17592186335050} {:answer/id #uuid "eefcef19-8d1a-5883-a20b-67ea52c964b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-\frac{5}{3}]\cup [0,\infty )" :db/id 17592186335085}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333632} :answer-field/id #uuid "aad2f438-ee37-59da-a7ab-a1d7bb45d223" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335552}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9ec246d1-243c-5637-8a53-160c017f85e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-66063" :question/problem "Find the range of the function $$

$$" :question/worked-solution "The range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

The points where $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-1$ are **local maximums** of the graph of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡x.$ For now, we're interested in the local maximums (not local minimums) of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ because we see that $f(x)$ contains a vertical reflection.

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{3{x}^{4}+2}{{x}^{3}-7x} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(\frac{3{x}^{4}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{7x}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(3x+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{7}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(3x+0)}{(1-0+0)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,3x \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186335944 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0948bf66-b9eb-50e0-aa36-a645d1dd4d71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186333074} {:answer/id #uuid "7f2618e2-1548-5494-9496-e1c7e62150fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186334121} {:answer/id #uuid "89c810fb-1fda-543b-a4ab-03e4899ffff7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\infty " :db/id 17592186334214} {:answer/id #uuid "c6d2b174-a819-5c3c-8807-a772dccc544a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "Does not exist." :db/id 17592186334717} {:answer/id #uuid "f53a2a74-5ee8-5629-9c0f-607f722db1d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\infty " :db/id 17592186335140}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186335140} :answer-field/id #uuid "315d67e3-a8ca-5508-a7b2-478fa5b39f63" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335337}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "66754a6b-36e3-52c9-b059-874445c5d773" :question/math-academy-id "q-68043" :question/problem "Calculate $\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{{x}^{3}+x}{2{x}^{2}+x+4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{2}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$

\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}\left(-\frac{2x}{9\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\right) & =\lim_{x\to 0}(-\frac{2}{9}\cdot \frac{x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}{\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\cdot {[\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}]}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\cdot {1}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}

In this case, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{2}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{4{x}^{2}+6x+1}{1-2{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{6x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(4+\frac{6}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{6}{x}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(4+\frac{6}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2)} \\  & \to \frac{4+0+0}{0-2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is  $y=-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186335976 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c842fc6-bdb7-5fd1-95ec-a8a6c5c213af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{arcsec} (7x)+C" :db/id 17592186333694} {:answer/id #uuid "8817bce9-1d12-59f6-a5d1-e12cf7bf9ea0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{arcsec} (7x)}{7}+C" :db/id 17592186334193} {:answer/id #uuid "d4994be2-56ea-5429-8d7d-0f2980d19115" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{arcsec} (49x)}{7}+C" :db/id 17592186334851} {:answer/id #uuid "d5ef86d7-cffa-55cc-8343-9157ea5e011e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{arcsec} (7x)}{49}+C" :db/id 17592186334864} {:answer/id #uuid "eff32ea7-4fa2-5bab-91d2-777e88bff4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{arcsec} (49x)+C" :db/id 17592186335089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333694} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebde86f4-5f82-5ab1-8866-0726b82f2be1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335652}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1090f68a-a5e7-5187-bfa4-8579cbfba1e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-69475" :question/problem "$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{7\,\text{d}x}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}=7\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\operatorname{arcsec} ,$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec} (u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $7x.$

So, let's substitute $u=7x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

Multiplying both sides by $(4x-1)(x+3)(x+1)$ gives

$$

For $x=\frac{1}{4}$, we get 

$$

For $x=-3$, we get 

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
u=\frac{v}{|\,v\,|}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,v\,| & =\sqrt{{v}_{x}^{2}+{v}_{y}^{2}+{v}_{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+0+9} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $v$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{|\,v\,|} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot ⟨-4,0,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{4}{5},0,\frac{3}{5}⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{f}(t) & =⟨\sqrt{t},\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{ln}t,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\ \mathbf{g}(t) & =⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{t},\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the constant multiple rule and the sum rule, we have

$$
(\mathbf{f}(t)+4\mathbf{g}(t))^{'}={\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)+4{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t).
$$

Let's find the derivatives of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{t},\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\hspace{0.222em}4{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf{f}(t)+4\mathbf{g}(t))^{'} & ={\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)+4{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{t},\hspace{0.222em}0⟩+4⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\hspace{0.222em}4{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{t},\hspace{0.222em}0⟩+⟨4,\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}},\hspace{0.222em}16{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+4,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{t}-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}},\hspace{0.222em}0+16{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1+8\sqrt{t}}{2\sqrt{t}},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{t-4}{{t}^{2}},\hspace{0.222em}16{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338809 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "619a4c51-2e05-537d-92f8-05b27adc0576" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186467812} {:answer/id #uuid "b91d959d-53f8-55db-a51e-4ff6ad7ddc62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186467813}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186467812} :answer-field/id #uuid "9fdac921-475b-5331-a99d-ec7b6d2ed4c0" :answer-field/key "$(-\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2})$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468627} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f35e836d-9bb8-578a-a543-2f4893a1ac7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186467814} {:answer/id #uuid "bb49ae2b-5562-5a17-b362-7dd84e0030a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186467815}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186467815} :answer-field/id #uuid "cfdd3471-0795-5b0b-9ab3-357659c59d0f" :answer-field/key "$(1,\frac{\pi }{2})$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468628} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7240a062-fdde-5f4a-b323-b6fe3a7554d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186467816} {:answer/id #uuid "0d23fd2f-ce53-5110-991d-3c8e82483cb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186467817}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186467816} :answer-field/id #uuid "67a4358a-90d6-55fb-8b57-f1e67df2bf37" :answer-field/key "$(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{6})$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468629}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "cc9d880f-4b58-5f10-97af-057cfca9838a" :question/math-academy-id "q-70714" :question/problem "Which of the following points lies on the graph of the function $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x?$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "In order for a point $(a,b)$ to lie on the graph of the function $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x,$ the following conditions must hold:

- The reflected point $(b,a)$ must lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ meaning $a=\operatorname{sin}⁡b.$

- The $y$-value of the point must lie in the range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x,$ which is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$

With this in mind, let's check each of the points.  

- First, we consider the point $(-\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2}).$ We note the following:

- The point $(-\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2})$ does **not** lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$  $\,\times $

Therefore, the point $(-\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2})$  does **not** lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x.$

- Next, we consider the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{2}).$ We note the following:

- The point $(\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\,✓$

- The range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x$ is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{2}$ lies within this range. $\,✓$

Therefore, the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{2})$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x.$

The line segment $\overset{―}{XY}$ is a diameter of a circle. Given that $X$ and $Y$ have coordinates $(7,3)$ and $(-1,3)$, respectively, what is the equation of the circle?" :question/worked-solution "The general equation of a circle with radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ is  

$$
(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}={r}^{2}.
$$

Using the distance formula to compute the distance between the points $X(7,3)$ and $Y(-1,3),$ we find that the length of the diameter is 

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{{(7-(-1))}^{2}+{(3-3)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{8}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So the radius of the circle is 

$$
r=\frac{8}{2}=4.
$$

Since the center of a circle is the midpoint of the diameter, to find the center we use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
(\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2},\frac{{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}}{2})=(\frac{7+(-1)}{2},\frac{3+3}{2})=(3,3)
$$

So our circle has radius $r=4$ and center $(a,b)=(3,3),$ and therefore it is represented by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2} & ={r}^{2} \\ (x-3)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ (x-3)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338868 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00e4a49e-453f-5b68-98b1-7a31adb93775" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x-3)^{2}-{y}^{2}=10" :db/id 17592186336038} {:answer/id #uuid "450d803a-0dda-576f-ae85-76770d27f4a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=10" :db/id 17592186336677} {:answer/id #uuid "7ee14867-8540-55f0-b7a0-7100bebee222" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=10" :db/id 17592186337181} {:answer/id #uuid "87685e0e-a82f-5609-beee-7cd2ee774d09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=10" :db/id 17592186337255} {:answer/id #uuid "adc4df30-8770-5d9e-9c11-b2f992c2a043" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=10" :db/id 17592186337592}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337181} :answer-field/id #uuid "0625c9ee-953d-5a19-becb-0ce059539921" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338285}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4b08908d-2189-5c82-98e7-76da156bba41" :question/math-academy-id "q-70990" :question/problem "![](images/a6/a6a21dbf4785a270a0ae03066df1f92df73974532f9a75aa8e470cef42ea5e14.png)

\displaystyle \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{11}=1,
$$ find its intercepts with the $z$-axis." :question/worked-solution "To find the $z$-intercepts, we plug $x=0$ and $y=0$ into the equation:

$$

$$

Hence, we get the solutions $z=-\frac{11}{6}$ and $z=\frac{11}{6}.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $z$-axis are $(0,0,-\frac{11}{6})$ and $(0,0,\frac{11}{6}).$"} {:db/id 17592186338922 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10a0d643-3fba-5025-8ba0-fe80f13a0f5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186336191} {:answer/id #uuid "1a106852-4afd-52ed-ab68-75af9121d300" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,-2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186336273} {:answer/id #uuid "7079191a-2817-517c-b22b-ed0b7decbd3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,1,-2⟩" :db/id 17592186337033} {:answer/id #uuid "903c10f0-0ae9-5406-ba48-0978c42fa7c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,0,1⟩" :db/id 17592186337339} {:answer/id #uuid "a5b520c6-d634-55fb-9a73-9aac376cbf2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186337536}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336191} :answer-field/id #uuid "cc44ecd5-8b94-53f1-aa64-9fdcc88bcaac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338643}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3dcde73b-e9a7-56a8-9973-7e22f495be27" :question/math-academy-id "q-71234" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{x(y-x)}{2x(y+1)}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,0) & =\frac{(-1)(0-(-1))}{2(-1)(0+1)} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,0) & ={f}_{y}(-1,0)(y-0) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-1 \\ z &=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $y-2z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨0,1,-2⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,-2⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\,j+k \\  & =⟨0,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,2,1⟩.$"} {:db/id 17592186338929 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "157bc3da-2d1c-5137-b516-d8ff7c42bad7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})" :db/id 17592186336235} {:answer/id #uuid "3cfe7ebf-3262-597f-b2fd-edf534fd618c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\mathbf{i}" :db/id 17592186336607} {:answer/id #uuid "4baa559e-cde4-5072-9145-09ac20cb641a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})" :db/id 17592186336735} {:answer/id #uuid "829583d7-8e78-579d-9221-64ce8b48dc24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})" :db/id 17592186337220} {:answer/id #uuid "e26af925-4997-53e5-8b3d-7425b92d8e93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186338003}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336735} :answer-field/id #uuid "e48649d2-bf76-55fc-aef9-b0aff8e82c8d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338680}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "22cfc584-e8e6-55e0-a1d3-35d71c5742a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-71370" :question/problem "Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$, can be found by computing $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\text{ }i+2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338930 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "049b7f23-d6a7-5be3-a6ca-ac19b8a84234" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186336070} {:answer/id #uuid "123c36c6-7310-581c-8de4-b675e090dc56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{i}" :db/id 17592186336203} {:answer/id #uuid "4b49d759-d015-5843-b6e9-3497dc09edfe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{i}" :db/id 17592186336730} {:answer/id #uuid "6e16ffd6-406d-50b5-9b6a-0f4b899fc6bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\mathbf{i}" :db/id 17592186337009} {:answer/id #uuid "ccd3f738-ef19-5d09-afcb-04a5b6bdd7fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(-2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{i})" :db/id 17592186337828}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337009} :answer-field/id #uuid "60184a90-8959-560b-aa4a-378830d13dbb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338445}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "436e814d-020d-5b28-b909-495bbb1c431a" :question/math-academy-id "q-71374" :question/problem "Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x+3y-2xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(1-2y)\text{ }i+(3-2x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(\frac{3}{2},1) & =(1-2(1))\text{ }i+(3-2\left(\frac{3}{2}\right))\text{ }j \\  & =-i\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(\frac{3}{2},1)}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(\frac{3}{2},1)‖} & =\frac{-\mathbf{i}}{1}=-\mathbf{i}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338933 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0dfa2d9c-c5a6-5bae-b0d2-a5aba5899793" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y=1" :db/id 17592186336165} {:answer/id #uuid "521e5638-e80d-5edb-bd60-91e3b7a98567" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-2y=1" :db/id 17592186336787} {:answer/id #uuid "9255b74e-b684-545c-a101-b50d053e917e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y=1" :db/id 17592186337362} {:answer/id #uuid "928ea3e2-97a0-57df-ae69-6fb23ba7d7dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y=1" :db/id 17592186337365} {:answer/id #uuid "c360c2bb-962a-5e23-b0d5-b54534c74210" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y-x=1" :db/id 17592186337766}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337362} :answer-field/id #uuid "59dddcfe-8a5c-5160-b7d7-f42966cf2e3f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338431}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2de4f7e4-2884-5220-a39a-17359a9ea964" :question/math-academy-id "q-71388" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2x+y-1=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y-1 & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\ -1 & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y)\,j \\  & =(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-2)\,i+(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-1)\,j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}-{0}^{2}}}-2)\,i+(-\frac{0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}-{0}^{2}}}-1)\,j \\  & =-i-j \\  & =⟨-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-1,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-1} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ 1-x & =-y \\ x-y & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338936 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "923db4e3-1672-5a50-9581-8d103a4e9394" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186337357} {:answer/id #uuid "a0ca54cd-1662-5f06-ad4a-139620f93cc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-x+y-1=0" :db/id 17592186337484} {:answer/id #uuid "a201c603-2105-5c16-ac28-6ea1909ee0e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-1=0" :db/id 17592186337500} {:answer/id #uuid "f0aa3752-46b2-55e2-872a-d4d7eb4de111" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y+1=0" :db/id 17592186338139} {:answer/id #uuid "f7b5b220-5b4e-5b43-8acc-b11f2fdd7f50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y+1=0" :db/id 17592186338205}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337500} :answer-field/id #uuid "a093c235-9586-5c2c-a6e1-6f61aa48334d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338573}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "47afea57-2ac6-5bfd-8472-520b5199e74f" :question/math-academy-id "q-71393" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338939 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "217b6b69-1258-52ca-92cb-84d166055cab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186336344} {:answer/id #uuid "8847c9cc-20d2-574c-a780-1b2f9a38d565" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{j}+2\,\mathbf{k}" :db/id 17592186337260} {:answer/id #uuid "9b429560-704b-5928-a704-fbc5ba05c495" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{k}" :db/id 17592186337439} {:answer/id #uuid "edd7d436-4244-565c-b127-7c866996e6d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{j}+2\,\mathbf{k}" :db/id 17592186338108} {:answer/id #uuid "f0dcdca1-0652-5268-9a5c-8bdbc0a1e227" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\mathbf{i}-2\,\mathbf{j}+2\,\mathbf{k}" :db/id 17592186338140}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337260} :answer-field/id #uuid "b348b668-7c03-56ec-b406-92e416034172" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7acbac43-bc81-5177-9def-8ee007ede43b" :question/math-academy-id "q-71404" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186338952 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23400f54-8b3f-5ebc-b598-c7818f4586c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186336361} {:answer/id #uuid "34196f13-9af3-5e84-930f-7cdc02f6b4ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\text{ }\mathbf{i}+y\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186336521} {:answer/id #uuid "78b044f0-5569-5fa2-b926-c4fa16e63d1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186337118} {:answer/id #uuid "86424757-d1c0-5142-865b-bc737655d636" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186337246} {:answer/id #uuid "8a45146a-092c-5746-a1f7-52f22a8062eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\text{ }\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186337277}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337118} :answer-field/id #uuid "0fa16c79-d297-52a5-b07c-cccb5e15aa03" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338305}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "91443473-cbb1-5ab2-b98b-379cda895777" :question/math-academy-id "q-71476" :question/problem "Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=(2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\frac{1}{xy},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}h(x,y)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=h\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)+f(x,y)\mathrm{∇}h(x,y) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}((2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j})+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(\frac{2xy+{y}^{2}}{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{j})+(-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(\frac{2x+y}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{x+2y}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j})+(-\frac{x+y}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{x+y}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(-\frac{x+y}{x}+\frac{2x+y}{x})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(-\frac{x+y}{y}+\frac{x+2y}{y})\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\  & =\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338956 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08503ca9-6377-5e96-8351-fd9fe91d34ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5e\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186336101} {:answer/id #uuid "25e254e6-ce2c-53bc-b986-9e21106f9cb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5e" :db/id 17592186336385} {:answer/id #uuid "814fdfa5-49d1-591b-ac3b-a5b01f92486b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7e" :db/id 17592186337206} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d00a90-be82-533f-bf58-fa7a51abb135" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\sqrt{e}" :db/id 17592186337537} {:answer/id #uuid "ea3312e5-2c6e-58ba-97ae-2c49c6ebf7ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\sqrt{5e}" :db/id 17592186338076}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336385} :answer-field/id #uuid "b373a9bf-c725-5f21-89df-bf7fd1bb7643" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338606}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "869dc3d2-8d4d-5276-972b-32891f99547b" :question/math-academy-id "q-7152" :question/problem "The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,2{t}^{2}+9⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=e.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+9)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=e,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(e) & =⟨2e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+e,4e⟩ \\  & =⟨3e,4e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=e$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(e),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(e)| & =\sqrt{(3e)^{2}+(4e)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{e}^{2}} \\  & =5e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338967 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "127b09f8-c603-5ae3-a931-2ffad6e69ed6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "a=⟨24t,\,24{t}^{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186336207} {:answer/id #uuid "329468a4-5599-55c9-b2ee-ef34fe3cecfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "a=⟨12{t}^{2},\,8{t}^{3}+3⟩" :db/id 17592186336511} {:answer/id #uuid "58287b4a-9178-58af-a0a4-2bd375529c06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "a=⟨8t,\,12{t}^{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186336840} {:answer/id #uuid "7148a811-bb91-5a42-b751-a19fd842e5b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "a=⟨24t,\,12{t}^{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186337042} {:answer/id #uuid "e1eeb3c4-77e3-54ab-87dc-f42e09560100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "a=⟨12t,\,8{t}^{2}+3⟩" :db/id 17592186337998}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336207} :answer-field/id #uuid "0c83a258-ba11-5726-8806-40f77faa7b49" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338300}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ebadf146-dfb2-587d-835d-939f20781040" :question/math-academy-id "q-7164" :question/problem "The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨4{t}^{3}-21,2{t}^{4}+3t⟩.
$$

Calculate the acceleration vector $a.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}-21),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}+3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨12{t}^{2},\,8{t}^{3}+3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{t}^{3}+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨24t,\,24{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338982 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ec82676-385f-5f6a-ac9c-ba79308bee12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{arccsc} x+C" :db/id 17592186336316} {:answer/id #uuid "4b573896-b33b-57e6-b631-b759facddb70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186336731} {:answer/id #uuid "5ee8c39b-aa90-5108-83c3-6a90312f3c04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡x-4\operatorname{arcsec} x+C" :db/id 17592186336894} {:answer/id #uuid "bcab4637-e9df-53b6-beca-07d40a0ec77c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡x-4\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186337710} {:answer/id #uuid "e8ee07c5-6041-5304-9bfc-c6a2b63f065a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{arccos}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186338064}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336731} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e3ae158-b764-50b7-b710-2eb3076e5cf8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338386}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "bd957e59-0a76-5e62-9a01-c59f0b889410" :question/math-academy-id "q-71759" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\frac{4}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}})\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
