\displaystyle \int \frac{2{x}^{3}+2x+1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2{x}^{3}+2x+1}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)+1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{2x\cancel{({x}^{2}+1)}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int x\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C \\  & ={x}^{2}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186339004 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27163c60-302f-5873-ad00-05f9fc6cf2b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}>0\}" :db/id 17592186516192} {:answer/id #uuid "2e168002-1ed1-57b4-8e6b-f6204db8e27b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}<0\}" :db/id 17592186516208} {:answer/id #uuid "844c12cc-6c29-5811-8962-30dc8d6a532a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}\ge 1\}" :db/id 17592186516393} {:answer/id #uuid "bea4c84f-b068-5e60-82b9-448a2bf9137c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}<1\}" :db/id 17592186516516} {:answer/id #uuid "f56fd478-739e-5168-a707-21a2be18cb60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}\le 1\}" :db/id 17592186516621}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186516393} :answer-field/id #uuid "24b11784-26f9-538f-8ba3-52d50b1c6d87" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7a7a1c0f-0f8c-51ee-845c-3e87e142c085" :question/math-academy-id "q-71859" :question/problem "Given the hyperboloid of one sheet  $$
\displaystyle \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{5}=1,
$$ find the domain of $z=z(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{5} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1 & =\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{5} \\ (z-1)^{2} & =5(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1) \\ (z-1) & =\pm \sqrt{5(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}-1 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8} & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the exterior of the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}=1$, including its boundary.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{8}\ge 1\}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186339068 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0393ffe1-3780-5ea9-bead-2e9d8cc73789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨t+1,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+7⟩" :db/id 17592186336064} {:answer/id #uuid "9cdf5c1b-08a6-5068-be63-9fbb6167bbc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨-{t}^{2}+t+1,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+17⟩" :db/id 17592186337451} {:answer/id #uuid "b54d447c-1396-5666-a786-52182fff58a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨2t+4,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}+7}{2}-5t⟩" :db/id 17592186337646} {:answer/id #uuid "d30cd474-d6ec-577d-8ad9-6def53bcff9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨t+4,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}+7}{2}-10t⟩" :db/id 17592186337876} {:answer/id #uuid "f5289858-06f1-53e2-9eff-73f26dbb9fda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨{t}^{2}+4,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}+7⟩" :db/id 17592186338176}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336064} :answer-field/id #uuid "33acc8bf-4b95-526e-8d12-725cd3bc669a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338375}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "405f63b7-3135-5e33-b233-49a1169c9188" :question/math-academy-id "q-7218" :question/problem "The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨0,5⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(3,-3)$ and has velocity $⟨1,0⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨0,5⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 0\,\text{d}t,\int 5\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{C}_{1},\,5t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨1,\,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{C}_{1},\,5(2)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,10+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=1$ and ${C}_{2}=-10.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨1,\,5t-10⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,\,5t-10⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\int (5t-10)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{C}_{3},\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(2)=⟨3,-3⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨2+{C}_{3},\,\frac{5(2)^{2}}{2}-10(2)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨3,-3⟩ & =⟨2+{C}_{3},\,-10+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=1$ and ${C}_{4}=7.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨t+1,\,\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}-10t+7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186339073 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "22af21f2-c772-5744-9b60-d0ab89fce37e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186336356} {:answer/id #uuid "2d6f8552-7389-5dc5-a66d-030e7a61ef80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186336468} {:answer/id #uuid "536af063-bc84-5b66-817f-5b4ed0c78236" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186336803} {:answer/id #uuid "de25af14-5eec-5c56-965e-0877a7ed6fd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186337965} {:answer/id #uuid "e9345be3-545b-5204-a397-4c3146bc97ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186338068}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186338068} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a2e198f-72eb-5722-8df8-1a5d71ccce2b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338491}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8de1a47a-93f8-567a-a7de-e31eac5537a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-72197" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A,
$$ where 
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y(\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186339074 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a0fc10a-2cbd-5633-bb2f-ea7aaaa841c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186336123} {:answer/id #uuid "16292cbd-8350-5bd3-96d9-795ef552cf0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186336240} {:answer/id #uuid "1e57b365-540c-5e8a-8331-f6790e70b06d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+2{y}^{3}}" :db/id 17592186336311} {:answer/id #uuid "23a544b4-0d38-57bb-983c-e904eb2a25c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186336367} {:answer/id #uuid "ee47ac7c-c346-5761-8902-7e42ed6ca55e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186338116}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336240} :answer-field/id #uuid "f6bf4581-0ffc-537f-82d9-87405f04b109" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338711}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "454b7cf5-7862-57c7-a910-8dbc0dac1fcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-72213" :question/problem "Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}=2{x}^{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}=2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ [x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)]+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$

$$
\displaystyle D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:    

$$

$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y(1-0)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =-2[\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\cdot (-1) \\  & =2-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ad191a02-5856-5306-8980-ab9514c55d3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-72571" :question/problem "Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(5,1)$ and is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(1,5)$ and $(-3,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "Perpendicular lines have slopes which are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(1,5)$ and $(-3,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{-1-5}{-3-1} \\  & =\frac{-6}{-4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=-1\,⇒\,m=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(5,1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-5) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{10}{3} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we want to write the equation in standard form. So, we will bring the $x$ term to the left-hand side and multiply both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{13}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}x+y & =\frac{13}{3} \\ 3\cdot (\frac{2}{3}x+y) & =3\cdot \frac{13}{3} \\ 2x+3y & =13\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186341871 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05d966cc-8fed-5585-9802-da0009c421f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-\frac{63}{8}" :db/id 17592186339178} {:answer/id #uuid "7a5bdb47-642c-5847-b415-7acd09462b3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+4" :db/id 17592186340221} {:answer/id #uuid "ab6c10e8-5890-5117-ba59-b6c73fa45d62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=\frac{1}{4}-2t" :db/id 17592186340689} {:answer/id #uuid "e28cd841-ca6d-595a-825e-c4c1810fa0a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+1" :db/id 17592186341135} {:answer/id #uuid "f7f93847-8a6b-5df2-9c42-ff3305643c26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(t)=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{7}{8}" :db/id 17592186341320}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341320} :answer-field/id #uuid "741f9a31-4ea0-5b35-9dc9-dd1dfde7fb98" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341584}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "35ab132d-9e7c-5e1c-baf1-f58667f680d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-7284" :question/problem "A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}t-{t}^{2},$ where $t>0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=-7$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{4}t-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(3)=-7.$ Substituting this into the above gives

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(3{x}_{i-1}+{y}_{j-1}-1)Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(3{x}_{i}+{y}_{j}-1)Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0}) \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}-{x}_{0})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
3{x}_{i-1}+{y}_{j-1}-1\le 3\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-1\le 3{x}_{i}+{y}_{j}-1
$$

which simplifies to 

$$
3{x}_{i-1}+{y}_{j-1}-1\le \frac{3}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-1\le 3{x}_{i}+{y}_{j}-1.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\frac{3}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-1]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le \frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,+\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{3}{2}({4}^{2}-{1}^{2})(4-2)=45 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})(4-1)=18 \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =(4-1)(4-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 45+18-6\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 57\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=57.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186341884 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1dfd4429-470e-5160-b38b-71b5f4ecfede" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-324" :db/id 17592186339391} {:answer/id #uuid "51b20d0f-2079-5380-89c1-4228fc80f297" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-84" :db/id 17592186339877} {:answer/id #uuid "a63a68b0-99d3-5209-8346-b98d891452b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-144" :db/id 17592186340635} {:answer/id #uuid "b1d86d13-7214-5706-ae6b-1a73663bc8c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-360" :db/id 17592186340747} {:answer/id #uuid "d88fee66-be60-57a1-ad55-13ef4e820d82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-168" :db/id 17592186341051}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340635} :answer-field/id #uuid "e86449e4-c0a9-5b52-a8c2-80a206761f0f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341793}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f6a79a2d-bcfd-5ef3-be20-8c72ffbf021f" :question/math-academy-id "q-72906" :question/problem "Let $R=[-5,-1]\times [0,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(5{x}_{i-1}+2{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(5{x}_{i}+2{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
5{x}_{i-1}+2{y}_{j-1}\le 5\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 5{x}_{i}+2{y}_{j}
$$

which simplifies to 

$$
5{x}_{i-1}+2{y}_{j-1}\le \frac{5}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 5{x}_{i}+2{y}_{j}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\frac{5}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
L(f,P)\le \frac{5}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P).
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{5}{2}((-1)^{2}-(-5)^{2})(3-0)=-180 \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({3}^{2}-{0}^{2})(-1-(-5))=36\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le -180+36\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le -144\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=-144.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186341893 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "368d6f09-f86f-5a1f-934f-edb2ada2ecdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,\frac{1}{2},1⟩" :db/id 17592186339616} {:answer/id #uuid "4016e3b4-303c-5e7d-bc9c-f626ddc0e67a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,-1,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186339702} {:answer/id #uuid "5a087a29-e907-5bbd-8024-d1c0e3d6066a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186339946} {:answer/id #uuid "7f49b16e-bca9-5992-802b-f9800e9b025a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,\frac{1}{2},-1⟩" :db/id 17592186340272} {:answer/id #uuid "b28c83dc-7bea-5c71-a4cc-8b4d73503adb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},-1⟩" :db/id 17592186340752}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339946} :answer-field/id #uuid "7d72ac37-7d4a-57f8-a026-426aa0ba98f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341600}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6577a967-44f3-50e6-9603-cd6d17cab94e" :question/math-academy-id "q-72983" :question/problem "Solve the system of equations represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x$, $y$, and $z.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y+z &=-1 \\ y+z &=1 \\ 2z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that
 

$$
2z=1\,⟹\,z=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=1\,⟹\,y=1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we substitute $z=y=\frac{1}{2}$  into the first equation to get

$$
2x+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-1\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}(-1-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})=-1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-1$, $y=\frac{1}{2}$, and $z=\frac{1}{2}.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨-1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.$"} {:db/id 17592186341901 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d39e1d2-809f-5155-a07c-2be82fe6f5c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{7}\right)" :db/id 17592186339382} {:answer/id #uuid "40729786-50b6-5ff5-b256-a96bf88930f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{6\pi }{7}\right)" :db/id 17592186339704} {:answer/id #uuid "ab3fcfc4-5970-535a-9851-ae25c946b062" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{14}\right)" :db/id 17592186340688} {:answer/id #uuid "dc526537-6440-5beb-89ba-a669341bd361" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{6\pi }{7}\right)" :db/id 17592186341086} {:answer/id #uuid "f54d10f1-3bdb-508e-83f2-6340ec8fe28b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{7}\right)" :db/id 17592186341292}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341086} :answer-field/id #uuid "6bdfe7ee-6a1b-5a6c-8716-9c970e741c65" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341565}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "188c3216-6730-58aa-bfa7-8985bab845cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-7305" :question/problem "Express $$
\displaystyle 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{7}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{7}\right)
$$ as a single trigonometric ratio." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{3\pi }{7}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{7}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{7}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{7})=\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{6\pi }{7}\right).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186341918 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c11bc78-d2c8-508a-b8fb-990c82485b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[-5{\left(\frac{4j}{n}\right)}^{-4}\cdot \frac{4}{n}]" :db/id 17592186339511} {:answer/id #uuid "672f2c27-138f-5c55-aef5-0b2361a5154e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[-5{(-2+\frac{4j}{n})}^{-2}\cdot \frac{4}{n}]" :db/id 17592186340041} {:answer/id #uuid "ab869e72-931c-52bc-97fc-2e5c42e4486e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[-5{(4+\frac{2j}{n})}^{-2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}]" :db/id 17592186340692} {:answer/id #uuid "ee951d44-ea61-556b-94d7-e1dd4325b6f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[-5{(-4+\frac{2j}{n})}^{-2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}]" :db/id 17592186341232} {:answer/id #uuid "eee0bce5-f344-5783-ba0f-f51aa7490a07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[-5{\left(\frac{j}{n}\right)}^{-2}\cdot \frac{1}{n}]" :db/id 17592186341237}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341232} :answer-field/id #uuid "a983d74d-4019-5c4d-aa85-405465fd5a9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341675}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9f9a39ce-97fb-5b82-8335-1f0d956000c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-73160" :question/problem "What is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-4}^{-2}-5{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x
$$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{-2}-5{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-5{x}^{-2},$ the lower bound is $a=-4,$ and the upper bound is $b=-2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{-2-(-4)}{n}=\frac{2}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-2}-5{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(-4+j\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(-4+\frac{2j}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[-5{(-4+\frac{2j}{n})}^{-2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}

$$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot (1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x

We then use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot (1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (1+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x){|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & (\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186341960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a6893eb-1f05-5d46-b268-8de656696696" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-\frac{3}{4}|+C" :db/id 17592186339652} {:answer/id #uuid "5218164d-7fa9-5394-b4ca-310da4a12e7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-\frac{3}{4}|+C" :db/id 17592186339882} {:answer/id #uuid "ad0db077-2bfb-5216-b827-716e01eb989a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x}{4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-\frac{3}{4}|+C" :db/id 17592186340704} {:answer/id #uuid "d2b73d5d-2019-5c03-8f5c-39d4c27f932d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-\frac{3}{4}|+C" :db/id 17592186340993} {:answer/id #uuid "d4814811-e099-564e-a5ea-04bd6b9d15d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-\frac{3}{4}|+C" :db/id 17592186341007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340993} :answer-field/id #uuid "926e9445-ed34-57bf-a68d-46ca2b6964c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341636}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3e1b813e-8df8-5d81-a96c-2b239f38f3b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-73390" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{8x-1}{4x-3}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we pull out the factor of $4$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8x-1}{4x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8x-1}{4(x-\frac{3}{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{8x-1}{(x-\frac{3}{4})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{3}{4} & 8 & -1 \\  & ↓ & 6 \\ \hline  & 8 & 5\end{array}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8x-1}{(x-\frac{3}{4})} & =8+\frac{5}{(x-\frac{3}{4})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8x-1}{4x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int (8+\frac{5}{x-\frac{3}{4}})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8\int \text{d}x+5\int \frac{1}{x-\frac{3}{4}}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8x+5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-\frac{3}{4}|]+C \\  & =2x+\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-\frac{3}{4}|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186341961 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "48658c86-5fff-5d1e-ad97-ca9615485d8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-9\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C" :db/id 17592186339773} {:answer/id #uuid "8d8c23eb-6ff2-5bd1-ab4a-f009409818c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x+9\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C" :db/id 17592186340399} {:answer/id #uuid "a839708e-6d86-5a57-b693-6f0e21e650eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C" :db/id 17592186340655} {:answer/id #uuid "ced86a89-239e-50b2-894e-628af504a0d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C" :db/id 17592186340966} {:answer/id #uuid "daa4acb0-2d88-582f-a718-be7e56ba1265" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C" :db/id 17592186341071}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341071} :answer-field/id #uuid "ea2bfd72-4857-53aa-b6a7-f5d94cbdaa7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341797}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "40d2e0b8-4256-5b72-ae20-79f2c7d72c06" :question/math-academy-id "q-73391" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{x-1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{3(x-\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & \frac{2}{3} \\ \hline  & 1 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{array}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} & =1+\frac{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$

$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & -3 \\ \hline  & 1 & -4\end{array}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x+3)} & =1+\frac{(-4)}{(x+3)} \\  & =1-\frac{4}{(x+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x+6}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186342007 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f092e91-4f61-5603-80d5-8a93282c6a99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186339399} {:answer/id #uuid "5d2c2bab-1eca-5488-9001-c674cb08e279" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186339967} {:answer/id #uuid "896af8fb-37f5-589c-b238-bbb774191209" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186340354} {:answer/id #uuid "9f3d592d-784d-5142-ab34-93f237937bc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186340566} {:answer/id #uuid "c8d18828-18be-5809-990c-92d134b043c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186340907}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339399} :answer-field/id #uuid "6d3c55f3-ba0b-5134-9af5-27dd30e3aab6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "661506d6-91ed-5312-9a5a-a709acc23a76" :question/math-academy-id "q-73539" :question/problem "Evaluate $\lim_{x\to 0}\left(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4x}\right).$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that as $x\to 0,$ both numerator and denominator approach $0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{\sec }^{2}⁡\theta -1}{{\theta }^{2}} & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{\tan }^{2}⁡\theta }{{\theta }^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\left(\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta }\right)}{{\theta }^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}}\cdot \frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta }) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }{{\theta }^{2}}\cdot {lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{1}{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}

Let's now evaluate the limits separately:

- Consider the second limit. Evaluating it directly, we get

$$

\displaystyle \lim_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we can simplify the limit using trigonometric identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}(\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ÷\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }÷\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}

Notice that as $\theta \to 0,$ both numerator and denominator approach $0.$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186342019 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27e36dff-223f-5b4e-b1b4-209444ae4750" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186339475} {:answer/id #uuid "295c3085-d512-5a69-92dc-71d06b0bdf20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186339493} {:answer/id #uuid "83e36855-c02f-53e9-947d-e5e2682c194d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186340315} {:answer/id #uuid "9b3f0e3a-443b-558d-9213-98e89a32d936" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186340527} {:answer/id #uuid "daea0c65-3b56-5a21-bd69-1ef30a29e1c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186341072}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339475} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0dec351-1e40-54db-9221-0fdc8d5c0c71" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341691}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9f9ea65f-55fc-5861-a64a-a45dd398be77" :question/math-academy-id "q-73578" :question/problem "Evaluate the repeated integral
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}(-\frac{1}{2}-(-1))\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186342021 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23119422-3823-57bd-ae60-3a70da203882" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186339428} {:answer/id #uuid "3233eb3a-80c4-5e2c-afa0-25c63262aae6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186339569} {:answer/id #uuid "8c653da2-7477-595d-a51e-c3f66f8b5ff3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186340387} {:answer/id #uuid "cce2e1a4-aa36-57b6-badd-2c432cb8566b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186340942} {:answer/id #uuid "e95bda4b-27fc-570d-96c8-8ec990cd3092" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186341185}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340942} :answer-field/id #uuid "738ace53-c45e-5df6-a139-2497bca10161" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341583}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9d286237-0b02-5319-9c6e-7aa25af2bd91" :question/math-academy-id "q-73583" :question/problem "Evaluate the repeated integral

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$

$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186342024 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25d1e73b-e0ae-5dd1-8aa5-0411dedefcf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186339453} {:answer/id #uuid "45467690-7474-56f4-ae84-f1a272286059" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186339743} {:answer/id #uuid "5cef7967-e086-5164-96f7-20b9ba784e40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186339964} {:answer/id #uuid "7ba1d5d6-b3a4-56c2-b8e9-e4af54ad363c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186340240} {:answer/id #uuid "f47fc6a7-3bbd-5818-b278-d9d17cc9814a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt[3]{6}" :db/id 17592186341283}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339453} :answer-field/id #uuid "294db225-753f-529c-acb9-ca6c79515375" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341450}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "aee01977-ad27-5b85-b8b2-915e471c24f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-73591" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral $$

$$ where 
$D={(x,y)\,:\,{e}^{2}\le x\le {e}^{4},\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{6}}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}[{\int }_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{4}}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}[{\int }_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{4}}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{4}}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}{y}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}{y}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{4}-\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}{y}^{2}\cdot 2\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{2}{3}[{y}^{3}]_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}((\sqrt[3]{6})^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342027 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16c0dc97-1bfa-5226-9e8a-83188a4da218" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/id 17592186339328} {:answer/id #uuid "3785646e-da4d-5ce4-884b-7241e989b715" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}" :db/id 17592186339627} {:answer/id #uuid "6b813e4f-15f3-5ca2-a873-e38985156d55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/id 17592186340080} {:answer/id #uuid "7c522d09-2793-56be-8f5f-51c906dc7f1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}" :db/id 17592186340247} {:answer/id #uuid "7ce6c823-b30e-5a3f-ac0b-98f3964eefdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}" :db/id 17592186340254}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340247} :answer-field/id #uuid "dc74d58b-4531-5b1b-ba07-fd90641c83fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341768}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "69cbca99-1555-5b49-9e0d-f5bfd292b88d" :question/math-academy-id "q-73601" :question/problem "Evaluate the repeated integral $$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186342066 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12a76728-b839-5d06-89f1-9934eae3f027" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{arcsec} (6x)}{6}+C" :db/id 17592186339291} {:answer/id #uuid "665fe7b3-58d5-51b3-a6e6-d098ccd5df2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{arcsec} (6x)}{36}+C" :db/id 17592186340029} {:answer/id #uuid "689ac8e4-68fd-56b3-a68a-d04dadd83f44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{arcsec} (6x)}{2}+C" :db/id 17592186340060} {:answer/id #uuid "926a2dfc-a131-5563-ba53-5afa24278c9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{arcsec} (36x)}{6}+C" :db/id 17592186340442} {:answer/id #uuid "e3ae6232-f8ce-5ece-a30d-6e27d814267f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{arcsec} (36x)+C" :db/id 17592186341146}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340060} :answer-field/id #uuid "c6e02fde-8f73-598e-a892-0518e56b81c6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341728}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8cd85d7e-9002-5474-aae0-35e5eb480c8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-73715" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int \frac{3\,\text{d}x}{|6x|\sqrt{(6x)^{2}-1}}=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{3\,\text{d}x}{|6x|\sqrt{(6x)^{2}-1}}=3\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x|\sqrt{(6x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\operatorname{arcsec} ,$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec} (u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $6x.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

 $(\sqrt{\frac{12}{7}},0)$ and $(-\sqrt{\frac{12}{7}},0).$"} {:db/id 17592186342097 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52002c6b-9859-5b7b-a1de-586418b14736" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,3,28)$ only" :db/id 17592186339881} {:answer/id #uuid "551d2228-56ee-5488-91bb-0169794e5cbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-3,0)$ only" :db/id 17592186339910} {:answer/id #uuid "796a4945-abaa-5bd2-997d-087f2262b1b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,3,0)$ only" :db/id 17592186340210} {:answer/id #uuid "8a645bd4-5f4d-5164-aa70-44b211e15ecc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-3,0)$ and $(-1,3,28)$" :db/id 17592186340364} {:answer/id #uuid "c6b33a5b-7afb-5095-9268-a98f89267aca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-3,0)$ and $(3,1,20)$" :db/id 17592186340888}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339910} :answer-field/id #uuid "e58edcff-ee66-5f0c-86cd-1ec279fff31c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341787}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c589653c-432a-5bb8-acb2-94698429fbb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-73857" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10$ is the tangent plane horizontal?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2x-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2y+6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x-2,\,2y+6,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-2 &=0 \\ 2y+6 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=1$ while the second equation gives $y=-3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into our function, we get

$$
z={1}^{2}-2(1)+(-3)^{2}+6(-3)+10=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(1,-3,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186342100 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e7c281c-3ed2-505e-bb39-624565383d58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,1,1)$ and $(2,1,1)$" :db/id 17592186339538} {:answer/id #uuid "5d0e6d85-901c-5c92-bee2-2a7c391f4ac2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,1,1)" :db/id 17592186339965} {:answer/id #uuid "92fe27bc-7297-5bff-aa40-85efb366b3a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,1,1)" :db/id 17592186340449} {:answer/id #uuid "b73decc5-bf30-5593-9a84-120c9cd31d42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,1,1)$ and $(1,-1,1)$" :db/id 17592186340784} {:answer/id #uuid "e5166059-3d34-56f7-b88e-8c219479020b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,-1,1)$ only" :db/id 17592186341154}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339965} :answer-field/id #uuid "169b7bd1-0afe-5339-a2e8-b0915ac47bda" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341421}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9d930cb5-4a33-5f68-a149-002500eed8d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-73868" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨0,2,-2⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{x}{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨0,2,-2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨0,2,-2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}c\operatorname{ln}⁡y &=0 \\ \frac{cx}{y}+2cy &=2 \\ -c &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

And substituting $c=2$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
\frac{2x}{1}+2(2)(1)=2\,⟹\,x=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =(-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{1}^{2} \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-1,1,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186342112 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "43d96809-e3dd-5fef-aec9-43b2a849f964" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48" :db/id 17592186339725} {:answer/id #uuid "53143a70-d722-51cd-8e2b-e4e20cc2d282" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36" :db/id 17592186339893} {:answer/id #uuid "707f529c-3710-523a-9777-24e6935aad7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186340126} {:answer/id #uuid "ea6b0a98-b813-579e-9675-d74b38ae8281" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186341199} {:answer/id #uuid "f11c1ac8-7991-5f39-84b0-28a20d7bcaf6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186341253}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341253} :answer-field/id #uuid "eef3e121-56c7-5a3b-bf87-c4536c1b03a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341808}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7fa0bdb5-f053-5d67-8f95-d145fa39b1e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-73939" :question/problem "Let $\mathbf{a}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ What is $(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a})\cdot \mathbf{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, multiplying each component of $\mathbf{a}$ by $\frac{1}{2}$, we get

$$

To compute the dot product, we add up the products of corresponding components:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186342131 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aa1cdee6-ac73-548c-adcc-2f2217142d90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The entire $xy$-plane" :db/id 17592186340680} {:answer/id #uuid "278677bd-636d-5e6b-baa4-61d15bbe918b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}\ge 1\}" :db/id 17592186507645} {:answer/id #uuid "27a941c5-178a-59ae-85cf-65febbfce639" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}\ge 1\}" :db/id 17592186507646} {:answer/id #uuid "7d19b694-4700-571e-bc5e-8170015e653a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+{y}^{2}\le 1\}" :db/id 17592186507781} {:answer/id #uuid "b85f79a1-9c55-50f6-8994-c949dca618ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}\le 1\}" :db/id 17592186507853}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507646} :answer-field/id #uuid "3fd0265d-f2bf-5b7a-b5a0-01ae09a136be" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341494}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c94f24ee-6291-5f63-846b-0a8b39098945" :question/math-academy-id "q-74015" :question/problem "Given the hyperboloid of one sheet $$
\displaystyle \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{4}=1,
$$ find the domain of $z=z(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}-1 & =\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(z-1)^{2} & =4(\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}-1) \\ z-1 & =\pm 2\sqrt{\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}-1 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2} & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the exterior of the ellipse $$
\displaystyle \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}=1,
$$ which includes the boundary.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{7}+\frac{(y+8)^{2}}{2}\ge 1\}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342135 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "086eec50-0aed-5c9c-8440-0856e5e2064f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186339199} {:answer/id #uuid "172641f6-459f-542b-9ca3-87d09d7ddd86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186339333} {:answer/id #uuid "851577ba-1f6c-53a2-85ce-67be15b77c28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186340324} {:answer/id #uuid "a4ac1540-d34a-5782-8d87-4465aa7c8c41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186340624} {:answer/id #uuid "c11ca11c-bf97-531c-b363-2e4aa0364db5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30" :db/id 17592186340847}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339199} :answer-field/id #uuid "e9e44fb3-1f00-5e49-ac7c-21a4e249d75c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341795}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f55a19ff-3690-5ec5-bee0-56233af0bdf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-74039" :question/problem "If $u=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\,,$ $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\,,$ and $u\cdot u=30,$ then $$
\displaystyle \frac{(\frac{2}{3}u)\cdot u}{u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}v)}=
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that the dot product is linear.

To quickly compute the numerator $(\frac{2}{3}u)\cdot u,$ we multiply $u\cdot u$ by $\frac{2}{3}.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{2}{3}u)\cdot u & =\frac{2}{3}(u\cdot u) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 30 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

To quickly compute the denominator $u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}v),$ we compute $u\cdot v$ first and then multiply the result by $\frac{1}{2}.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}v) & =\frac{1}{2}(u\cdot v) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+{u}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}+{u}_{4}\cdot {v}_{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1\cdot 1+2\cdot 1+0\cdot 2+3\cdot (-1)+4\cdot (-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+2+0-3-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-4) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{(\frac{2}{3}u)\cdot u}{u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}v)}=\frac{20}{-2}=-10.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342170 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "525dd401-8559-527d-af93-7fef9e69ee27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{16}+\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186339886} {:answer/id #uuid "6a36174c-682b-5784-964c-645e66ae8121" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{2}+\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186340070} {:answer/id #uuid "93edef1f-9ccb-5c5a-aa03-e9a87fbc0b39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186340457} {:answer/id #uuid "be54c2a1-06c9-56df-9284-b03b2269f23b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{8}+\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186340824} {:answer/id #uuid "c37d75fb-95ca-5848-8a92-0af7cf07e8bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{16}+\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186340867}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339886} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec5708c4-c573-5a48-a243-f9a6b68c7be2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341803}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cd8afad0-6e25-593b-9edf-5db6bd394b38" :question/math-academy-id "q-74172" :question/problem "![](images/7e/7ecbb53bb87156d11f9a9d8021182cdfb8c0c1749cd028780377bb61f32adf43.png)

The graph of the function $f(x)$, which is defined on $[-3,6]$, is shown above. It consists of the arc of the semi-circle centered at $(0,0)$ with radius $3,$ and two line segments. Find the average value of $f(x)$ on $[-3,5].$" :question/worked-solution "The average value of a function on a given interval $[a,b]$ is

$$
{f}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the additive property of the definite integral, we write

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\underbrace{{\int }_{-3}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{{A}_{1}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{{A}_{2}}.
$$

The 1st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,3].$ The corresponding region is a semi-cirle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi \cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The 2nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [3,5].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the formula for the average value, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5-(-3)}\cdot (\frac{9\pi }{2}+2) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{16}+\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342179 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3ed626f5-d63f-5165-8577-be0fed212989" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{\pi }{4},-1)" :db/id 17592186339693} {:answer/id #uuid "3f4ba3ad-767a-5772-a0d5-c4bbef92fa7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{3\pi }{4},-1)" :db/id 17592186339699} {:answer/id #uuid "9c53bac8-092e-588f-8ae1-784810597fef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{7\pi }{4},-1)" :db/id 17592186340537} {:answer/id #uuid "a9dc55d8-ec0a-5fc1-88e9-221142810533" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,\frac{\pi }{4},1)" :db/id 17592186340675} {:answer/id #uuid "d7cf792e-bb0a-5d2f-9dcb-75a9b7b4bc90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{7\pi }{4},1)" :db/id 17592186341042}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340537} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c21b4f4-e5d5-5a57-ac84-f32164a155ad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341543}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6628a10e-0b07-5061-bbd3-ef23eb0ebd24" :question/math-academy-id "q-74196" :question/problem "![](images/3a/3a919c1ad631af6dfea304db2bdf0ad36fcbff6162f516e8591d7ce9cef3ecca.png)

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each of the subsets.

- The set $A$ is not a subspace. Indeed, the vector $u=⟨\frac{1}{4},0,0⟩$ is in $A$, since

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}<\frac{1}{2},
$$

but, $4u=⟨1,0,0⟩$ is not in $B$, since 

$$
\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}>\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, $A$ is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- The set $B$ is a subspace. It represents a plane, and a plane is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $5x-y-z=0$ since $5\cdot 0-0-0=0.$ So $0$ lies in $B.$

- The set $C$ is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. Indeed, $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the equation $5-x-z=0$ since $5-0-0\ne 0.$

In conclusion, the correct answer is $$
\displaystyle \begin{gathered}B=\left\{\begin{gathered}⟨x,y,z⟩\in {R}^{3}:\\5x-y-z=0\end{gathered}\right\}\end{gathered}
$$ only."} {:db/id 17592186342193 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26c30e3f-d29e-5013-9514-d17c3eee3460" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186339466} {:answer/id #uuid "376779f8-ab66-595c-9bd0-478fd63c0239" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\csc }^{2}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186339625} {:answer/id #uuid "447b1d64-6d6b-508d-818e-c81c4fc983e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186339733} {:answer/id #uuid "744da144-5af4-5254-8514-317a1d8d743d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186340164} {:answer/id #uuid "cf6a59f6-df8c-5517-879f-5849fb7de659" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C" :db/id 17592186340974}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339466} :answer-field/id #uuid "ede24e4d-4785-5cd1-8533-d9afadca7785" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341806}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "504ab9d3-58bf-5555-aee6-cd8fa47fea51" :question/math-academy-id "q-74281" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{1-{\cot }^{2}⁡x}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{1-{\cot }^{2}⁡x}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int (1-{\cot }^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we use the fact that $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1-{\cot }^{2}⁡x}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1-{\cot }^{2}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (1-\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡x}{{\sin }^{2}⁡x})\cdot \frac{1}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \left(\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡x-{\cos }^{2}⁡x}{{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \left(\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}{{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{{\sin }^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
-\int {\csc }^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\int {\csc }^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-(-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5a16e0c9-93e3-5941-9489-0dd0225ce52d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186339947} {:answer/id #uuid "6713678d-e4a2-510a-bc07-20071a50a4ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186340038} {:answer/id #uuid "8f2327ee-e90f-5d92-9bb3-814b74d13d2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186340416} {:answer/id #uuid "b96232b8-fdc2-5f52-b7c0-6ecc5d7059bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186340789} {:answer/id #uuid "bab5fa49-44d1-57fe-b02c-773f6204ed93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186340801}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340038} :answer-field/id #uuid "139020ad-e28f-5554-b72e-515964f83bc8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "319e0a68-f800-5f78-baec-4e9220398ab8" :question/math-academy-id "q-74398" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Rearranging the above formula, we get

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+C \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342198 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15bcdc8a-bf4e-535c-ae00-dfd78d725cf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+C" :db/id 17592186339320} {:answer/id #uuid "2052f191-69d3-5274-93bb-4d7bf5147eae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186339407} {:answer/id #uuid "6c2c6a56-2867-5d7e-b202-894c0c22b86a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+C" :db/id 17592186340084} {:answer/id #uuid "77323a6a-0c3a-5d0b-921f-d95f488da3db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+C" :db/id 17592186340189} {:answer/id #uuid "7a0ef93a-2868-5fe9-9178-956d59cd7f2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C" :db/id 17592186340217}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339320} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0076dd1-19fe-56e8-a626-1b35e9a9bd23" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341689}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ea8beebd-1dd9-5d27-af0f-4c6b17fc6bdd" :question/math-academy-id "q-74400" :question/problem "$$

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z
$$

Calculating $x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cba0666a-04f8-5761-91d5-608acf1e745f" :question/math-academy-id "q-74720" :question/problem "The point $U$ has Cartesian coordinates $(1,-\sqrt{3},2).$ What are the spherical polar coordinates of $U?$" :question/worked-solution "If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho $, $\theta $, and $ϕ$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{z}{\rho }
$$

First, we find $\rho :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(x,y)=(1,-\sqrt{3})$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So to find $\theta ,$ we first need to find the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{1}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi $ to get $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $ϕ$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{z}{\rho }\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $U$ are $$
\displaystyle (2\sqrt{2},\frac{5\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186344986 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0cf412ba-cb44-5810-90eb-470d798d6591" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,0⟩" :db/id 17592186342351} {:answer/id #uuid "38066b67-952e-5aaa-89e3-87ed3e2d7e87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186342700} {:answer/id #uuid "9e480808-eca1-5207-ab76-299e8586efe8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186343632} {:answer/id #uuid "d306b071-4ab7-5ed5-b27f-e66587823105" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186344089} {:answer/id #uuid "d6a03b41-a1b1-5998-84af-ee854f6b5424" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,0⟩" :db/id 17592186344121}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344121} :answer-field/id #uuid "195ce2b3-5781-555d-8433-34219cc57723" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344535}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "bcc4a25a-4ff4-59f4-a945-c409687d5f70" :question/math-academy-id "q-74851" :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨t,4⟩) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\right)\cdot ⟨t,4⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(⟨t,4⟩) \\  & =-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}+16)\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨t,4⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{0}{({0}^{2}+16)\sqrt{{0}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨0,4⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

  

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{1}{4}‖⟨1,0⟩‖ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(0)$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}⟨1,0⟩}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)} \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\cdot N(0) & =\frac{1}{4}⟨0,4⟩\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0+0) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\frac{4}{t})\,j \\  & =\frac{4}{t}\,i+(1-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}})\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{4}{t}\right)}^{2}+{(1-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{{t}^{2}}+{(1-\frac{8}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{16}{{t}^{4}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{8}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{16}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}({t}^{4}+8{t}^{2}+16)} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}{({t}^{2}+4)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+4)}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{({t}^{2}+4)}(\frac{4}{t}\,i+(1-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}})\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+4)}(4t\,i+({t}^{2}-4)\,j)\end{aligned}

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$"} {:db/id 17592186345048 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "307a5aa6-d86b-5bbb-92a3-e6f4a26d810a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(x+4)" :db/id 17592186342641} {:answer/id #uuid "58a43569-55e6-5bb8-afc8-ca5359491361" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x+4)" :db/id 17592186342980} {:answer/id #uuid "77dffce9-f2db-5153-9cd8-dd1e6ad0e1c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{{x}^{2}+7x+12}{x-2}" :db/id 17592186343275} {:answer/id #uuid "95999e23-a2db-5ef5-b9b6-6fe3d48b3d65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x+7}{x-2}" :db/id 17592186343546} {:answer/id #uuid "ee50544d-e6ea-5472-9355-2c79279eda1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(x+5)" :db/id 17592186344334}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343275} :answer-field/id #uuid "61952ac2-99cf-52a0-ba8f-8e4f89399cf4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344654}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "430b2a2e-1d17-5c4e-929d-cb9c9dc46185" :question/math-academy-id "q-75217" :question/problem "Calculate

for $x<0.$" :question/worked-solution "In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

Therefore, by FTC II, we have
