$$"} {:db/id 17592186345061 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0866e81e-41e2-5a24-9758-5fdc46ac8910" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(3)=⟨1,\,8⟩" :db/id 17592186342308} {:answer/id #uuid "6e4286f2-c750-5df9-ba1c-7c3ca66a526b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(3)=⟨2,\,8⟩" :db/id 17592186343185} {:answer/id #uuid "8038ea30-9c84-5f3f-9fe2-003ac69594ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(3)=⟨4,\,8⟩" :db/id 17592186343341} {:answer/id #uuid "9e97acbc-6419-521b-a1f3-c7d65b378a49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(3)=⟨2,\,7⟩" :db/id 17592186343637} {:answer/id #uuid "ed25a92b-3714-549a-8a14-6385a683daad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(3)=⟨1,\,7⟩" :db/id 17592186344323}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342308} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ff4fd96-bbea-5ad6-81ad-bd5b54f52cb4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344742}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "863d2b12-a7b6-532b-971d-62874cf250c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-75290" :question/problem "The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨4\sqrt{1+t},(1+t)^{2}⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=3.$" :question/worked-solution "The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\sqrt{1+t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((1+t)^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1+t)^{-1/2},2(1+t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+t}},2+2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=3,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+3}},2+2(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{2},\,2+6⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345063 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ad01848-8741-5cb8-87a5-f6517290d6eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186342468} {:answer/id #uuid "71c169d6-5705-5a09-9d3e-2b9fa9418633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186343220} {:answer/id #uuid "9a17635b-0972-57cb-b31e-499ad5931fc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186343594} {:answer/id #uuid "c7525d1b-d02f-5b0f-bcd5-f1d6c6826b5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186343988} {:answer/id #uuid "f91bc710-bf1b-51b9-8455-71a367e23015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186344430}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342468} :answer-field/id #uuid "af5f01ce-9357-53cf-ac88-d236cd72d59a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344801}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "af6a3602-6598-5ad6-8883-59a5609544bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-75302" :question/problem "A particle $P$ is moving in the $x$-$y$ plane. Its position vector relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by

$$
r=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ),4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨-4(0),4(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ we calculate the magnitude of $v\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)| & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345083 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d86c569-1b23-58e1-8325-4f3e7e75a69f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\,j-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\,k" :db/id 17592186342353} {:answer/id #uuid "225011dd-679b-5c4b-b454-3b0b1271da1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,k" :db/id 17592186342522} {:answer/id #uuid "60fd3304-972d-5e5d-9fb2-f58c18df414c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i" :db/id 17592186343059} {:answer/id #uuid "8b30390b-535a-5fbf-a016-d26514ebf39c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k" :db/id 17592186343449} {:answer/id #uuid "bf0dcad5-ba23-558d-b9a1-58b76db4a021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k" :db/id 17592186343917}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343917} :answer-field/id #uuid "818560be-6c53-5bbb-8884-04841718675f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344720}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e872eb2a-80c0-5fe7-b915-1fedf1110b20" :question/math-academy-id "q-75407" :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=1$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(1)=-i+j+\frac{1}{2}k,\,{q}^{′}(1)=j+k.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\right)\cdot q(t)+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{4t}{({t}^{2}+2)^{2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(1) & =-\frac{4(1)}{({1}^{2}+2)^{2}}\cdot q(1)+\frac{2}{{1}^{2}+2}\cdot {q}^{′}(1) \\  & =-\frac{4}{9}(-i+j+\frac{1}{2}k)+\frac{2}{3}(j+k) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}\,i+\frac{2}{9}\,j+\frac{4}{9}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{2}{9}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{81}+\frac{4}{81}+\frac{16}{81}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{36}{81}} \\  & =\frac{6}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(1)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(1) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(1)}{‖{T}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{4}{9}\,i+\frac{2}{9}\,j+\frac{4}{9}\,k}{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\cdot N(1) & =\frac{2}{3}q(1)\cdot (\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-i+j+\frac{1}{2}k)\cdot (\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{2}{3}\,i\cdot \,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j\cdot j+\frac{1}{3}\,k\cdot k) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345086 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c81bfce-9632-5e30-aca0-66bfd54ed5e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{3}}" :db/id 17592186342869} {:answer/id #uuid "6696bf37-f7ff-50df-9318-a659fdf44683" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186343107} {:answer/id #uuid "669b4061-b6a6-5c32-bcc9-77f78daffdf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{3e}" :db/id 17592186343108} {:answer/id #uuid "991af7f3-b4f6-515e-a7e8-d7d5a51f6ac3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3e}" :db/id 17592186343584} {:answer/id #uuid "c959123c-a4c9-5b03-b0d7-7a0e84a3f053" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{3}}" :db/id 17592186344004}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343108} :answer-field/id #uuid "619bf93e-94cf-5c5d-8b42-901d98684e52" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344655}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c985bafb-2593-5b73-b834-81a6aec3295e" :question/math-academy-id "q-75458" :question/problem "Find ${F}^{′}(e)$ if $$
\displaystyle F(x)={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{a}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $x.$

The integrand $\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{du}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{u}{2+{u}^{2}}\right)+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}}\right)+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2x+x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x).$

Finally, we can compute ${F}^{′}(e).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(e) & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡e}{2e+e(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2e+e} \\  & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{3e}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345091 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "375ef518-4d6a-56b5-8701-cd9802686411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨0,-1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186342695} {:answer/id #uuid "41e5f4d8-856b-52f5-85b3-07ac865cef2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}⟨4,0,3⟩" :db/id 17592186342784} {:answer/id #uuid "69d5fca1-eec8-5d54-b1fc-d0f9751e2efa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,0,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186343141} {:answer/id #uuid "745b8d3b-d175-5c42-a346-9db9b829c2bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨-1,1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186343245} {:answer/id #uuid "af1ce442-73ac-5780-9670-756b226a0a89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,1,0⟩" :db/id 17592186343779}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343779} :answer-field/id #uuid "74402250-c07b-5643-a659-e21ce9c35c06" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344702}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b15f4c73-c376-5fbd-b671-915cb2fd0f2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-75491" :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=⟨3,0,-4⟩,\,{q}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=⟨0,3,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\right)\cdot q(t)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{5}\cdot q\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{5}\cdot {q}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{q}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{3}{5}⟨0,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)‖ & =\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\frac{{T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{‖{T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{5}⟨0,1,0⟩}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)} \\  & =⟨0,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\cdot N\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\frac{1}{5}q\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3,0,-4⟩\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot 0+0\cdot 1-4\cdot 0) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345102 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "70c234f6-092e-5f46-865a-425945404213" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,0)$ and $(1,0)$" :db/id 17592186343206} {:answer/id #uuid "72377fdc-c5c4-5cad-be35-e357b4b262ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186343227} {:answer/id #uuid "8be39f08-c60d-56cb-867b-ae591af34e37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,-1)" :db/id 17592186343461} {:answer/id #uuid "9f960098-4e3f-597c-a84f-8d0dfb1daa4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,0)" :db/id 17592186343646} {:answer/id #uuid "ee8ce6f6-003a-5a0f-82e6-f33b9254bcdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,1)" :db/id 17592186344335}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343227} :answer-field/id #uuid "c1ca2441-2869-5b83-a4db-5247f47eb190" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344834}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2a9495b4-c709-53eb-875a-846142be09cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-75521" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular." :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\,j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j]\cdot (i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1-\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{1}{{t}^{2}} & =0 \\ t-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}} & =0 \\ {t}^{4} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1)=1\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j=\,i+j, \\ r(-1)=(-1)\,i+\frac{1}{(-1)}\,j=-\,i-j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1).$"} {:db/id 17592186345103 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0191e885-4eaa-5810-988a-c30eb71a3ed8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,3)$ and $(1,0)$" :db/id 17592186342262} {:answer/id #uuid "056a40fc-c58d-5c4c-ab62-664c240b4261" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,3)$ and $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2})$" :db/id 17592186342290} {:answer/id #uuid "33643afa-ac2e-5b9f-adc3-b2783e20d066" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0)" :db/id 17592186342671} {:answer/id #uuid "35947d12-1855-548c-b110-dedcae0828e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2})" :db/id 17592186342679} {:answer/id #uuid "83eb6ca0-8566-5ea4-a7c4-84d928c8be41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,0)$ and $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{3}{2})$" :db/id 17592186343366}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342671} :answer-field/id #uuid "b899eb10-9d4b-51ba-91ba-e034d3dbe1cd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344820}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4ed3b4a4-4334-5910-b956-ca1595cafddd" :question/math-academy-id "q-75524" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,t\in [0,\pi )$ find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular." :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =0 \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in [0,\pi )$, the only solutions are $t=0$ and $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=⟨0\,,\,3⟩, \\ r\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨1\,,\,0⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(0,3)$ and $(1,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186345119 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20e4799b-7cd0-5cb1-9266-f051a077fd2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186342510} {:answer/id #uuid "80b2d167-5da5-5f35-9fe6-52013ee0e068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186343347} {:answer/id #uuid "851e346c-b574-577c-81ee-b3cad8815d4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186343379} {:answer/id #uuid "cd8e36d8-288a-5694-bc61-5e66300fe6b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186344049} {:answer/id #uuid "e0c0f3fe-29c2-5c13-bb47-1de7b39c108c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The sequence diverges." :db/id 17592186344212}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344049} :answer-field/id #uuid "bc8cd83e-9262-564b-8790-28e8d46fbcb0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344825}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8c99b596-c493-5824-b816-7b21709913d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-75723" :question/problem "Does the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{e}^{3n}}-1$ for $n>1$ converge or diverge? If the sequence converges, what is its limit?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for large values of $n,$ we have

$$
n!≫{e}^{n}≫{n}^{m}≫\operatorname{ln}⁡(n),
$$

where $≫$ means "much greater than," and $m>0.$

We calculate the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\lim_{n\to \infty }(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{e}^{3n}}-1)=-1+\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{e}^{3n}}
$$

Both the numerator and denominator approach infinity as $n\to \infty .$ However, the denominator is growing much faster than the numerator, and we conclude that

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{e}^{3n}}=0.
$$

Hence, 

$$
-1+\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{e}^{3n}}=-1+0=-1.
$$

Therefore, the sequence converges and its limit is $-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186345128 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "151da108-2d1a-5bc5-b41f-3452f296556f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{ln}⁡5" :db/id 17592186342423} {:answer/id #uuid "6541d20f-1ff9-546c-9c03-a8ef80814ea5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/id 17592186343097} {:answer/id #uuid "b1b6e00e-897a-5d95-a121-a2ba216a3005" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡5" :db/id 17592186343797} {:answer/id #uuid "c2432a49-d9c3-5f08-881b-95bc366e4923" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/id 17592186343944} {:answer/id #uuid "eecb1e2a-7344-5ba9-8e2a-6cca8c0e342f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186344336}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343797} :answer-field/id #uuid "0bdd9cde-ccbc-562f-bc45-0c204929d46a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344518}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "33fe88ae-755e-5444-9db1-f4813a03f297" :question/math-academy-id "q-75825" :question/problem "Evaluate
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-1}^{3}\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
{x}^{2}-2x-8=(x+2)(x-4).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8} & =\frac{3x-6}{(x+2)(x-4)}=\frac{A}{x+2}+\frac{B}{x-4},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
3x-6=A(x-4)+B(x+2).
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(4)-6 & =A(4-4)+B(4+2) \\ 6 & =6B \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-2)-6 & =A(-2-4)+B(-2+2) \\ -12 & =-6A \\ A & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}=\frac{2}{x+2}+\frac{1}{x-4}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{x+2}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}(x-4)|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{3}\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}(x-4)|{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345129 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "241e4e41-3877-590f-b9fb-f9441f5491c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(12)" :db/id 17592186342541} {:answer/id #uuid "2a868b11-a8ff-5adf-ab9a-9bf43adf6226" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)" :db/id 17592186342591} {:answer/id #uuid "8689e7c8-b5a6-587c-8850-666b874ed56a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)" :db/id 17592186343396} {:answer/id #uuid "d624b7cc-f612-5da1-90f6-60de0f22b6c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{7}\right)" :db/id 17592186344113} {:answer/id #uuid "ec7baec1-72af-559b-b4c9-4860c48320be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(28)" :db/id 17592186344316}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343396} :answer-field/id #uuid "db324572-0ff6-5834-9630-8030d14c66f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344872}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "36f60655-da6b-51ba-a53b-de029dead882" :question/math-academy-id "q-75828" :question/problem "Evaluate
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{4}^{11}\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
5{x}^{2}+16x+3=(5x+1)(x+3).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3} & =\frac{14}{(5x+1)(x+3)}=\frac{A}{(5x+1)}+\frac{B}{(x+3)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
14=A(x+3)+B(5x+1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & =A(-3+3)+B(5(-3)+1) \\ 14 & =-14B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{5},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & =A(-\frac{1}{5}+3)+B(5\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)+1) \\ 14 & =\frac{14}{5}A \\ A & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}=\frac{5}{5x+1}-\frac{1}{(x+3)}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{5}{5x+1}-\frac{1}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{5}{5x+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{5x+1}{x+3}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{11}\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{5x+1}{x+3}|{|}_{4}^{11} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{4}{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345134 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "403fead1-28dc-51e8-883e-1ea78fb58c8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186342768} {:answer/id #uuid "51524fcb-5371-5134-98fd-7bc0b95c2398" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186342910} {:answer/id #uuid "6d345723-89f4-5351-84cf-b5bdbe44c4c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186343174} {:answer/id #uuid "bcca82d0-a051-5fde-94e1-fbf46764a754" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186343898} {:answer/id #uuid "dce93094-4d77-5ba6-b201-1d213789909e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186344178}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343174} :answer-field/id #uuid "db497c06-807c-5ce4-a68f-3dd5b362ea6c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344873}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "19f3a0d4-a9e3-5752-9f3d-c41b8d14446d" :question/math-academy-id "q-75924" :question/problem "Solve for $x$ where $\frac{x+7}{x}-\frac{1-x}{x}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $x,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+7}{x}-\frac{1-x}{x} & =4 \\ x\cdot (\frac{x+7}{x}-\frac{1-x}{x}) & =x\cdot 4 \\ x\cdot \frac{x+7}{x}-x\cdot \frac{1-x}{x} & =x\cdot 4 \\ \cancel{x}\cdot \frac{x+7}{\cancel{x}}-\cancel{x}\cdot \frac{1-x}{\cancel{x}} & =4x \\ x+7-(1-x) & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+7-(1-x) & =4x \\ 2x+6 & =4x \\ 4x-2x & =6 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. $$

$$

$$

$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(2m-3)+3(m+5) & =m+4 \\ 10m-15+3m+15 & =m+4 \\ 13m & =m+4 \\ 12m & =4 \\ m & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
n!≫{e}^{n}≫{n}^{m}≫\operatorname{ln}⁡(n),
$$

where $≫$ means "much greater than," and $m>0.$

We calculate the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$

$$

Both the numerator and denominator approach infinity as $n\to \infty .$ However, the numerator is growing much faster than the denominator, and we conclude that

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{4{n}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2n)}=\infty .
$$

$$
n!≫{e}^{n}≫{n}^{m}≫\operatorname{ln}⁡(n),

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(4).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(4)=x.$ For $x\ne -1,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(4) & =x \\ f(x) & =4 \\ \frac{2x+1}{x+1} & =4 \\ \frac{2x+1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1) & =4\cdot (x+1) \\ \frac{2x+1}{\cancel{(x+1)}}\cdot \cancel{(x+1)} & =4x+4 \\ 2x+1 & =4x+4 \\ 2x & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(4)=-\frac{3}{2}.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x+1}{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) & =\frac{1}{{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345210 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2deb5ecd-9fcb-5de8-a47f-2aac32b50a6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(-\frac{1}{2},2)$, radius: $\frac{3}{2}$" :db/id 17592186342625} {:answer/id #uuid "4f75afc8-c8e2-552b-bf47-67f0c0a13567" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(2,\frac{1}{2})$, radius: $\frac{3}{2}$" :db/id 17592186342897} {:answer/id #uuid "5fd46a16-dd73-5cd7-848b-a231cc8b9c89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(\frac{1}{2},2)$, radius: $\frac{3}{2}$" :db/id 17592186343050} {:answer/id #uuid "6734105b-9de9-5be8-a53a-4158d98ddacb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(-\frac{1}{2},-2)$, radius: $\frac{3}{2}$" :db/id 17592186343113} {:answer/id #uuid "f715325d-e759-56c1-bf0d-6cd6e0eee098" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(\frac{1}{2},-2)$, radius: $\frac{3}{2}$" :db/id 17592186344414}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343050} :answer-field/id #uuid "58052dca-b02a-538c-bcb6-2bc7ad90fc13" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344639}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9155ce6a-a592-5aef-9c65-bf69cca03a69" :question/math-academy-id "q-76369" :question/problem "Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}-x+{y}^{2}-4y=-2.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x+{y}^{2}-4y & =-2 \\ ({x}^{2}-x)+({y}^{2}-4y) & =-2 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =-2+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2} & ={\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ and its radius is $\frac{3}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186345211 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a4b4a86-f169-5c4f-87f5-d0b62ec60298" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}),$ radius: $\frac{3}{2}$" :db/id 17592186342323} {:answer/id #uuid "3ce40828-670c-5edd-87b2-c0cb375a82f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(\frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{2}),$ radius: $\frac{1}{2}$" :db/id 17592186342739} {:answer/id #uuid "3ed3b169-f0d4-5213-afa6-342dddae141a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}),$ radius: $\frac{1}{2}$" :db/id 17592186342758} {:answer/id #uuid "92eceef3-679c-5de1-b434-dd837f79c2d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{2}),$ radius: $\frac{1}{2}$" :db/id 17592186343524} {:answer/id #uuid "d14e25aa-c14c-530e-b787-28f9bb6a6b10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "center: $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}),$ radius: $\frac{3}{2}$" :db/id 17592186344078}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342758} :answer-field/id #uuid "0b2b3b34-415d-5dcc-bc53-182c2750c2e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344516}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "385da02b-d681-50b2-a172-67bb1e6a6af1" :question/math-academy-id "q-76370" :question/problem "Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+3x+{y}^{2}-y=-\frac{9}{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3x+{y}^{2}-y & =-\frac{9}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}+3x)+({y}^{2}-y) & =-\frac{9}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}) & =-\frac{9}{4}+{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4},$ $\,0\le x\le 4\sqrt{6}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}\right)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\frac{t}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}\right)}{t}=\frac{t}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}\frac{t}{4}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}t\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}$, $\text{d}u=\frac{t}{2}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186345218 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2157cbec-dd3c-50c6-8f66-e922ba1f66ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi -1" :db/id 17592186342514} {:answer/id #uuid "46847ff5-553b-5f26-9805-09a27496f196" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi -2" :db/id 17592186342819} {:answer/id #uuid "52b6665a-0ccb-5b28-87e4-9cb8ee2700ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi -1}{4}" :db/id 17592186342928} {:answer/id #uuid "a88c1662-aadb-5062-a115-55611ab6c159" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi +2}{4}" :db/id 17592186343722} {:answer/id #uuid "bfef22ae-f97c-5172-89a1-1bc5619b881d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi +1}{4}" :db/id 17592186343921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342819} :answer-field/id #uuid "09fe84d2-3042-5159-a1de-85adb6692d1b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344513}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5649582e-ddb6-5db4-a7c3-699a007eaafe" :question/math-academy-id "q-76433" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$

\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\end{aligned}

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{4{\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)}^{2}}{{t}^{3}}=\frac{4}{{t}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\sin }^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{\sin }^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{\sin }^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186345250 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b7fc9c2-4c69-54a4-80fc-bad3ecfa5ad1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/id 17592186342726} {:answer/id #uuid "4b8b986c-eacd-5892-87dd-71c0d9c6f4f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{16}" :db/id 17592186342859} {:answer/id #uuid "9734c89e-bf7d-518a-b7d4-04a6d670adf1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{8}" :db/id 17592186343564} {:answer/id #uuid "e6cf1f3f-478f-5826-b35f-1d2148451b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{31}{10}" :db/id 17592186344263} {:answer/id #uuid "ffef2d32-f612-5254-bfaf-7abf41405410" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21}{8}" :db/id 17592186344493}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344493} :answer-field/id #uuid "0c1cefb8-a187-5530-9672-96286f591e0f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344519}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "84bd9e35-b1ad-5104-8c53-a77a665c8e52" :question/math-academy-id "q-76749" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$

$$ where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$

$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{\cos }^{4}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8{\cos }^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{\cos }^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =16{\int }_{1}^{1/2}-{u}^{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-16\cdot \frac{1}{6}{u}^{6}{|}_{1}^{1/2} \\  & =-\frac{16}{6}({\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{6}-{1}^{6}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}\left(-\frac{63}{64}\right) \\  & =\frac{21}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345251 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0db51a33-3a41-59c9-81e2-4977416f0bbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{10}\right)" :db/id 17592186342356} {:answer/id #uuid "4e66f044-704b-5e52-82fd-7775a345573b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{5}\right)" :db/id 17592186342884} {:answer/id #uuid "611b54d2-27f5-5778-b31a-a615fefd7d7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{5}\right)" :db/id 17592186343061} {:answer/id #uuid "7ada0cf6-550a-5410-8925-e1587a2111ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)" :db/id 17592186343294} {:answer/id #uuid "7d3428c5-5eb7-5f6a-939d-3f6b641fe810" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{5}\right)" :db/id 17592186343317}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343061} :answer-field/id #uuid "8031f084-7386-5995-b791-a49b6fd8c3ab" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344719}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "71319f17-956d-5226-b02f-5e0082742e93" :question/math-academy-id "q-7675" :question/problem "Express $$
\displaystyle 8\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)
$$ as a single trigonometric ratio." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{5}$ into the above, we get

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{5})=\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{5}\right).
$$

Therefore,

$$
8\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)=4\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{5}\right)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{5}\right).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345254 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "68904330-d856-56ab-ab89-95598aff7f05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}" :db/id 17592186343132} {:answer/id #uuid "7643286e-f9ff-585d-9aca-43eda7f2b710" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186343260} {:answer/id #uuid "ccc1b583-ed2c-5e36-a6b5-501f45d92300" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}" :db/id 17592186344043} {:answer/id #uuid "eba40804-2b69-5b03-8ebc-fcc8b5946e91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi +1}{2}" :db/id 17592186344303} {:answer/id #uuid "ec2c9374-53c5-5786-8c80-f18bc786264b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{2}" :db/id 17592186344309}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344043} :answer-field/id #uuid "e39c6e76-f79f-5404-bd14-1344e4f9c50e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344892}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "21e9d3c4-49da-5fcb-92fe-c05185c24062" :question/math-academy-id "q-76767" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\theta  & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}\theta =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}-0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}+(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345259 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "107d5a2a-4f6f-52c4-a7ea-a3c986f47360" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186342381} {:answer/id #uuid "12208fda-53a7-5d69-9f6a-dbdffb153e06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186342399} {:answer/id #uuid "768320a8-bc68-56f3-9b17-f4dad32ac2f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186343266} {:answer/id #uuid "9381484a-6981-59d3-b123-6f51531c898a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186343530} {:answer/id #uuid "bd7ef7a7-f907-538f-b138-4c1ddb333884" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186343904}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342381} :answer-field/id #uuid "20642a04-5ca1-5221-ae4c-b1d1be5781d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344550}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "06fe26ef-4ec2-5c23-a26d-637e986a7e20" :question/math-academy-id "q-76906" :question/problem "Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}4,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2t\operatorname{cos}2t-\operatorname{sin}2t,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2},\hspace{0.222em}2t\operatorname{sin}2t+\operatorname{cos}2t⟩
$$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186345268 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10fd546e-6850-53e8-ae1a-3f4f4b165e06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186342387} {:answer/id #uuid "2b35bb1a-43d0-59e2-a75f-6da5905e2d86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186342598} {:answer/id #uuid "2d466b44-fd60-581c-aea2-39afd97d6ab7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi -12" :db/id 17592186342615} {:answer/id #uuid "b7d7dc1f-2c50-5c7c-88af-db176d4c240b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186343851} {:answer/id #uuid "ff3bdff6-e0d5-5365-ae66-b27cbfab7afd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}-12" :db/id 17592186344486}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344486} :answer-field/id #uuid "8cefcc8e-0177-5dec-979d-65559f35b4e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344737}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1c70d6fc-ab49-5aab-b1d0-4a65a7ea2b5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-77032" :question/problem "![](images/08/08c3195e7325d853f61562b1f62460cb0796f14377286228f2b7cd40983202ac.png)

Evaluate the line integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $F(x,y)=3\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$  traversed from the point $A(4,0)$ to the point $B(0,4).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =3\,i+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\,i+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =3\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\,dt \\  & =[12\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(0+\frac{\pi }{2})-(12+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-12\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345270 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b5a67bb-0704-5374-80b7-f3c08e8d80a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186342601} {:answer/id #uuid "46234d75-8481-586d-a8d6-e8817f41182e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186342815} {:answer/id #uuid "8ba3f5f9-1429-57ca-8bd7-30d8b83aa72f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186343454} {:answer/id #uuid "d2b57ee9-5770-5bad-bc47-e53eff6914ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186344087} {:answer/id #uuid "e992c30b-4dd9-5634-88df-cea97771fa79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186344283}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342815} :answer-field/id #uuid "05a88dee-a59b-585a-bbc1-cb4004578b85" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344504}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "50a8400d-aac2-5c82-9900-5410f81b5445" :question/math-academy-id "q-77064" :question/problem "Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨10,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}-1,\hspace{0.222em}2t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\  & ={t}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(1,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(0,-2).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{7}{3},
$$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x-{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the horizontal line segment from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t) & =\mathbf{0}+t(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{0}) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,0⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,0⟩ \\  & =t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=t$ and $y=0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t)) & =({x}^{2}+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x-{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =({t}^{2}+0)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t-{0}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & ={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =({t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\mathbf{i}) \\  & ={t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{1}}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t+\frac{7}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0)+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345286 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ccbd978-8163-5c7e-baae-b8ad95985a86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186342350} {:answer/id #uuid "453e49ec-25af-50ef-847c-f9e8f100fa90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186342807} {:answer/id #uuid "78d2918a-06f4-5e2f-8f95-8ce2e0a1d53e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186343281} {:answer/id #uuid "7c924cb2-9540-5923-aef1-54902d61b6c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186343312} {:answer/id #uuid "a953ff99-deba-55f2-9b54-5b5b5650e514" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186343729}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342350} :answer-field/id #uuid "10c5cc9a-ab7f-5bd2-8f67-b0bc3b91ae44" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344525}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8fc56ee5-fc5d-5429-bfdb-4254f7ee30fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-77191" :question/problem "![](images/04/0457cb819e6f39ef9c0978e356cff788e1cf5edbef9cbf844a054ab777b70eac.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of the line segment from the point $B(0,1)$ to the point $D(1,1).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{3}{2},
$$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,

$$

$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =⟨-2,0⟩+t(⟨0,1⟩-⟨-2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨-2+2t,t⟩ \\  & =(-2+2t)\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-2+2t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t)) & =(x-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(y-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =((-2+2t)-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t-(-2+2t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+2t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =(-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =-2-t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{1}}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t+\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2-t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2} \\  & ={[-2t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =[-2(1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0]-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345287 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a04d171-7f37-5d9d-a2f8-61194e6e93c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "28" :db/id 17592186342463} {:answer/id #uuid "2dbc28ff-5d76-56ae-8ecf-64a2fdcb3e2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186342623} {:answer/id #uuid "a4e002a4-bd25-5f07-8e74-c15da484745e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "56" :db/id 17592186343691} {:answer/id #uuid "b2aa47f5-56ab-5309-a1ff-ddb6c0030709" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186343807} {:answer/id #uuid "c97a2a57-f756-5bf4-8ca0-819491201663" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186344007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186342463} :answer-field/id #uuid "9bc43f6a-48ec-5f1d-9fa3-8b18c022ec80" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344765}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3fbb4ec8-936e-5c4c-830d-f88706e61780" :question/math-academy-id "q-77219" :question/problem "![](images/23/2324d20426a6ef6110714341f256ed3943c66d4068cdb9bd3d1763f8f528f5a1.png)

from  $t=1$ to $t=2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}2t+2t\operatorname{sin}2t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}2t-2t\operatorname{cos}2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4t\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.222em},4t\operatorname{sin}2t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(4t\operatorname{cos}2t)}^{2}+{(4t\operatorname{sin}2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+16{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}} \\  & =4t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t>0$ for $t\in [1,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-5\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{25}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4}) & =0.\end{aligned}

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4}=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})(\lambda -\frac{5}{2}) & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =\frac{5}{2}$ is a repeated root.
