$$"} {:db/id 17592186348404 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "099529b2-f2d8-571a-8051-1abe76e80e34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186345427} {:answer/id #uuid "1c89dd2c-b2a6-55ce-9cde-64a9db39f22a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186345598} {:answer/id #uuid "2af3437a-013c-5c2c-ba66-e91d3d0b3776" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186345732} {:answer/id #uuid "e08432ed-6cab-5f33-bc9d-ccb5e07f25a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186347321} {:answer/id #uuid "e22f899c-983b-59f9-b450-dbd732e6a167" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{25}" :db/id 17592186347340}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345732} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f5bdbcf-f249-5c99-b7cb-71c1723c6391" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347774}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "19bd97de-146f-5b50-9592-8b78d39231d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-80523" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s$, where

$$
r(s)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right),\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)⟩,\,0\le s<10\pi .
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right))⟩ \\  & =⟨-5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{5},\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right))⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{5},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟩ \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =|-\frac{1}{5}|\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right))}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)+{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{5}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348411 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4803543c-d61e-5f5c-968e-bc681feef549" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2s}}" :db/id 17592186345969} {:answer/id #uuid "4ca68699-5d12-50bb-b538-dd82a35e755d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2s}}" :db/id 17592186346010} {:answer/id #uuid "724bf20d-270c-5376-b989-0685a8f99019" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2s(1-2s)}}" :db/id 17592186346362} {:answer/id #uuid "7f95752a-9af9-56bd-b358-ebcec0812d80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2s(1-2s)}" :db/id 17592186346470} {:answer/id #uuid "fd88f132-9956-5edd-b9a1-d15e9c7f24c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186347583}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346362} :answer-field/id #uuid "c8a7def3-c10e-5e3b-9fa8-80d05175b949" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347953}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "61dc28ce-9be1-5118-b764-acd32225832e" :question/math-academy-id "q-80545" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s,$ where

$$
r(s)=⟨\frac{1}{3}(1-2s)^{3/2},\,\frac{1}{3}(2s)^{3/2}⟩,\,0<s<\frac{1}{2}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{1}{3}(1-2s)^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{1}{3}(2s)^{3/2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot (1-2s)^{1/2}\cdot (-2),\,\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot (2s)^{1/2}\cdot 2⟩ \\  & =⟨-(1-2s)^{1/2},\,(2s)^{1/2}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-(1-2s)^{1/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}((2s)^{1/2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1-2s)^{-1/2}\cdot (-2),\,\frac{1}{2}(2s)^{-1/2}\cdot 2⟩ \\  & =⟨(1-2s)^{-1/2},\,(2s)^{-1/2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, the curvature is  

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{((1-2s)^{-1/2})}^{2}+{((2s)^{-1/2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(1-2s)^{-1}+(2s)^{-1}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{1-2s}+\frac{1}{2s}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2s(1-2s)}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348420 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0abddb8f-91f8-5ee8-9e90-e4eb6046e101" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186345435} {:answer/id #uuid "17002d3c-d0d8-5485-aa3f-3748e9b1113a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186345554} {:answer/id #uuid "63123636-56ca-5c3f-9905-b24651986635" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186346214} {:answer/id #uuid "cb7edda9-0cf7-5d75-bb2c-a28098da660f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186347131} {:answer/id #uuid "d6757e65-24a6-5b28-8adf-6e8e535e245a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186347241}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346214} :answer-field/id #uuid "90af9d53-8403-569d-8a7b-66ffcbfd6f0e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347856}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0e0662ae-2a01-57b3-bb86-0addfedab9d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-80607" :question/problem "Consider the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by arc length $s.$ Find the curvature at the point where $s=1$ if the unit tangent vector of the curve is given by

$$
T(s)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{s}^{2}}}⟨1,s⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given that the curve $r(s)$ and its unit tangent vector $T(s)$ are parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature: 

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖
$$

Now, we differentiate $T(s)$ with respect to $s$ and evaluate it at $s=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{s}^{2}}}⟨1,s⟩) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{s}^{2}}}\right),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{1+{s}^{2}}}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{s}{(1+{s}^{2})^{3/2}},\,\frac{1}{(1+{s}^{2})^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{(1+{s}^{2})^{3/2}}⟨-s,1⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{(1+{1}^{2})^{3/2}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we obtain the curvature:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =‖{T}^{′}(1)‖ \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}‖⟨-1,1⟩‖ \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348424 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00941107-e9c6-5933-9b3b-706a63234ba7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "38" :db/id 17592186345358} {:answer/id #uuid "04e48a0b-e477-5875-bccf-2afaa6e18026" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "22" :db/id 17592186345391} {:answer/id #uuid "0517197d-6ae6-5927-9dc2-64a247347fd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186345394} {:answer/id #uuid "a965b668-471d-54ec-81ea-2f7db68ebe67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "26" :db/id 17592186346828} {:answer/id #uuid "fa5975e9-7302-5301-927b-8ef8cd0130c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48" :db/id 17592186347561}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345358} :answer-field/id #uuid "5e31db97-e6fd-5344-986a-bb11c57faba1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347768}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3c76c336-dd88-5200-b5c5-bdf849ab058b" :question/math-academy-id "q-80627" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{R}\frac{2+6y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,
$$  where $R=[1,2]\times [2,4].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{2+6y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}6y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{2}{x}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{2}{2}-\left(-\frac{2}{1}\right)) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}6y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{2}^{4}6y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3{y}^{2}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =3({4}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{2+6y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A=2+36=38.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348429 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "311172a8-7e55-513e-8ad0-0a5ffe1f23c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},-1)" :db/id 17592186345785} {:answer/id #uuid "a87153a0-e08e-53d1-9b65-4f3d8b63db1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186346817} {:answer/id #uuid "c99f2895-b196-5066-8383-d5366c43e803" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},-1)" :db/id 17592186347107} {:answer/id #uuid "d35b0a5f-5b16-52e7-ae86-6ec97e1d9b78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},1)" :db/id 17592186347200} {:answer/id #uuid "f4319ac2-54b4-5918-88cd-fb73b81e377e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},1)" :db/id 17592186347517}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186347517} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a9f84a4-996e-5b49-a227-bb8512ac548b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347877}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d15295c3-5868-57e4-8227-d3f5fdb96a55" :question/math-academy-id "q-80646" :question/problem "Determine the stationary point of $f(x,y)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-4xy+{y}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "The stationary points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T},$ where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is $D={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}∣x>0},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2}{x}-4y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4x+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{x}-4y & -4x+2y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the stationary points, we need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$
Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{x}-4y &=0 \\ -4x+2y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving for $y$ in the first equation, we get

$$
\frac{2}{x}-4y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2x}.
$$

Then, substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+2\left(\frac{1}{2x}\right) & =0 \\ -4x+\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) & =0 \\ 4x & =\frac{1}{x}. \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{1}{2x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2} & \,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=1 \\ x=-\frac{1}{2} & \,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has two solutions, $(\frac{1}{2},1)$ and $(-\frac{1}{2},-1).$ We reject the point $(-\frac{1}{2},-1)$ because it does not lie in the domain of $f(x,y).$

In conclusion, $f$ has one stationary point, $(\frac{1}{2},1).$"} {:db/id 17592186348432 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20de5545-98b6-5d2c-a9e8-23d31442168f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186345643} {:answer/id #uuid "2d81058b-a41c-51b2-be5e-6cff35dadddc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186345754} {:answer/id #uuid "54870244-8e6a-5eb5-886f-6d29b6406c80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186346068} {:answer/id #uuid "85571f00-f73a-5cc6-b5a7-62f53afb2e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186346511} {:answer/id #uuid "fd707ea9-df6c-5eee-8eee-f57ee98f24d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186347580}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345643} :answer-field/id #uuid "803110be-ead5-5fd3-b4dd-d98cc2e1f996" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347831}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c8f1c2d8-aadd-57cc-878c-19c22388e69f" :question/math-academy-id "q-80661" :question/problem "Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2},\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=\frac{3}{2},
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}\frac{f(x,y)}{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}\frac{f(x,y)}{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348435 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29ff34e9-a4f9-5efb-ad29-b203ff520685" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,0)$ and $(2,1)$" :db/id 17592186345726} {:answer/id #uuid "34cc476b-a22c-50b8-b73e-550217b646bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,0)$ and $(1,2)$" :db/id 17592186345808} {:answer/id #uuid "5b57b927-3b0b-54c7-bf20-a0a9152b21b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,1)$ and $(2,-1)$" :db/id 17592186346128} {:answer/id #uuid "773c91c3-0748-5043-8dfd-d9ad13a415b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,-2)$ and $(1,1)$" :db/id 17592186346397} {:answer/id #uuid "ceb2afa7-2bcc-5d34-b559-37635169834d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-2,0)$ and $(2,1)$" :db/id 17592186347160}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345726} :answer-field/id #uuid "3829a637-2a8a-579c-8d17-1ea1059a7384" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347699}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a1fd2252-93e6-52b7-b6db-b0208e66793d" :question/math-academy-id "q-80685" :question/problem "Determine the critical points of $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}y+6{y}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "The critical points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(a)$ does not exist, where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =3{x}^{2}-6xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-3{x}^{2}+12y.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6xy & -3{x}^{2}+12y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$ such that ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ does not exist. Note that, in our case, ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so we just need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$

Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6xy &=0 \\ -3{x}^{2}+12y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving for $y$ in the second equation, we obtain

$$
-3{x}^{2}+12y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Then, substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6x\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\right) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-\frac{6{x}^{3}}{4} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(1-\frac{x}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}(2-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0 & \,⟹\,y=\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}=0 \\ x=2 & \,⟹\,y=\frac{{2}^{2}}{4}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has two solutions, $(0,0)$ and $(2,1).$

In conclusion, $f$ has two critical points, $(0,0)$ and $(2,1).$ Note that since ${f}^{′}(x)={0}^{T}$ at these two points, they are also both stationary points."} {:db/id 17592186348444 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "22141837-7250-500e-8f49-e3a949023800" :question/math-academy-id "q-80753" :question/problem "Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-y)=4xy-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y-2x)=4xy-2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(yx{e}^{x}+{y}^{2})=x{e}^{x}+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1){e}^{x}+2xy)=x{e}^{x}+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}-x)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is '“${f}_{x}(x,y)=yx{e}^{x}+{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=(x-1){e}^{x}+2xy$” and “${f}_{x}(x,y)=x-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}-x$” only'."} $$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) &=x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({({t}^{2})}^{2}+t)\cdot 2t+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+t)\cdot 2t+3{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{5}+5{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{(1)^{6}}{3}+\frac{5(1)^{3}}{3}+(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{5}{3}+1]-[0] \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351193 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50bcb0c7-dd3c-5662-8952-a62b864ea1b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}+{x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}" :db/id 17592186349177} {:answer/id #uuid "6bd9c288-0a2f-5b6a-8280-dfa7a6d79d4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}-{x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}" :db/id 17592186349441} {:answer/id #uuid "900b6cf9-f6a5-50fe-b972-4ff38adff462" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{3x/2}+B{e}^{-3x/2}+2x{e}^{3x/2}" :db/id 17592186349740} {:answer/id #uuid "d4c956e7-5ac6-5d5a-9667-fe7bf9e6a95b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}" :db/id 17592186350311} {:answer/id #uuid "fe1a6459-4165-58cc-bce3-9389de599355" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{-3x/2}+B{e}^{-x/2}+{e}^{3x/2}" :db/id 17592186350681}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350311} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ace36a3-9980-5ddb-840c-9facce6be643" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350886}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ff9e60ce-0c56-5edd-8dd6-d60ae5843660" :question/math-academy-id "q-8102" :question/problem "Find the general solution to the equation

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{9}{4}y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4} & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{3x/2}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $\frac{3}{2}$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (2x+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (2+6x+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (2+6x+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2}-3(\alpha (2x+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}){e}^{3x/2})+\frac{9}{4}(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}) & =6{e}^{3x/2} \\ (2+6x+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2}-6x-\frac{9}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{9}{4}{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{3x/2} & =6{e}^{3x/2} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{3x/2} & =6{e}^{3x/2} \\ 2\alpha  & =6 \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{3x/2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351200 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "54182a39-39fb-5be5-9664-fa162218a7fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}-\frac{4}{49}{e}^{-x}" :db/id 17592186349214} {:answer/id #uuid "679cf4da-701b-5bdc-92f7-957782af3225" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{-5x/2}+B{e}^{5x/2}+\frac{8}{49}{e}^{-x}" :db/id 17592186349401} {:answer/id #uuid "69114ebe-fbaf-5d5b-9d6c-9cf6ad123ae0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}+\frac{16}{49}{e}^{-x}" :db/id 17592186349416} {:answer/id #uuid "aef6bfbf-3637-5f9a-b416-eec0ecf46416" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{-5x/2}+B{e}^{5x/2}-\frac{4}{7}{e}^{-x}" :db/id 17592186349992} {:answer/id #uuid "ba31321f-bf40-5676-95d0-1848e2cd51e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}+\frac{2}{7}{e}^{-x}" :db/id 17592186350099}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349416} :answer-field/id #uuid "e48ff23b-ca88-5ca4-868e-d79bc82bd7dd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351106}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5ad9bde6-0f28-5d02-9140-ff3f90ecfdc9" :question/math-academy-id "q-8103" :question/problem "Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{25y}{4}=4{e}^{-x}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{25y}{4}=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4} & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\frac{5}{2}$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{-x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-1$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-\alpha {e}^{-x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha {e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha {e}^{-x}-5(-\alpha {e}^{-x})+\frac{25}{4}\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ (1+5+\frac{25}{4})\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{49}{4}\alpha {e}^{-x} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{49}{4}\alpha  & =4 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{16}{49}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{16}{49}{e}^{-x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{5x/2}+Bx{e}^{5x/2}+\frac{16}{49}{e}^{-x}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351208 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "332cef0f-7e74-5874-a5dd-9dcaf39eb621" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186348904} {:answer/id #uuid "6c3c177b-b307-5e69-88e2-f72b3ea017f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186349444} {:answer/id #uuid "718346f6-13c9-5b5e-a1b1-cf2a751071ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}" :db/id 17592186349494} {:answer/id #uuid "ba9420a7-4596-5a37-8320-623f88d3e445" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186350102} {:answer/id #uuid "d0e6b5e2-07c0-52a8-81d2-8322be2ebdb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186350282}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350102} :answer-field/id #uuid "9604317f-a341-5a08-a23b-384909662e3d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350963}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0b1df791-ae8a-5761-94bd-f7868c7dce6d" :question/math-academy-id "q-81059" :question/problem "What is the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}?$" :question/worked-solution "The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right).
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351215 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4d86d14f-109f-5fbc-a1b8-fa0a976df1b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186349154} {:answer/id #uuid "72017b2e-c440-5764-99f9-76f9513b9aa8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186349496} {:answer/id #uuid "8a15a52a-6673-5f9d-95a7-02892ff67d34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186349699} {:answer/id #uuid "8c155c2c-3cab-50b9-babe-50ea740e776f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186349713} {:answer/id #uuid "c6fd627c-a6b3-5cec-bc46-c9b0ad435ed7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186350199}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349496} :answer-field/id #uuid "bea3995e-f8db-5dc4-a647-999ecab54336" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351039}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "346018a5-76ad-5ea5-a1fa-213af5e9b80a" :question/math-academy-id "q-81097" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is a portion of the circle parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡t+{\cos }^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\pi -0 \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351216 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17becf89-3701-509a-a9a8-440484064ed9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186348648} {:answer/id #uuid "20742a72-7769-5476-9ce9-3b1881e0470b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186348727} {:answer/id #uuid "47810cbc-2cf1-5cf8-8896-58252baa012e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186349094} {:answer/id #uuid "ee29d359-0faa-5f3d-aacd-2a4fd062f399" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186350529} {:answer/id #uuid "f83e5f36-bde0-573a-91de-bf6ecdf50c44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186350622}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349094} :answer-field/id #uuid "81d0252a-6745-5c15-b97f-a22408b67a5b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350931}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7a071a2f-be85-5b88-9507-97c63159bbb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-81098" :question/problem "If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-x$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(2,2),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}2xy\,dx+x\,dy=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-x.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) &=x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{i}+(2t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2t({t}^{2}-t)\cdot 1+t(2t-1)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{t}^{3}-t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}]-[0] \\  & =8-2 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351218 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "499b11ec-b714-5e35-93a8-a00dd90bd487" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186349115} {:answer/id #uuid "4b3d1df7-d187-5a76-9ff2-d586354e93f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}-1" :db/id 17592186349135} {:answer/id #uuid "a07e3936-f719-59ae-bec5-b46ca80359cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e+1" :db/id 17592186349872} {:answer/id #uuid "ce5f8cad-b0d3-57e8-8823-669fc1f82f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186350261} {:answer/id #uuid "dc675675-601c-5a06-9c0d-83e3763e65c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186350373}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349135} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a5f8fc5-bd8c-52a6-b3a1-caea03d05cdf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350917}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "88864edb-1c9c-588d-bdc6-1eef5e251f66" :question/math-academy-id "q-81102" :question/problem "If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(2,3),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi y}{2}\right)\,dy=
$$" :question/worked-solution "The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =\mathbf{j}+t(2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\mathbf{j}+t(2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}) \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi y}{2}\right)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi y}{2}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi y}{2}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}\cdot 2-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi (1+2t)}{2}\right)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{e}^{2t}-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t))dt \\  & ={[{e}^{2t}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{e}^{2(1)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (1))]-[{e}^{2(0)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (0))] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)]-[1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+0]-[1+0] \\  & ={e}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351232 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1df8bb31-8697-5de1-ab64-b0087cf80766" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=8\operatorname{cos}⁡x-12\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186348709} {:answer/id #uuid "874922fb-eaa0-5b59-abee-6a91e4fb56fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=15\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186349678} {:answer/id #uuid "94b3734c-9c2d-512c-bbc9-599f1fb7dcf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=25\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186349779} {:answer/id #uuid "99c423b9-af51-597d-81a1-f34b58f190f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡x-16\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186349823} {:answer/id #uuid "e518fb89-2b7b-5c49-8938-6f2390ac3371" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡x+12\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186350456}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349823} :answer-field/id #uuid "e013f61e-ba7b-5c71-b166-0d277744875d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351097}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "19bd44fa-2632-53a7-82f0-7e7751665f68" :question/math-academy-id "q-8113" :question/problem "Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y}{4}=25\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation." :question/worked-solution "The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $25\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4}=25\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-\frac{3}{4}\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -\frac{3}{4}\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=25\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}\alpha -\beta &=25\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -\frac{3}{4}\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-12$ and $\beta =-16.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡x-16\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351239 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09e4e475-fd3e-59f0-820b-1982debe60cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}" :db/id 17592186348528} {:answer/id #uuid "0f62e3ce-84e7-595a-a7a5-457b174d16ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+4{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}-\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}" :db/id 17592186348582} {:answer/id #uuid "5798b2cd-2f47-5240-8fbd-f9a9d3c0182f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+2{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}-\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}" :db/id 17592186349252} {:answer/id #uuid "681d6106-231c-5bfd-baa9-0f66bdd3c674" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{4}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}" :db/id 17592186349404} {:answer/id #uuid "c2eb28a4-0e25-554d-a241-d0105cba2580" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-2{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}" :db/id 17592186350175}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348528} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbea5af6-49b4-5f17-84c3-27b7e8ed8bf1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351034}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3169dc8c-e50f-57c2-bbce-69548992f510" :question/math-academy-id "q-81157" :question/problem "Find the fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of ${\sin }^{2}⁡(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=a$ is given by

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}(a)}{4!}(x-a)^{4}.
$$

Here, we have $a=\frac{\pi }{2},$ so

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.
$$

So we need to work out $f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),$ ${f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),$ ${f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),$ ${f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ and ${f}^{(4)}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={\sin }^{2}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & ={\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{2}\right)=-2 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{(4)}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{2}\right)=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${P}_{4}(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =1+(0)(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\left(\frac{(-2)}{2!}\right){(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{0}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{8}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4} \\  & =1-{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351246 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a282ef1-02b6-5cec-8cbc-46098cc6ef59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186348666} {:answer/id #uuid "40da84d6-775a-5706-89d5-80bd2154dd2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186349035} {:answer/id #uuid "4c02b26f-4d12-56ba-a748-19be6fae7d6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186349141} {:answer/id #uuid "75937d77-6bd6-5532-b889-5e04ecdd593b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186349528} {:answer/id #uuid "d88c479e-9826-5a0a-aedc-792be5540e2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186350346}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349141} :answer-field/id #uuid "250e9511-1fcb-590f-8c12-c551fd4300a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350776}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f750ea59-b3de-591d-8c26-90afaaf302f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-81171" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{(2x+y+1)}{x}\,dx+dy,
$$ where $C$ is a portion of the parabola parametrized by $r(t)=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j$ for $t\in [0,2].$" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\,dx+dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{2x+y+1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2t+{t}^{2}-1+1}{t}+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+t+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+3t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[2t+\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[2(2)+\frac{3}{2}(2)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[4+6] \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351249 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b6156b9-9f78-59f9-8142-98f1233741d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186348543} {:answer/id #uuid "10a3e3a4-0310-552e-ab24-a02eb3c757db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186348591} {:answer/id #uuid "8aa1d276-43a7-559f-a05c-be52490034d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186349704} {:answer/id #uuid "c2eafcc9-b6ef-56c6-ac30-42c1bc19d6f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186350174} {:answer/id #uuid "f8c7f6ed-9846-5d42-9784-c5ff2760afa2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186350629}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350174} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ab55e1a-0618-5db2-9d17-8d651e9f287a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350972}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fde6cd1e-82de-5878-af27-eda97f1dc77e" :question/math-academy-id "q-81177" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{\pi }{4}].$" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}{\cos }^{2}⁡t-{\sin }^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){|}_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351250 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5480a9aa-ad9e-5901-99ef-a4b557010682" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2+6\pi " :db/id 17592186349219} {:answer/id #uuid "9515cda8-658c-596e-82bc-d1176ae74422" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2+10\pi " :db/id 17592186349782} {:answer/id #uuid "d708ba15-3640-5e0f-a2cc-8efebb555009" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+12\pi " :db/id 17592186350330} {:answer/id #uuid "e9a9cd99-2cbe-59b5-8edc-4b78ef09dc96" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+14\pi " :db/id 17592186350495} {:answer/id #uuid "f55e6f64-fa6a-5856-9b77-a53e676b505a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+16\pi " :db/id 17592186350593}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350495} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ed4da5c-67f9-5122-bb2a-f6a68757af78" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350790}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bbe13972-64bc-5d76-9613-e21318b0221e" :question/math-academy-id "q-81180" :question/problem "If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=\pi {x}^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(1,\pi )$ to point $B(2,4\pi ),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\,dx+3x\,dy=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\pi {x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) &=x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\pi {t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{i}+2\pi t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\,dx+3x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi {t}^{2}}{2{t}^{2}}\right)\cdot 1+3t\cdot 2\pi t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}1+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & =[t+2\pi {t}^{3}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =[2+2\pi (2)^{3}]-[1+2\pi (1)^{3}] \\  & =[2+16\pi ]-[1+2\pi ] \\  & =1+14\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351255 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "007c15b8-5581-5d5e-b9b9-20eee41ea6c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186348458} {:answer/id #uuid "082db701-17a8-5bfd-8d51-0f9db11a73c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186348516} {:answer/id #uuid "1b63928e-c54b-546f-a018-4d155b2013d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186348679} {:answer/id #uuid "83473f2c-636b-50f3-bc7d-a4ffeaa05151" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186349648} {:answer/id #uuid "9be4dc92-527b-522b-8645-b3d9e5f62909" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186349834}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349834} :answer-field/id #uuid "10ba579e-2517-548c-a3d7-b08e597033da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350739}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8452eaa3-7ef9-5d96-b24f-03672a6ae137" :question/math-academy-id "q-81195" :question/problem "Given that ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{bmatrix}$ and ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $\det (A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\det (A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}7-\lambda  & 5 \\ -4 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2-4\text{i} & 5 \\ -4 & -2-4\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ (-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -2+4\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -2-4\text{i}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+4\text{i})(-2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351267 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19aefefa-5028-5a51-9e4a-e7a5f85a0ecd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\sqrt{3},4)" :db/id 17592186348661} {:answer/id #uuid "31c265f3-9b60-519e-8c42-a2074afe1991" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\sqrt{2},4)" :db/id 17592186348888} {:answer/id #uuid "61e897c5-e855-5435-b9a3-3ce1fe3df228" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{9}{2})" :db/id 17592186349343} {:answer/id #uuid "6bdd275f-98a8-5d3a-be25-406316b4b4e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{5}{2},\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186349442} {:answer/id #uuid "a8ea7143-6d50-55a0-8054-cb45eeb37658" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\sqrt{2},\frac{9}{2})" :db/id 17592186349952}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349442} :answer-field/id #uuid "7ce1ae29-1a77-542a-a894-431caec80306" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350924}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e4c53f6c-deac-537d-ad18-d2272f3b99d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-81221" :question/problem "![](images/6e/6e9d2238ca77532c3adda8d35f94061d108c3e15432ce48fdc33885ddf4f4e48.png)

The diagram above shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(5,\frac{7\pi }{6})$ and $m∠AOB=\frac{5\pi }{6},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$" :question/worked-solution "First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(5,\frac{7\pi }{6}),$ we must have $r=5.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $5,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $5.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle clockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{7\pi }{6},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\frac{7\pi }{6}-\frac{5\pi }{6}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(5,\frac{\pi }{3})$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\displaystyle {∬}_{R}\frac{3-4y{x}^{3}}{y}\,\text{d}A,
$$  where $R=[1,2]\times [1,e].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{3-4y{x}^{3}}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{3}{y}-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{3}{y}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}4{x}^{3}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{3}{y}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{3}{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[3\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}4{x}^{3}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{1}^{2}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(e-1)[{x}^{4}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =(e-1)({2}^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =15(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{3-4y{x}^{3}}{y}\,\text{d}A=3-15(e-1)=18-15e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351279 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "231305d1-2a44-5129-8672-9f940eca8d39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186348746} {:answer/id #uuid "2bc171e2-f20a-5041-baf5-e5eefb5b2caf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186348831} {:answer/id #uuid "6f9eff26-2f2c-510b-975b-f511ee4eb4d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186349470} {:answer/id #uuid "8e1ff3ef-923b-5606-b2ea-728957655b37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186349726} {:answer/id #uuid "f819e8dd-1aca-5a9d-bed9-3528ec5560c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186350621}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350621} :answer-field/id #uuid "075229f6-a119-5672-9399-3d6b92199cb2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350718}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2a2e88a4-19f3-55df-8ef8-28fa3b7c0024" :question/math-academy-id "q-81254" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral $$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(1,9)\times (-1,1)$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,9)\times (1,4).$ So, we can write

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186351284 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07cf5972-f40e-5217-8db4-af4d714d0f29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,5)\cup (5,\infty )" :db/id 17592186348511} {:answer/id #uuid "4ff5e665-aaa0-5a32-9ee9-f1bfeace33e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,-3)\cup (-3,\infty )" :db/id 17592186349171} {:answer/id #uuid "86623a7d-5813-5d35-94af-16d6fb07a0e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,\frac{1}{5})\cup (\frac{1}{5},\infty )" :db/id 17592186349673} {:answer/id #uuid "c3ecf398-d445-5f07-9e39-0e0872bbfc4b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186350178} {:answer/id #uuid "e061e2c5-0620-5228-ad52-cedd9b116361" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,-\frac{1}{3})\cup (-\frac{1}{3},\infty )" :db/id 17592186350417}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349673} :answer-field/id #uuid "0a944731-6928-5c95-9932-5dd54d8c5f7b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350725}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f524ac1c-6637-5a2f-a68c-7f9c181d3393" :question/math-academy-id "q-81297" :question/problem "What is the domain of the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{5x-1}?$" :question/worked-solution "A reciprocal function is defined for all values of $x$ except for those that make the denominator zero. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values of $x$ that make the denominator zero.
