\displaystyle (-\infty ,\frac{4}{5})\cup (\frac{4}{5},\infty ).
$$ What is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "A reciprocal function is defined for all values of $x$ except for those that make the denominator zero. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}kx-4 & =0 \\ kx & =4 \\ x & =\frac{4}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point that must be excluded from the domain is $x=\frac{4}{k}.$ 

On the other hand, we can see that $x=\frac{4}{5}$ is excluded from the domain. Equating this to $\frac{4}{k},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{k} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{1}{k} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351288 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "054cfdb8-9523-5fd3-8ee5-f3584ca875a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186348495} {:answer/id #uuid "1a58f340-5f07-524b-9972-7aec7a072fe6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186348668} {:answer/id #uuid "413f25e1-e820-5b99-b415-72140d39e76a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186349040} {:answer/id #uuid "630cd449-0bac-53d3-aade-e06771d4eb3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186349353} {:answer/id #uuid "df055118-5d65-5cb6-afdd-037e1bc8f8e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-\pi " :db/id 17592186350398}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348668} :answer-field/id #uuid "bb3e7c8f-9e68-503e-917d-bfcf6dae85d1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351030}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f40afbe3-1000-5dc9-b06f-6a8edbf20249" :question/math-academy-id "q-81315" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dx\,dy.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{y}dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}[x]_{0}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}(y-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}y\,\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}y\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dy & ={[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-1-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351289 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26bbc4db-b814-52bd-b3ff-a786602bad48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186348779} {:answer/id #uuid "26bde5b4-36d6-575c-9652-f9261a189321" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{4}" :db/id 17592186348780} {:answer/id #uuid "294ee22b-5415-5f7c-87fb-cf75ba45c624" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186348805} {:answer/id #uuid "2962217e-731b-56f6-b321-15ce00f3d9e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{4}" :db/id 17592186348807} {:answer/id #uuid "4acd7113-2239-595d-9214-c7d08e0c617c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{17}{5}" :db/id 17592186349130}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348807} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9bcc58f-cf39-5a29-98cc-d059c827153d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350997}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "80f565d3-72fd-5b66-9620-41422767e4db" :question/math-academy-id "q-81320" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,dx\,dy.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{{y}^{3}}dx]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}[x]_{1}^{{y}^{3}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}({y}^{3}-1)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(y-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(y-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})\,dy & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{y}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(8+\frac{1}{4})-(\frac{1}{2}+1) \\  & =\frac{27}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351294 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "459cf9f3-fcf5-5525-b868-19e4cb73db91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{32}{15}" :db/id 17592186349081} {:answer/id #uuid "686bf042-9c4a-576c-9cf9-63394d84810d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{5}" :db/id 17592186349407} {:answer/id #uuid "6ec91b61-533c-5e77-8551-51ae48166546" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{32}{15}" :db/id 17592186349463} {:answer/id #uuid "79a8120b-b105-5a41-8d2b-ef56cd255962" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{16}{5}" :db/id 17592186349568} {:answer/id #uuid "bb52c336-ef0e-58b1-891f-33e5ebb71ca7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186350112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349463} :answer-field/id #uuid "6fdf6e49-b247-581f-8fa7-0908217951a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350898}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2de4beff-bfff-5979-9819-12dd21169f8d" :question/math-academy-id "q-81353" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-x}^{3x}\sqrt{x+y}\,dy\,dx=
$$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-x}^{3x}\sqrt{x+y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-x}^{3x}\sqrt{x+y}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{2}{3}(x+y)^{3/2}]}_{-x}^{3x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{2}{3}(x+3x)^{3/2}-\frac{2}{3}(x-x)^{3/2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}(4x)^{3/2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{16}{3}{x}^{3/2}\,dx \\  & =\frac{16}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3/2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{16}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3/2}\,dx & =\frac{16}{3}{[\frac{2}{5}{x}^{5/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}(\frac{2}{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351295 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6ba8975f-1dcf-5982-82b5-4619f25392af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186349440} {:answer/id #uuid "909c8869-f444-52b1-8e81-f3f7d8cd7ea7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186349746} {:answer/id #uuid "9cd6c44c-c13b-51de-a23a-1e56014ae0e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{81}{2}" :db/id 17592186349844} {:answer/id #uuid "a3dbc989-fd06-546f-a58e-5a71b4609f5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "19" :db/id 17592186349910} {:answer/id #uuid "d230d5cd-76aa-5b60-afae-1d4ccdb5bb52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{41}{2}" :db/id 17592186350291}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349844} :answer-field/id #uuid "cef03a78-3898-53d7-a31f-076237c237e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351068}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bba1a6f7-479e-5c7c-a4a7-2bc8097d537b" :question/math-academy-id "q-81361" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA,\,
$$
where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{e}^{y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x{[{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}-{e}^{0})dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x(x-1)dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx & ={[{x}^{3}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(64-24)-(1-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =40+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351296 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a7ddc79-cbfd-59b5-9638-d178b71104a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e" :db/id 17592186348536} {:answer/id #uuid "4b79160f-37ab-5192-8514-437d9b279188" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186349138} {:answer/id #uuid "544819eb-b6d1-5a40-bb3a-d34d78eef696" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{2}" :db/id 17592186349218} {:answer/id #uuid "a06fce6a-f06f-595a-9863-76102c8d8305" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186349871} {:answer/id #uuid "f06aa1a1-4329-543e-8ec1-01bf70f9f867" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186350550}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349871} :answer-field/id #uuid "08077c01-ccff-5e05-a424-ef1243bb7696" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350720}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b8f9d362-d296-527d-b3eb-8711496d6537" :question/math-academy-id "q-81367" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral
$$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA,
$$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines
$x=e,$ $y=e$ and the curve $y={e}^{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/aa/aa635ca5ef3198fea56d684b034de476a72e4ace2a4c51b37c6c59977036eb76.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=e$ intercepts the curve $y={e}^{x}$ at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$1\le x\le e.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/b7/b78021a06c9fea100b75c66a619c425345cda3666d84da018895be15a53af06d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le e,\,e\le y\le {e}^{x}\}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}[{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{y\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)]}_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx & ={[\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡x}{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡e}{2}-\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351305 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d87a379-101b-5044-a9cf-203aed1b7e63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186348705} {:answer/id #uuid "a21692a1-8c6c-5432-be24-63a9c726b966" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186349892} {:answer/id #uuid "ced492d5-0a6a-537c-9c30-9a615a606cb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186350263} {:answer/id #uuid "e0000c97-8188-5a05-9aab-54e12e3e1983" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186350412} {:answer/id #uuid "eec46d31-f46d-57c5-812e-af32b178cd7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186350535}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348705} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a03f15d-4ffa-5e5c-9200-f6e35eacce93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350944}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "90525ec7-d18b-5266-b954-a33a5311f7df" :question/math-academy-id "q-81395" :question/problem "![](images/ff/ff3b9f52ed01d991d1fff18e78c494488b53703669b6bb326b5436a19c952a18.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}x\,dA,\,
$$
where $D$ is the region enclosed between the curves $3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ and ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ as shown in the picture." :question/worked-solution "Notice that $D$ is a type II region. Since $x\ge 0,$ we obtain the following equations in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9 & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}} \\ 3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9 & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{3-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}} & =\sqrt{3-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}} \\ 9-{y}^{2} & =3-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{y}^{2} & =6 \\ {y}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line the $x$-axis, the $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le 3.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](images/91/91f377562a1e94218b7be886cd63638e8881b0c4fac231a810bb6bff3a1fe643.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\sqrt{3-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}}\le x\le \sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}x\,dA={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{3-{y}^{2}/3}}^{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}x\,dx\,dy
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{3-{y}^{2}/3}}^{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}x\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{\sqrt{3-{y}^{2}/3}}^{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}x\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{\sqrt{3-{y}^{2}/3}}^{\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}(9-{y}^{2}-(3-\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}))\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}(6-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}(6-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2})\,dy & =\frac{1}{2}{[6y-\frac{2}{9}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(18-6-0) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351313 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23dce36f-61ba-5015-8efe-10f5e58c37e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186348754} {:answer/id #uuid "33cc441d-205f-5f43-93b6-2ecef88de694" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186348911} {:answer/id #uuid "36156b9a-2d25-558c-9ab8-4629169c5f62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186348933} {:answer/id #uuid "e060bf48-f76f-5437-8da3-75acd9dc4f37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186350416} {:answer/id #uuid "fecdefff-5446-5487-8fea-206fa2f01600" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186350689}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350416} :answer-field/id #uuid "93100b95-ae42-53dc-b4eb-19f8569529d0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350958}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "62741b76-bd79-5cef-9d76-2003787fe433" :question/math-academy-id "q-81506" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6}).$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=3.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=\frac{\pi }{6}?$" :question/worked-solution "The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{6}].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & =\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3+{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{6})]}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =3+([\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{6})]-[\operatorname{sin}⁡(0-\frac{\pi }{6})]) \\  & =3+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{6}\right)) \\  & =3+(0-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)) \\  & =3+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is $x=\frac{7}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186351319 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e6cd0c5-ce1f-5d3a-b6f1-3a89e0b5f754" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=n\cdot {720}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186348713} {:answer/id #uuid "4d45e2b5-e9d4-5b3f-b67e-5e26df2dceac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=n\cdot {90}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186349152} {:answer/id #uuid "51334a88-913f-55d4-8662-d179d2358561" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {45}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186349184} {:answer/id #uuid "7f7694a2-f54e-508d-b344-bd1d687a7f95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=n\cdot {180}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186349617} {:answer/id #uuid "975cdbff-46b0-5f28-8af3-9f16bb6d6b9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {720}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186349805}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348713} :answer-field/id #uuid "d2edbed1-c9c4-5765-85ec-f61c946b0343" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351073}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "64a8f363-4b61-59a9-9418-863b08cb8a8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-81523" :question/problem "Which expression gives all of the zeros of $y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4}+{90}^{∘})?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer." :question/worked-solution "First, let's start by defining a new variable $X$ as

$$
X=\frac{x}{4}+{90}^{∘}.
$$

So, we need to calculate the zeros of 

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡X.
$$

The zeros of this function are given by the following expression:

$$
X={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the zeros of our original function, we rewrite $X$ in terms of the original variable $x$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$

Assume that $n$ is an integer." :question/worked-solution "First, let's start by defining a new variable $X$ as

$$
X=4x+\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

So, we need to calculate $X$-values at the maxima of

$$

The $X$-values at the maxima are given by the following expression:

$$

$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the $x$-values at the maxima of our original function, we rewrite $X$ in terms of the original variable $x$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi  \\ 4x+\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi  \\ 4x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{16}+n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}

$$ Which expression gives all of the values of $x$ at which $f(x)$ attains its minimum value? Assume that $n$ is an integer." :question/worked-solution "First, let's start by defining a new variable $X$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+\frac{{f}^{⁗}(a)}{4!}(x-a)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{(4)}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\begin{aligned}v\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =3-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =3-2\cdot (-1) \\  & =5\,\text{ft}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $5\,\text{ft}/\text{s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186351357 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19bc219a-35b4-506a-8788-1ce7920044b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)=12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y}+C" :db/id 17592186348662} {:answer/id #uuid "697a9c9c-4964-5cc5-b1e1-e9e4ce855bc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)=3{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{y}+C" :db/id 17592186349423} {:answer/id #uuid "b9d3d365-e63f-5485-9f7c-bb976d8dbf45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)=12{x}^{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}-\frac{x}{y}+C" :db/id 17592186350095} {:answer/id #uuid "dfcbf686-54eb-5d98-ad26-4a8fcc350136" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)=3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+\frac{1}{y}+C" :db/id 17592186350408} {:answer/id #uuid "e346b178-9934-5d6b-b8a5-f42de5668c87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)=12{x}^{3}y-\frac{x}{y}+C" :db/id 17592186350445}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350408} :answer-field/id #uuid "a2cd2466-47dd-5469-8369-868df3afb4d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350984}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8cb4b31d-3aca-59fb-b7c0-b708932a190d" :question/math-academy-id "q-81737" :question/problem "Find $f(x,y)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ where $$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\left(\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}\right)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ g(y) & =\frac{1}{y}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=\frac{1}{y}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+\frac{1}{y}+C.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351361 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d3d344f4-8ed3-593a-aed4-5228049f941e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438616} {:answer/id #uuid "b51feba4-149e-552b-ba57-a034975c6254" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438617}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438617} :answer-field/id #uuid "f0efaccc-6c1e-515a-a6b3-27b5fea347ab" :answer-field/key "$F=xy\,i+(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439337} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fceaa12c-f1cb-5a20-a916-433cb5161bb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438618} {:answer/id #uuid "fdca841c-e44f-5760-937f-556b1d7dbb00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438619}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438618} :answer-field/id #uuid "75fbead4-be61-5190-81c8-ff7df1836c09" :answer-field/key "$G=(4x+{y}^{2})\,i-4x{y}^{2}\,j$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439338} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "42ce1c69-5a9a-5668-a6d1-ef1043e559b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186438620} {:answer/id #uuid "1cc59867-4b98-5161-bf03-738307481109" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186438621}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186438620} :answer-field/id #uuid "521321bd-40ca-5972-9cfb-572b598d4cdd" :answer-field/key "$H=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,j$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186439339}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7be69df3-7414-5358-b771-962bb47016d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-81746" :question/problem "Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields.  

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=xy$ and $Q=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=4x+{y}^{2}$ and $Q=-4x{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-4{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $G$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$ and $Q=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $H$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F=xy\,i+(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j$ only."} {:db/id 17592186351369 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "125b9147-6355-50f2-ba8c-748686fc87f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186348607} {:answer/id #uuid "6df205c3-6135-5d2b-b3fd-a8bcf211e047" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186349456} {:answer/id #uuid "8a2bfe7d-c973-5e74-8dfd-79e2236afc46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186349700} {:answer/id #uuid "90178deb-05ed-554a-b6da-bcd3010a2bf1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186349741} {:answer/id #uuid "f59a2f53-d71c-5744-ba75-d029ceccffcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186350594}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350594} :answer-field/id #uuid "c92c3f4e-98f4-5231-9b54-c6264a5301cf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351057}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "adc09746-e915-53ae-9b39-14d8d6a2a18e" :question/math-academy-id "q-81774" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}x\,dA,\,
$$
where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le {x}^{2}+1\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le {x}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[y]_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(1-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351370 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3bbdf4f1-67f9-5d2a-bf83-eb8d28b28a47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{7}" :db/id 17592186348986} {:answer/id #uuid "573657d5-697b-5eba-898d-46073aab023e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{15}" :db/id 17592186349248} {:answer/id #uuid "7c47bd07-3fce-51b3-a645-67a2c66e05fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186349588} {:answer/id #uuid "d52b4cbf-899a-54c0-9363-592dcf222fc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186350317} {:answer/id #uuid "ebba4e4d-3512-52c9-8f1e-c437d4291d5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186350505}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349248} :answer-field/id #uuid "6f29377f-f8a7-5e8e-ae20-7f215e0b9245" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350895}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d7ea77d5-2143-55d3-8743-b4a1643dda58" :question/math-academy-id "q-81776" :question/problem "![](images/6a/6accbfcccdf910acca3aab9f1a12d0ab35c4da683fe78d6ca2d7ada88f28767c.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,dA,
$$
where $D$ is the finite region above the $x$-axis enclosed by the curve $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and the line $x=0.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the curve with the line $y=0.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/db/db0dd47348fb2f9a97c9e0514f74adae05830de7e03f1aea2886eaa95701200e.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}
$$

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[y]_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(1-{x}^{2}-0)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\,dx & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351371 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23b5c7c3-c26e-582d-bb2e-8f042816f6a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186348753} {:answer/id #uuid "42d940c0-05b6-554b-bc8c-35dfa257887d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186349052} {:answer/id #uuid "84a7742a-fffe-5f11-907a-8c766b4d7f0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186349657} {:answer/id #uuid "b908f026-083b-5f77-bf2f-152d5cac9615" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186350085} {:answer/id #uuid "cb714fbc-b873-50d4-b078-4528eaedae9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{3}" :db/id 17592186350236}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349657} :answer-field/id #uuid "793a0df5-dacd-550d-b9d0-996f94f43180" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350916}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3119c509-e446-518c-94fc-dda5b6ec1994" :question/math-academy-id "q-81778" :question/problem "![](images/78/786dd06154d1bda5483ed992dce8922c9629f759b498a3f713c35612311c1ee6.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA,
$$
where $D$ is the finite region below the line $y=2$ enclosed by the lines $y=x$ and $x=0.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the line $y=x$ with the line $y=2.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/92/92b1eda4ccf9e62e1f7310b1ba9bef5cc6c434755e74196d1829a30f2c4a3c53.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2\}
$$

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,dx & ={[\frac{8x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{12}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-\frac{4}{3}-0 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351382 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a14671a-8217-5f47-b97a-df09b3468a65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}+2x+36=0" :db/id 17592186348532} {:answer/id #uuid "0d403a57-1fff-53c8-9104-23dd37892e1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}+6=0" :db/id 17592186348561} {:answer/id #uuid "0f7803d1-2e02-5852-80f6-d8b9f8cd9b92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}+x-6=0" :db/id 17592186348583} {:answer/id #uuid "25b1a803-7e57-56a4-91f6-762db9f82e2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}+36=0" :db/id 17592186348771} {:answer/id #uuid "7c85c232-c965-5a98-87a6-388a20393c41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}-36=0" :db/id 17592186349590}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348771} :answer-field/id #uuid "c2800f31-30ff-5ba1-86c6-e76a0a8718e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351046}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "620a6533-87d2-5c52-b06c-bca99f3a99df" :question/math-academy-id "q-8186" :question/problem "A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-\,\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $5,$ find the equation." :question/worked-solution "Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=-\,\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}})(x+\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{\left(\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}}\right)}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{36}{5}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{36}{5} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $5.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5({x}^{2}+\frac{36}{5}) & =0 \\ 5{x}^{2}+36 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351404 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0651159c-ebe0-5b0d-bd84-9e495f369370" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186348503} {:answer/id #uuid "80249071-56e9-52e0-acf3-620988a4071e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186349620} {:answer/id #uuid "ab90514b-ed10-50fc-8f70-df74f47dfb2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186349967} {:answer/id #uuid "c92e6bf9-60d7-5d7f-b3f3-81bbe0074f86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186350217} {:answer/id #uuid "df686207-2055-5b87-a6b5-ed7d15522a09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186350402}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350217} :answer-field/id #uuid "e01bf0ce-6049-5af3-b9b1-9a170659c91e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351098}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d3abb825-5e1f-5f44-b3d6-edf93dd36e5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-82223" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle {∬}_{|x-1|+|y|\le 1}\,\,6(x+y)\,dA=
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a sketch of our region.

![](images/c9/c9072d2b8f1b49770403280af13d3d8e681247f168e796c056eb697fe28b8ba9.png)

  

The  region $D={(x,y)|\,\,|x-1|+|y|\le 1}$ can be  partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/d1/d16296029378c7adb891affba63683971ff972b5ed0268641ac3b677c694b5f8.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2-y}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le y\le 0,\,-y\le x\le y+2}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{|x-1|+|y|\le 1}6(x+y)^{2}\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}6(x+y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}6(x+y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-y}6(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-y}^{y+2}6(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[3(x+y)^{2}]_{y}^{2-y}\text{d}y+{\int }_{-1}^{0}[3(x+y)^{2}]_{-y}^{y+2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(4-4{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{-1}^{0}3(2y+2)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3{[4y-\frac{4{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1}+4{[(y+1)^{3}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =8+4 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 1}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary is

$$
y={x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{y}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/0b/0bed4692a7a6851ef2b66cb3842ebac6b2ef7ef4ff30bed41e84b7cb71c4f5c0.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{3})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{3})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{3})[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{3})}{4}[{x}^{4}]_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{3})]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)).\end{aligned}

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 8,\,\sqrt[3]{y}\le x\le 2\}.

$$

$$

and the bottom boundary is

$$

$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. Its type I representation is

$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/05/05ec37a8f4fd33c05a2438df5c5fbc697f8b560fde0b9fe73922a0db56a09c2c.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{8}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{4}}[{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{4}}[y]_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}\,{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{4}{e}^{{x}^{4}}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({e}^{16}-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351414 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a938191-8b3e-56f4-8081-1b075590a46d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\sqrt{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186348537} {:answer/id #uuid "6372be94-fc66-5e25-833f-cd89953352e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186349357} {:answer/id #uuid "72422885-4513-5417-8d3b-281b44c8f96d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186349498} {:answer/id #uuid "e17059d3-0090-564d-b35e-0ba90c89cdec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186350426} {:answer/id #uuid "e74331bb-7eb9-5a3e-aa55-42f1700dca23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\sqrt{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186350470}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350426} :answer-field/id #uuid "be2b944c-41ea-501f-b2aa-bc5f7a5ea041" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351038}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "86817391-743e-56b5-bd59-9c333eb5f19a" :question/math-academy-id "q-82336" :question/problem "The position vector $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

To find the acceleration at time $t=0,$ we substitute $t=0$ into the above:

The region $D$ is enclosed by the the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=|x|,$ as shown in the picture. Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}2x\,dA.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](images/2f/2fcb30778db2f051a7a819ae701808af59ac18d27c25a9c57ce678caa6c3ee3b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le -x\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x\}.
$$

 

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2x\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2x\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2x\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2x[-x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2x[x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(-2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{-1}^{0}+{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =((0-(-\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{4}))+((\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{4})-0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the sum rule and write our repeated integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z+{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

Since the domain of integration $R=[0,1]\times [0,2]\times [-1,1]$ is a rectangular box, and each integrand can be expressed as $f(x)\cdot g(y)\cdot h(z),$ we can rewrite our sum of repeated integrals as follows:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}z\,+\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}z
$$

Let's evaluate each of these separately:

- For the first product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}z & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot (2-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}z & =(1-0)\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =1\cdot \frac{8}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{16}{3}=\frac{20}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351461 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8c16586d-cc25-53cc-9362-6437b79c060a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|-\frac{4}{x+2}+\frac{2}{(x+2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186349714} {:answer/id #uuid "998be8ec-a9f8-5319-9eef-2aae1574b0de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x+2}+\frac{2}{(x+2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186349821} {:answer/id #uuid "adea4ada-7cc7-5da3-98b6-914d4acd1442" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\frac{2}{(x+2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186349984} {:answer/id #uuid "bef94dca-73fa-5d10-89d2-be9a6b332a16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|-\frac{1}{x+2}+\frac{2}{(x+2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186350141} {:answer/id #uuid "f5a58b23-169d-5e0d-b12a-3d71909e57c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|-\frac{4}{x+2}+K" :db/id 17592186350596}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349984} :answer-field/id #uuid "21898db2-5323-5985-8c96-07b477ebe19f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350768}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e554a089-5768-5395-81cb-0926b256840b" :question/math-academy-id "q-82894" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{(x+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{(x+2)^{3}}=\frac{A}{x+2}+\frac{B}{(x+2)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x+2)^{3}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+2)^{3}$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}+4x=A(x+2)^{2}+B(x+2)+C.
$$

Plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)^{2}+4(-2) & =A(-2+2)^{2}+B(-2+2)+C \\ -4 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2}+4(0) & =A(0+2)^{2}+B(0+2)+C \\ 0 & =4A+2B-4 \\ 2A+B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=-1$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{2}+4(-1) & =A(-1+2)^{2}+B(-1+2)+C \\ -3 & =A+B-4 \\ A+B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the equations $2A+B=2$ and $A+B=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2-1 \\ A & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting back into $A+B=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+B & =1 \\ B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{(x+2)^{3}}=\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{4}{(x+2)^{3}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{(x+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{4}{(x+2)^{3}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{4}{(x+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\frac{2}{(x+2)^{2}}+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant."} {:db/id 17592186351462 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1c4446c1-f2a3-525f-9123-dceb2419d6ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|-\frac{1}{x-2}+K" :db/id 17592186348691} {:answer/id #uuid "857e90e6-8a4c-5a40-91e1-23ea6b1779f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186349664} {:answer/id #uuid "da4bacf6-d4df-5a38-86af-4279df6ecb63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{x-2}-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186350362} {:answer/id #uuid "eb768012-9e91-5e35-96b0-49c43ad32bc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186350501} {:answer/id #uuid "ef264592-2ad4-5048-82cf-b89309361a14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|-\frac{1}{x-2}-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+K" :db/id 17592186350541}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350541} :answer-field/id #uuid "8d74949b-6468-57bc-bf6a-67536d2dd796" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350946}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "585e985a-767c-5259-99e8-0c60ba5df1b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-82895" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{(x-2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{(x-2)^{3}}=\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x-2)^{3}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-2)^{3}$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}-3x+3=A(x-2)^{2}+B(x-2)+C.
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)^{2}-3(2)+3 & =A(2-2)^{2}+B(2-2)+C \\ 1 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=1$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{2}-3(1)+3 & =A(1-2)^{2}+B(1-2)+C \\ 1 & =A-B+1 \\ A-B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=3$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3)^{2}-3(3)+3 & =A(3-2)^{2}+B(3-2)+C \\ 3 & =A+B+1 \\ A+B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations $A-B=0$ and $A+B=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =0+2 \\ 2A & =2 \\ A & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

 
and substituting back into $A-B=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1-B & =0 \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{(x-2)^{3}}=\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{(x-2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|-\frac{1}{x-2}-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+K,\end{aligned}
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal." :question/worked-solution "Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 1+1\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot 2+1\cdot (-1)+(-3)\cdot (-2)+1\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\left(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -4 \\ -8 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -3 \\ -7 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}=\hat{x}.\end{aligned}

\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $$
\displaystyle I=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I) \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2\pi }}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-\frac{{e}^{2(0)}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{2{e}^{2\pi }}{5}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}({e}^{2\pi }+1)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351477 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "45574f83-e9b0-571e-9177-3e8f29da4762" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}({e}^{3\pi }-1)" :db/id 17592186349078} {:answer/id #uuid "749d9a5a-b627-5ced-afbb-1b2d484b769e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}(3{e}^{3\pi }+1)" :db/id 17592186349518} {:answer/id #uuid "8619e840-beaa-50f3-85de-a2da120d8673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{10}({e}^{3\pi }+1)" :db/id 17592186349670} {:answer/id #uuid "9c158255-35fc-589c-9c34-ad69454a0bd0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{3\pi }-10" :db/id 17592186349838} {:answer/id #uuid "bdb35a76-9436-5097-9167-f370b974f37a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{e}^{3\pi }+1" :db/id 17592186350133}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349670} :answer-field/id #uuid "c4590fb3-0490-57c1-ab15-66cd749766c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351047}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "82defc42-da2f-5d1e-93f8-b4bb11e56282" :question/math-academy-id "q-83013" :question/problem "Evaluate $$

\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3J.\end{aligned}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3I.\end{aligned}

$$"} {:db/id 17592186351478 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23815347-d93f-58ba-b1c7-e3ed64d48844" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{10}({e}^{-\pi /3}+1)" :db/id 17592186348752} {:answer/id #uuid "4d7073ff-ed85-58f2-b155-46bd8775ace3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}({e}^{-\pi /3}+3)" :db/id 17592186349153} {:answer/id #uuid "8588b43f-4e08-5267-af90-836fa5f9e2b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{-\pi /3}+10" :db/id 17592186349666} {:answer/id #uuid "92fc068b-a45e-5637-a0e8-f2f88ee3ad76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{-\pi /3}-5" :db/id 17592186349758} {:answer/id #uuid "a76c1c18-aaf5-5760-be34-52e784dcaf6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}({e}^{-\pi /3}-1)" :db/id 17592186349937}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348752} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6af00b3-29da-55ac-a3ba-02da31bf42c0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350990}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "742e2e60-8650-5364-af0a-ff31062d8fcb" :question/math-academy-id "q-83014" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $$
\displaystyle I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)-\int \left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}\right)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}(\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\left(-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}\right){|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}))}{10}+\frac{{e}^{-0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0))}{10} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{-\pi /3}}{10}+\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}({e}^{-\pi /3}+1)\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2}=2{x}^{1/2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C \\ {y}^{3/2} & =3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2})}^{2/3} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+K)}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\frac{3C}{2}.$

Use this family on a connected interval where $3\sqrt{x}+K>0$. This condition preserves the positive square-root branch used before raising both sides to a power. $$
\frac{{x}^{2}+x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}=\frac{Ax+1}{{x}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{x-1},
$$

where $A$ is a constant to be found, calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{x}^{2}+x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the constant $A.$ Multiplying both sides of the given equality by $({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+3 & =(Ax+1)(x-1)+{x}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2$  into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2}+2+3 & =(A(2)+1)(2-1)+{2}^{2}+4 \\ 9 & =2A+1+8 \\ 9 & =2A+9 \\ A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{0x+1}{{x}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the fact that $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right),
$$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351487 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3e2299b9-bba1-5ac4-a81a-757c178c81b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}-\frac{1}{60}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯" :db/id 17592186349012} {:answer/id #uuid "78b853f4-18f6-5ee1-a3dd-563cddb837e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{18}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}-\frac{1}{240}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯" :db/id 17592186349562} {:answer/id #uuid "88535081-3090-5fcd-a7a6-c126efd784d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{12}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}-\frac{1}{240}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯" :db/id 17592186349687} {:answer/id #uuid "997233b1-72e6-57b1-a513-ea0436ea1e25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{9}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}-\frac{1}{27}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯" :db/id 17592186349820} {:answer/id #uuid "f7cbf4aa-a5ef-5829-9721-0f1fd67cad81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{6}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}-\frac{1}{120}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯" :db/id 17592186350618}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350618} :answer-field/id #uuid "d662b76f-600e-5ce0-89ea-ae55894c30e7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351079}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5f218cc7-60a5-53f7-bb6e-74dc39f98842" :question/math-academy-id "q-83187" :question/problem "Find the first three non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ centered about the point $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{(4)}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0 \\ {f}^{(5)}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{(5)}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0+(-1)(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{0}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2} \\  & +\frac{1}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{0}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}+\frac{(-1)}{5!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯ \\  & =-(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{6}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}-\frac{1}{120}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351490 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c3ce7f6-052a-53dc-ab90-78b1c368b3be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-x+2)+K" :db/id 17592186348552} {:answer/id #uuid "37e450ff-a2ee-5816-98e2-7f6b60feb761" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-x+2}+K" :db/id 17592186348950} {:answer/id #uuid "7944aef5-1b48-5eaa-8786-1f16c8f0df33" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-x+2)+K" :db/id 17592186349565} {:answer/id #uuid "c52c4abb-407b-54b1-b666-8b9885971332" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-x+2)+K" :db/id 17592186350187} {:answer/id #uuid "f3fb68cd-a58a-58e8-bb4b-1b5d1cec1ee8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}-x+2}+K" :db/id 17592186350584}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349565} :answer-field/id #uuid "948ac1d5-6ed0-51e5-8f96-8969c582b9e2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350961}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "dc91504d-2e13-5e38-b0d6-dba8bbe089a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-83230" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{4{x}^{2}-3x+4}{x({x}^{2}-x+2)}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a negative discriminant:

$$
D=(-1)^{2}-4(1)(2)=-7<0
$$

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}-3x+4}{x({x}^{2}-x+2)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}-x+2}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $x({x}^{2}-x+2),$ and we get

$$
4{x}^{2}-3x+4=A({x}^{2}-x+2)+(Bx+C)x.
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=2,$ and $C=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}-3x+4}{x({x}^{2}-x+2)}=\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}-x+2}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4{x}^{2}-3x+4}{x({x}^{2}-x+2)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}-x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}-x+2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|.
$$

For the second integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}-x+2.$ Then $\text{d}u=(2x-1)\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}-x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{1}{u}\right)\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-x+2| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}-3x+4}{x({x}^{2}-x+2)}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}-x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-x+2)+K\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351497 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "146d90b3-5c9d-5707-a406-0a9382d46855" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-4x-3|+K" :db/id 17592186348621} {:answer/id #uuid "281a60ee-7789-534b-95a2-91d514a22a70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+\frac{1}{2({x}^{2}-4x-3)}+K" :db/id 17592186348793} {:answer/id #uuid "32e9fad0-e594-54e4-aa9b-28a2b1a366f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x+3}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-4x-3|+K" :db/id 17592186348901} {:answer/id #uuid "d38e1ec9-6e77-5bcf-910d-a08c7d3657c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-4x-3|+K" :db/id 17592186350305} {:answer/id #uuid "ec5dfce4-5487-5c82-997c-f390363c48e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{x+3}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-4x-3|+K" :db/id 17592186350510}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350305} :answer-field/id #uuid "62a82bb8-91d2-5271-9a80-81d19c7f9b98" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350871}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7e6be0c4-0435-506d-8ce1-14ee1c45fe6c" :question/math-academy-id "q-83367" :question/problem "$$
