$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,8)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(2,8)+∇f(2,8)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,8)=8.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{xy}}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(2,8)=\frac{8}{\sqrt{2\cdot 8}}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{xy}} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(2,8)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\cdot 8}}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,8)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,8) & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(2,8)+∇\,f(2,8)\cdot ⟨x-2,\,y-8⟩ \\  & =8+⟨2,\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,\,y-8⟩ \\  & =8+2(x-2)+\frac{1}{2}(y-8) \\  & =2x+\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362307 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bfef024-1b6c-555f-8a26-33bf987ce229" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186360947} {:answer/id #uuid "5b8d1fdb-1e8d-5f02-9ea7-c3c298ae432f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{4}" :db/id 17592186361248} {:answer/id #uuid "af862e42-0cba-5667-86e1-bcba2137990c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186361614} {:answer/id #uuid "c253a7fe-6f5f-512c-aff1-bf5aa8dd058e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186361708} {:answer/id #uuid "ed37a445-de09-58c0-b587-33b13984c10f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186361889}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360947} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf9e95f8-2048-5fb9-b5b3-a7a136bdb4eb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362172}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "61a53a3d-9f1a-5b06-bcde-4575632a0617" :question/math-academy-id "q-98665" :question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{\cos }^{3}⁡t,{\sin }^{3}⁡t⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ and $‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\cos }^{3}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\sin }^{3}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{\cos }^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3{\sin }^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =⟨-3{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,3{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right),3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-1,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖ & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{\cos }^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{\sin }^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{\sin }^{2}⁡t-3{\cos }^{3}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{\cos }^{2}⁡t-3{\sin }^{3}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-3{\cos }^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-3{\sin }^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨6\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right){\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}-3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{3},6\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right){\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}-3{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ and ${r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\times {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =\left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩\times \left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & ={\left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)}^{2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \,-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}\,-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{8}\cdot 2\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{4}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\times {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖ & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\times {r}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)‖}=\frac{{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{3}}{\,\frac{9}{4}\,}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362308 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6322d2b9-0dbb-585f-957a-9fa0c4bee467" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2\pi }" :db/id 17592186361283} {:answer/id #uuid "854b0a9d-582d-5023-88c3-48df26e8d38e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{\pi }" :db/id 17592186361432} {:answer/id #uuid "93be4c00-a297-5b56-8159-07ed88841f05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\pi }" :db/id 17592186361493} {:answer/id #uuid "a1dbe3b4-d1e5-5d40-8555-88b3f0839ea7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{\pi }" :db/id 17592186361559} {:answer/id #uuid "b3a9ede2-c544-5b6a-a210-e0ddfc93f1e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2\pi }" :db/id 17592186361635}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361432} :answer-field/id #uuid "eefd2a88-5ea0-541a-90a0-81a3376a3da9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a52b4e8f-8a80-5361-a7aa-97f65400f662" :question/math-academy-id "q-98668" :question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\pi $ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t),$ we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ),\,{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{\pi },\,-{e}^{\pi }⟩ \\  & ={e}^{\pi }⟨-1,\,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & ={e}^{\pi }\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t))⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-2{e}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,2{e}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & ={e}^{\pi }⟨0,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & ={e}^{\pi }⟨-1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times {e}^{\pi }⟨0,\,-2,\,0⟩ \\  & ={({e}^{\pi })}^{2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ \,0 & -2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{2\pi }\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ \,0 & -2\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =2{e}^{2\pi }\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2{e}^{2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}=\frac{{(\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\pi })}^{3}}{\,2{e}^{2\pi }\,}=\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362311 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00bbaa91-9d31-5875-9261-e253520000fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=-2" :db/id 17592186360832} {:answer/id #uuid "396b3a78-1982-5c1f-85b2-74a967c1969d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=-1" :db/id 17592186361097} {:answer/id #uuid "4ed27a06-c6ac-539f-8162-be16b0283151" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=-3" :db/id 17592186361182} {:answer/id #uuid "ec94ac4a-711a-5da9-bb53-7e3d650234c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solutions" :db/id 17592186361887} {:answer/id #uuid "f3a49ab8-cea0-59f7-95ab-694ceae5725a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=2" :db/id 17592186361926}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361887} :answer-field/id #uuid "ed7e11bc-5c03-5f5e-8796-5952fcf17931" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362192}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "657ec21d-728e-5f9c-8336-09507044d024" :question/math-academy-id "q-98697" :question/problem "Solve the equation $$
\displaystyle \frac{4}{x-2}-\frac{6}{x(x-2)}=\frac{3}{x}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(4x-2,\,x(x-2),\,x)=x(x-2).
$$

- The values $x=2$ and $x=0$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{x-2}-\frac{6}{x(x-2)} & =\frac{3}{x} \\ x(x-2)\cdot (\frac{4}{x-2}-\frac{6}{x(x-2)}) & =x(x-2)\cdot \frac{3}{x} \\ \frac{4x(x-2)}{x-2}-\frac{6x(x-2)}{x(x-2)} & =\frac{3x(x-2)}{x} \\ \frac{4x\cancel{(x-2)}}{\cancel{x-2}}-\frac{6\cdot \cancel{x(x-2)}}{\cancel{x(x-2)}} & =\frac{3\cdot \cancel{x}(x-2)}{\cancel{x}} \\ 4x-6 & =3(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $x,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-6 & =3(x-2) \\ 4x-6 & =3x-6 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

However, since $x=0$ is not a valid solution, our equation has no solutions."} {:db/id 17592186362312 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17043857-3227-572b-b4b7-6ed400421ab4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "w=-1" :db/id 17592186360933} {:answer/id #uuid "35f1c23e-4f90-5bc5-a18f-a8492ea035e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "w=-3" :db/id 17592186361079} {:answer/id #uuid "74d18717-fb29-5681-a346-e6ed7697370a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solutions" :db/id 17592186361351} {:answer/id #uuid "8ec7f463-3427-592f-90f0-c6c4b74d7bc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "w=1" :db/id 17592186361471} {:answer/id #uuid "f3bae244-6b93-50b4-a686-78c3894fb2f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "w=0" :db/id 17592186361927}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361351} :answer-field/id #uuid "a54d9c25-2457-5ba9-aa66-2f2a91622cdc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362136}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "305f4a20-a5d5-5769-aa7d-36e413111285" :question/math-academy-id "q-98699" :question/problem "Solve the equation $$

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(4)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(4)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\sqrt{t-3}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{t-3}},1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(4) & =⟨2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(4)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{t-3}}\right),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{(t-3)^{3}}},0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(4) & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(4)$ and ${r}^{″}(4)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(4)\times {r}^{″}(4) & =⟨2,1,0⟩\times ⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(4)\times {r}^{″}(4)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, the radius of the osculating circle at  $t=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(4) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(4){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(4)\times {r}^{″}(4)‖}=\frac{(\sqrt{5})^{3}}{\,1\,}=5\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362320 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "118da805-8d4d-5712-a36c-cd77c1c5bcc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=1" :db/id 17592186360902} {:answer/id #uuid "221ed9dd-6363-58f5-a13f-28ea35802178" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=-3" :db/id 17592186360987} {:answer/id #uuid "2b8d4542-dea0-5420-b58c-12dbab7429c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solutions" :db/id 17592186361030} {:answer/id #uuid "3432d0b7-a400-5e44-af3e-694272f1758a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=2" :db/id 17592186361067} {:answer/id #uuid "7608caaa-0a67-5ff3-8a2a-4143e6b8492c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=3" :db/id 17592186361359}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361030} :answer-field/id #uuid "ca620ff8-9a8a-5856-bc6f-86f00cb0ed6b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362168}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c2197596-2744-5571-ba37-b2f03d9b6d9e" :question/math-academy-id "q-98716" :question/problem "Solve the equation $$

\displaystyle \frac{2}{N+1}-\frac{1}{{N}^{2}+N}=\frac{1}{N}.

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-1 &=2\lambda x \\ -1 &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y &=-\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1$ and solve for $\lambda ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4{\lambda }^{2}}+\frac{1}{4{\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{2}{4{\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \lambda  & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives

$$
x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\,y=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}),\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}).

| $\,(x,y)\,$ | $$

$$

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $$

$$ and its maximum value is $1+\sqrt{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186362339 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "075b3513-d2fc-5e9a-8ff0-2aab5db7cb27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186360862} {:answer/id #uuid "0cbd7eda-9a45-5683-9e40-626dab02003b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186360888} {:answer/id #uuid "b71306f7-0408-5b68-938c-45f1c168c526" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-40\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186361654} {:answer/id #uuid "cff3bb4a-f1d0-5588-993c-52723759352e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-20\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186361766} {:answer/id #uuid "dae90de0-58c1-535a-ae69-fa7602e42e25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186361811}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360888} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e5dea45-a64a-5e4a-aa7f-b189e201e4ac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362109}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "10fa34d1-bf77-58e6-9792-74938feb848e" :question/math-academy-id "q-99039" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=4x+16y\,$ on the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "We must find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4.$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-z,-y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x &=2\lambda x \\ -z &=2\lambda y \\ -y &=2\lambda z\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(\lambda -1) &=0 \\ y(4{\lambda }^{2}-1) &=0 \\ z &=-2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- First, assume that $\lambda \ne 1$ and $\lambda \ne \pm \frac{1}{2}.$ Then, the solution of the above system is $x=y=z=0.$ But this contradicts the constraint $g(x,y,z)=1.$

- Next, assume that $\lambda =1.$ Then, by the second and third equations, we must have $y=z=0.$ Also, by the constraint $g(x,y,z)=1,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}=1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.
$$

This gives the critical point $(\pm 1,0,0).$

- Finally, assume that $\lambda =\pm \frac{1}{2}.$ Then, by the first and third equations, we must have $x=0$ and $z=∓y.$ Also, by the constraint $g(x,y,z)=1,$ we have

$$
{y}^{2}+(-y)^{2}=1\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (\sqrt{t}+t)\,\text{d}t,\int {2}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨2,\,0⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{7}{6}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=\frac{5}{6}$ and ${c}_{2}=-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$ Consequently

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector." :question/worked-solution "The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{2{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{8{e}^{4t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}},\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨1,\,-2{e}^{2t},\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(1)^{2}+{(-2{e}^{2t})}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{4{e}^{4t}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨1,-2{e}^{2t},0⟩}{\left(\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{4{e}^{4t}+1}\right)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}⟨1,\,-2{e}^{2t},\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{2t},1,0⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}⟨1,\,-2{e}^{2t},\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}\,\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2{e}^{2t} & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2{e}^{2t} & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}\left[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2{e}^{2t} & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}2{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}2{e}^{2t} & 1 \\ 1 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }\right] \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}⟨0+0,-(0-0),-4{e}^{4t}-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}⟨0,0,-(4{e}^{4t}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362388 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05c6c8cf-4f52-5e19-a6a0-f83a65ac7c9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{40}{3}" :db/id 17592186360854} {:answer/id #uuid "8b8f97b0-83e6-564c-b5dc-769853af4472" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{32}{3}" :db/id 17592186361452} {:answer/id #uuid "b973b826-6371-5d1b-9cf5-4fbc6c3551b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186361664} {:answer/id #uuid "c4634de2-da5c-55c6-aef1-e625b6a8efec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186361721} {:answer/id #uuid "f7a4b955-59cf-5672-b582-f4d572b0d22d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{64}{3}" :db/id 17592186361944}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361452} :answer-field/id #uuid "77178a41-d25c-5f86-93be-403ec472bfe7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362081}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "da377ea7-a436-56fd-bc10-dd4b8618d147" :question/math-academy-id "q-9978" :question/problem "![](images/79/79889a1366311f6175a3cc736d5cd800a19a9d843daffc824d36c0690f0e3310.png)

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5c3132dd-8104-5475-a04a-6ba3130fe419" :question/math-academy-id "q-99822" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={\sin }^{2}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=1
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{1},{f}_{2}⟩=0.$*

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨{\sin }^{2}⁡t,1⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity ${\sin }^{2}⁡\alpha =\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\alpha )}{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}]{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{2}-(0-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -0-(0-0)] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” only."} {:db/id 17592186362393 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))
$$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2t)}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)}{4}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{4})-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$

$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $$

- Statement “$S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is true. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t),$ ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ and ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is orthogonal.

"8889f645-9334-518f-83dc-7064dd4f1d1d" :question/math-academy-id "q-99848" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2},\,{f}_{3}(t)=t-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{3}
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-2,2]$ of continuous functions over $[-2,2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-2}^{2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}t\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}{|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-\left(\frac{(-2)^{4}}{4}\right) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,t-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}t\cdot (t-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}({t}^{2}-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}{t}^{5}){|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}{2}^{5}-(\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}(-2)^{5}) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is true. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t),$ ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ and ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product”; “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product”; “$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product”."} {:db/id 17592186362397 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}(t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-t){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-2-(0-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” only."} {:db/id 17592186362408 :tutorial/content "The general power series solution of the differential equation $y' - y  =0$ is

$$
y =\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.
$$

As we determined previously, the coefficients of this series satisfy the recurrence relation

$$
a_{n+1} =\dfrac{a_n }{n+1  }, \qquad n= 0,1,2, \ldots
$$

Since we are looking for the general solution of the differential equation, we can set the first term of its power series solution to an arbitrary number. So, we can set $a_0=C,$ where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Now, using the recurrence relation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{{a}_{0}}{0+1}=\frac{C}{1}, \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1+1}=\frac{C}{1\cdot 2}, \\ {a}_{3} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{2+1}=\frac{C}{1\cdot 2\cdot 3}, \\  & \,\,⋮ \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{C}{n!}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =C+\frac{C}{1}\,x+\frac{C}{1\cdot 2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{C}{1\cdot 2\cdot 3}\,{x}^{3}+⋯+\frac{C}{n!}\,{x}^{n}+⋯ \\  & =C(1+x+\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+⋯+\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}+⋯) \\  & =C({\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}).\end{aligned}
$$

Recall the definition of the standard Maclaurin series of the exponential function:

$$
e^{x} = 1+x+\frac{1}{2!}x^2+\cdots + \dfrac{x^n}{n!} + \cdots = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{x^n}{n!}
$$

So, finally, we can write the general solution of our differential equation as 

$$
y = C e^x.
$$

The solution of a differential equation is not always a recognizable standard series. But if we are able to find the recurrence relation for the coefficients, we can always present the solution as a general power series." :tutorial/id #uuid "c2e2a098-2d5c-5f2c-bcbe-81be39b99ea0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15960 :tutorial/title "Finding the Power Series Solution Using the Recurrence Relation"} {:db/id 17592186362410 :tutorial/content "Consider the volume of the solid region enclosed by the $xy$-plane, the plane $z = 4 - x - y ,$ and the planes $x=0,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ and $y=1.$

Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region.

First, the phrase **enclosed by the $xy$-plane** tells us that the bottom of the solid is
$$
z=0.
$$

The plane
$$
z = 4 - x - y
$$
is the top of the solid.

Also, the planes
$$
x = 0 ,  x = 2 ,  y = 0 ,  y = 1
$$
describe the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. So the base region is the rectangle
$$
D = \{  ( x , y ) : 0 \le  x \le  2 , \text{ } 0 \le  y \le  1 \}  .
$$

Therefore, for each point $(x,y)$ in this rectangle, the variable $z$ runs from the bottom surface to the top surface:
$$
0 \le  z \le  4 - x - y .
$$

So the volume is
$$
V = {\iiint }_{R} \text{d} V = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{4 - x - y} \text{d} z  \text{d} y  \text{d} x .
$$

Now we evaluate:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}V &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} {[ z ]}_{z = 0}^{z = 4 - x - y} \text{d} y  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} ( 4 - x - y )  \text{d} y  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {[ ( 4 - x ) y - \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} ]}_{y = 0}^{y = 1} \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} ( 4 - x - \frac{1}{2} ) \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} ( \frac{7}{2} - x ) \text{d} x \\  &  = {[ \frac{7}{2} x - \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} ]}_{0}^{2} \\  &  = 7 - 2 \\  &  = 5.\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the solid is $5.$

In problems like this, the planes involving only $x$ and $y$ usually describe the base region in the $xy$-plane, while the $xy$-plane and the surface or plane involving $z$ describe the lower and upper bounds for $z$." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca3b6881-db7f-536a-b48b-77adde0a1b19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15981 :tutorial/title "Setting Up Volume from a Verbal Description"} {:db/id 17592186362483 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8d38de0f-5de0-5773-b07e-b5d1a45f588e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186362485}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362485} :answer-field/id #uuid "08b51766-5aec-52ac-81b0-b241e0d6ebbd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362484}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8ab3a634-4399-5235-8052-11670b252c18" :question/math-academy-id "q-167886" :question/problem "The cost, in dollars, to manufacture the mesh for a cylindrical heater $r=f(\theta ,z),$ where $(\theta ,z)\in C,$ is given by

$$

$$

How much did it cost to make the mesh for the cylindrical heater?

." :question/worked-solution "We found that the surface of the heater can be described in cylindrical polar coordinates as

$$
r=3,\,(\theta ,z)\in C,
$$

where
$C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

Hence, the cost to manufacture its mesh is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A
$$

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{C}\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A.
$$

The function under the first integral is constant, so we have

$$
{∬}_{C}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(C)=2\pi \cdot 3=6\pi .
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $z.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A & =\frac{(3-0)}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }\cdot {[{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }((2\pi )^{2}-0) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $\theta .$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A & =(2\pi -0){\int }_{0}^{3}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\pi ({3}^{2}-0) \\  & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2\pi }(6\pi +6\pi +18\pi )=15.
$$

Therefore, the cost to manufacture the mesh of the cylindrical heater is $\$15.$"} {:db/id 17592186362489 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71948d5e-02be-51dc-b11c-503e671f7d19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x/3" :db/id 17592186362491}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362491} :answer-field/id #uuid "1b017a4d-e67e-5487-80c5-eb76509d584e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362490} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "307fd8a5-abeb-553b-a401-f90d8d28581a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186362493}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362493} :answer-field/id #uuid "d2a44b4a-6420-526a-8932-c62fb58e471c" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362492} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "220d31f3-2b87-5137-986e-02a43c004603" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y/3" :db/id 17592186362495}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362495} :answer-field/id #uuid "fb8df416-9cb6-541c-aa33-a5474ab16ffe" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362494}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ed75dd18-34d6-5d52-a9e6-519946daa110" :question/math-academy-id "q-167888" :question/problem "A heating element $E$ lies on the intersection of the cylindrical heater and the plane $z=2.$ Use your answer to part 4 to find an outward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}(x,y)$ to $E$ that lies within this plane. Express your answer in terms of $x$ and $y.$

*Hint: The matrix ${R}_{z}(ϕ)$ representing a counterclockwise rotation of $ϕ$ radians about the $z$-axis is given by*

$$
{R}_{z}(ϕ)=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & -\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
$\mathbf{n}(x,y)=\hspace{0.222em},$

$\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$" :question/worked-solution "We found that a parametrization of the cylinder is given by

$$
\mathbf{f}(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}\theta ,z⟩\hspace{2em}(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $\mathbf{r}(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
\mathbf{r}(\theta )=\mathbf{f}(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $\mathbf{r}(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
\mathbf{r}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf{r}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{'}(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we normalize the vector found in Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{n} & =\frac{\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}}{||\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{y}{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+0\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362496 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0368d3ef-7ff9-5da6-857d-96776c228a1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}xy" :db/id 17592186362498}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362498} :answer-field/id #uuid "47f7b160-4a23-58c9-94a1-d65bba0f866a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362497}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9d35a688-8b95-5b4b-a5d5-a0c9f931f061" :question/math-academy-id "q-167889" :question/problem "Water flows over the element $E$ according to the vector field

$\text{d}s.$" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $E$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $E$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{E}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit vector to $E.$

![](images/2c/2cd5e4c7ab86cdb999e239e986713a51c07b8decb629b1ee4a656077590f04bb.png)

In our case, we have

$$

$\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/46/4693916207540a6453c6c3775824ba577e62fea0a18b07e96f8814901d9ad80e.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x+(-2xy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\hspace{0.167em}0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, by applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2y-(-4y))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2y\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362527 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d5f60037-9e3d-54bb-a440-952c5cda1375" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-128" :db/id 17592186362529}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362529} :answer-field/id #uuid "810d80f0-caf3-5923-a0a0-ee211445f690" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362528}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "358104ea-eaad-5a15-86b6-df0552400d81" :question/math-academy-id "q-168627" :question/problem "The flux of $G$ through the duct surface is$\,$

                                        ." :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $G$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $G$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}G\cdot \,\text{d}S={∬}_{S}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $G=⟨0,0,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $G$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides.

![](images/9e/9e894018baf5f651e2d43cb48a324a5470c9061e6da10f666978519b3bff4c7f.png)

Let's consider the flux of $G$ through these two sides.

* Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}G\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-32⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =-xy-32.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $G$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot \text{d}{S}_{1} & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}(-xy-32)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(xy+32)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(xy+32)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y+32x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+64)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}+64y]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =-132.\end{aligned}
$$

* Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}G\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $G$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}G\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-132+4 \\  & =-128.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362539 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5190752e-a1c8-5dd8-b834-158e58825739" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6xy" :db/id 17592186362541}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362541} :answer-field/id #uuid "02bbd186-1d4e-5461-bc79-ce35c2890910" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362540}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "231df40f-8e86-536b-af50-43d6f14cbda6" :question/math-academy-id "q-169203" :question/problem "Use Green's theorem to write down the integral that gives the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along the border $C$ of the plot $D,$ shown in the diagram above.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

* the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

* the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parameterizing the line segment $L,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}t,\,y=-\sqrt{2}t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the line from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2}).$ Therefore, $\mathbf{n}$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf{T},$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x{y}^{2} \\  & =3(\sqrt{2}t)(-\sqrt{2}t)^{2} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =-{y}^{3} \\  & =-(-\sqrt{2}t)^{3} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}t)=\sqrt{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{2}t)=-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{L}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{L}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (-\sqrt{2})-(2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (\sqrt{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-12{t}^{3}-4{t}^{3})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-16{t}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =-4[{t}^{4}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4(1-0) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362555 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ff3661cf-178f-52bd-85c7-48d75d20b100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186362557}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362557} :answer-field/id #uuid "53b1b3ff-21b1-5213-8b9c-584dd6a1a1eb" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186362556}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "98f26745-fe03-53ee-9421-2717c110e542" :question/math-academy-id "q-169207" :question/problem "![](images/83/8354a964dc235f1c9676754cf7d163cb4a54f05bd5899ff398acb11a4287861d.png)

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cccbf905-9f63-54b3-9f8d-d6f0dbce85ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-106251" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,-1)-f(0,2,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,0,-1⟩-⟨0,2,1⟩) \\ 2-(-7) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,-4y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ x & =-\frac{y-2}{2}=-\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t,\,\,y=2-2t,\,z=1-2t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t,\,\,{c}_{2}=2-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-2t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t)+8(2-2t)-4(1-2t) & =9 \\ 2t+16-16t-4+8t & =9 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =2-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(\frac{1}{2},1,0).$"} {:answer/id #uuid "827f14ed-373b-54f0-87eb-ba05ac897597" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},1,0)" :db/id 17592186362604} {:answer/id #uuid "9fa8cd0a-d89b-5bf5-ac6c-3d535195e448" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{5}{6},\frac{1}{3},-\frac{2}{3})" :db/id 17592186362606} {:answer/id #uuid "532d3b94-1153-561c-80f6-cf5aaf59db52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},-\frac{2}{5})" :db/id 17592186362608} {:db/id 17592186362867 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364fe6cb-9d03-53ce-a165-42f5c54b95ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3e}{16}" :db/id 17592186362869} {:answer/id #uuid "c21264c7-8089-52ce-9a48-6dad38c7f2ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186362870} {:answer/id #uuid "ef9db4ec-3467-518d-a30c-e4d04ca7e957" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{2}" :db/id 17592186362871} {:answer/id #uuid "b4b710cd-dff5-5c54-9db5-d82e41461d08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186362872} {:answer/id #uuid "c0fe8a21-d6a2-507f-9611-cdd51fb00208" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{16}" :db/id 17592186362873}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362873} :answer-field/id #uuid "08dd7829-9567-51b3-9a69-757f02b76b0e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362868}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "65eb7d35-cf19-5d83-87df-2f6cd4fcb07e" :question/math-academy-id "q-114317" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1/4}x{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{4x} & ⇒ & v=\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}-\int \left(\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}\right)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/4}x{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & ={\frac{1}{4}x{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4}-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/4}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{4}x{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4}-{\frac{1}{16}{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4(1/4)}-0\cdot {e}^{4\cdot 0}]-\frac{1}{16}[{e}^{4(1/4)}-{e}^{4\cdot 0}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{e}{4}-0]-\frac{1}{16}[e-1] \\  & =\frac{e}{16}-\frac{e}{16}+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362887 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "be70cf20-a712-5709-b35b-937dc2c0d369" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186362889} {:answer/id #uuid "6b6ddf74-4770-595f-899b-116441f857f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186362890} {:answer/id #uuid "15446dd9-5015-5403-b01a-d1888f4b4aea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+2\pi " :db/id 17592186362891} {:answer/id #uuid "02430b8b-e95e-5e00-bf36-982ce578dff0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186362892} {:answer/id #uuid "98bb0d83-f17c-55b7-8962-d5f1322270b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186362893}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362893} :answer-field/id #uuid "0a37bc31-d8c2-5721-a783-ab38279822c0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362888}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7f9dc4af-4f4e-5627-b6ea-707abe485f5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-115593" :question/problem "Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=0.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to estimate the value of $f(1).$" :question/worked-solution "The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=0,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ then $$
\displaystyle {f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=\operatorname{csc}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{sec}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=2.
$$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=2(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & ≈L(1) \\  & =2(1-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362921 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f3fb44a-5490-5c19-8dee-85b2abd2004f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468906} {:answer/id #uuid "4ccb2efc-9aa5-581b-9dc6-3bccac908663" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468907}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468906} :answer-field/id #uuid "416ef8e1-f182-5bc0-84b4-7491d68b70e9" :answer-field/key "${y}^{′}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470065} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b29f257d-ce75-5d81-9686-9ed494387614" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468908} {:answer/id #uuid "e8823ee4-d8ab-5aa2-a2f8-a5040cb6e2c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468909}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468908} :answer-field/id #uuid "bdb2b31b-82e4-563c-9c5a-d93987854026" :answer-field/key "${y}^{′}=-\frac{1}{y-1}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470066} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5ffdd4bd-e260-5e69-8280-f2f66fdbf870" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468910} {:answer/id #uuid "c7ce93f0-7bb1-5161-8005-5dfa196e656f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468911}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468911} :answer-field/id #uuid "de5792cc-f766-54d2-a12e-8e918370da4a" :answer-field/key "${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}-1}$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470067}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "81af22bb-892f-5bfc-b62b-3a9ae21c3aa9" :question/math-academy-id "q-116029" :question/problem "![](images/2b/2b25629c102be82d96b7ca94d5ab5ce499d327837ed53c6b4adb69ee214db81d.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "![](images/1b/1bf59ce83d7a82899587095217c080a5942f28a9c36c6971ec07ae5e8988e7fc.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- The slopes of the slope field become vertical as $y\to \pm 1.$

- The slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The slopes of the slope field are positive for $y\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )$ and negative for $y\in (-1,1).$

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. Notice that

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-1}=\frac{1}{(1-\frac{1}{y})}\to 1\,\text{as}\,y\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{y-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become vertical as $y\to -1.$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}-1}$ gives the required behavior. Notice that ${y}^{′}\to 0$ as $y\to \pm \infty ,$ and ${y}^{′}\to \infty $ as $y\to \pm 1.$ Also, the right-hand side of this equation is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )$ and negative for $y\in (-1,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186362928 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bb8c523b-6100-5004-846d-16fdc0ebd7d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e" :db/id 17592186362930} {:answer/id #uuid "027b7b92-0d26-5393-930d-ee8c7cae8cc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186362931} {:answer/id #uuid "56440c67-b574-5dbb-b2cc-6eec73dc0b74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{2}" :db/id 17592186362932} {:answer/id #uuid "d17156b3-2b9e-5ddd-9360-6b2c3d97a07c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186362933} {:answer/id #uuid "2353d310-e427-5375-acbb-9db1cba5d1cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{e}" :db/id 17592186362934}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362931} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e85fd67-ba77-5ee8-8b3e-d72489a044dc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362929}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6e8240bf-cbf5-5e93-ab51-651e9e2ebe6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-118059" :question/problem "$$

$b=⟨6,5⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{169-{y}^{2}}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨6,5⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(6,5)-f(0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨6,5⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\ \sqrt{169-{5}^{2}}-\sqrt{169-{0}^{2}} & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ 12-13 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ -1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨6,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,-\frac{y}{\sqrt{169-{y}^{2}}}⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,\,-\frac{{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ -1 & =⟨0,\,-\frac{{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}}}⟩\cdot ⟨6,5⟩ \\ -1 & =-\frac{5{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}} & =5{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve this radical equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{169-{{c}_{2}}^{2}} & =5{c}_{2} \\ 169-{{c}_{2}}^{2} & =25{{c}_{2}}^{2} \\ 26{{c}_{2}}^{2} & =169 \\ {{c}_{2}}^{2} & =\frac{169}{26} \\ {{c}_{2}}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the radical equation, we notice that ${c}_{2}=-\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}$ does not satisfy the equation. Therefore, the only solution is ${c}_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{1}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-0}{5-0} & =\frac{x-0}{6-0} \\ \frac{y}{5} & =\frac{x}{6} \\ y & =\frac{5}{6}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{5}{6}{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2},$ we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2} & =\frac{5}{6}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{26}}{2} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{3\sqrt{26}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $$
\displaystyle (\frac{3\sqrt{26}}{5},\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2}).
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "184cb44b-fc79-5576-987d-837cad0c48b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{3\sqrt{26}}{5},\frac{\sqrt{26}}{2})" :db/id 17592186363061} {:answer/id #uuid differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={z}^{3}-3{z}^{2}+3z-xy-1$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,-1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,-1,0)-f(0,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,-1,0⟩-⟨0,0,1⟩) \\ 0-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-y,\,-x,\,3{z}^{2}-6z+3⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-{c}_{2},\,-{c}_{1},\,3{{c}_{3}}^{2}-6{c}_{3}+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =⟨-{c}_{2},\,-{c}_{1},\,3{{c}_{3}}^{2}-6{c}_{3}+3⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =-{c}_{2}+{c}_{1}-3{{c}_{3}}^{2}+6{c}_{3}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{(-1)}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ x & =-y=1-z\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t\,\,y=-t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t\,\,{c}_{2}=-t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $-{c}_{2}+{c}_{1}-3{{c}_{3}}^{2}+6{c}_{3}-3=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-(-t)+t-3(1-t)^{2}+6(1-t)-3 & =0 \\ t+t-3+6t-3{t}^{2}+6-6t-3 & =0 \\ -3{t}^{2}+2t & =0 \\ -t(3t-2) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem.

- For $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =0, \\ {c}_{2} & =-0=0, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-0=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(0,0,1).$

- For $t=\frac{2}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{2}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{2}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(\frac{2}{3},-\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3}).$"} {:answer/id #uuid "fc456ae1-f295-56dd-b806-65585c6ede47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} #uuid "86c222b1-ebbd-591c-81fe-2d687175781c" :question/math-academy-id "q-149821" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta $ for $$
\displaystyle \frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\csc }^{2}⁡\theta +{\csc }^{2}⁡\theta {\cot }^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\csc }^{2}⁡\theta (1+{\cot }^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\csc }^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{\csc }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-[\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)] \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186363405 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4e1d6f24-a734-5128-a639-c1475cde6fe7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id "![](images/8f/8f955ee719a4e69f0d09c678f0a74023f137efd7b5ae36d49b98706156384173.png)

Consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown above.

$$
f(x)=\begin{cases}x+\frac{1}{2},\, & 0<x<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1
$$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1
$$ is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{0}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is true. Since statements “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” and $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1
$$ are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$”; $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1;
$$ “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function”."} {:db/id 17592186363437 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12c1ef0d-50f2-5c9a-b4b9-0991f9c0a289" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi /2,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi /4}" :db/id 17592186363439} {:answer/id #uuid "47fdcbeb-40a9-5611-b056-78b64e916319" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \pi /2,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }" :db/id 17592186363440} {:answer/id #uuid "836f0c92-4ede-5cf1-96e6-62274df2003b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }" :db/id 17592186363441} {:answer/id #uuid "cc70d968-925f-59dc-8142-ed88f79b74df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }" :db/id 17592186363442} {:answer/id #uuid "2d121f58-2417-5bb0-9cf6-0e82dabbaada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 6,\,0\le \theta \le \pi /2,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi /2}" :db/id 17592186363443}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186363440} :answer-field/id #uuid "c5c47e22-687f-55b2-a676-a0660995722a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186363438}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9cdc8440-2f90-5caf-ad31-d7cf53f0ded0" :question/math-academy-id "q-161820" :question/problem "![](images/69/691d275e70d43453e016d16e393f42aa6001cfbc3ee46ad99a5bc294a9e85be9.png)

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $(0,0,-1).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2z=0$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2z & =0 \\ {\rho }^{2}+2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & =0 \\ \rho (\rho +2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/14/1499d492c526bad77e81aca1128b6160cc574a209ad7706e8d89b3012112e1df.png)

 

Notice that inside our region, the spherical polar coordinates vary within the following domains:

- $\rho \in [0,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]$

- $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$

- $ϕ\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]$

Therefore, we have

$$
\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186363465 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "92fa23c5-f5ca-52b3-b9c6-f9d5a4e10d47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186363467} {:answer/id #uuid "96364a64-4346-5e93-8663-7f3c260832d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}-3" :db/id 17592186363468} {:answer/id #uuid "0cbfda04-b7ed-5845-b354-cec468c5c6bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3+\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186363469} {:answer/id #uuid "b806c0e9-8a1c-528e-a67e-89e1eba6df52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-3\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186363470} {:answer/id #uuid "1bc8ece8-ce75-5ec7-a65b-0906f086e127" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186363471}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186363469} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ca7b7a8-4b09-595e-a90a-557478166188" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186363466}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "0965ed17-df89-5de8-b0cd-60d291248cdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-162797" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+x+y$ given that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x+1,2y+1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$ This point belongs to our region.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global maximum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=3
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=1 \\ h(x,y,z) &=1\end{aligned}\right.

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨3,2,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,2,1⟩+\mu ⟨8x,4y,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3 &=\lambda +8\mu x \\ 2 &=2\lambda +4\mu y \\ 1 &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{4\mu } \\ \mu y &=0 \\ \lambda &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the second equation above, we must have $y=0.$

Next, we substitute $y=0$  into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =1 \\ 4{x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- If $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y+z & =1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}+2(0)+z & =1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}+z & =1 \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{1}{2}),\,(-\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{3}{2}).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-3 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ 3(t+1)(t-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+({1}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =\,i-2\,j,\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following special limit:
