\displaystyle {\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\cos }^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x={\cos }^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={\cos }^{4}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta {\cos }^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\cos }^{2}⁡\theta ({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={\cos }^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}{|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364413 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "49adc8e9-1dc5-5cb5-9175-f91e269efe35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "192" :db/id 17592186364415} {:answer/id #uuid "e94aff50-1cf2-58b3-85e2-e76471a133a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96" :db/id 17592186364416} {:answer/id #uuid "7fdf46cb-8dea-538a-974a-83bf0db567f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "256" :db/id 17592186364417} {:answer/id #uuid "119dacc9-0e3b-5285-87d0-21d3cc26e860" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "512" :db/id 17592186364418} {:answer/id #uuid "bddd3fe2-39af-5dc8-a534-e22068d4a73c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "384" :db/id 17592186364419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364415} :answer-field/id #uuid "7944764b-8f2e-517b-9311-deccaafc6156" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13c81ebd-eba4-55aa-a40f-bfa1b49cc9df" :question/math-academy-id "q-76763" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$ along the polar curve $r=4$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{3}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =256{\cos }^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(4)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}256{\cos }^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 4\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =1\,024{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\cos }^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1\,024{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\cos }^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =-1\,024{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-1\,024\cdot \frac{1}{4}{u}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =-256(\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =-256\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) \\  & =192\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "de3bafdd-839c-5480-9641-adee3b28a372" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})" :db/id 17592186364455} {:db/id 17592186364634 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f65503b-cf8e-52cc-b535-c4e4ac1577d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{14}{15}}" :db/id 17592186364636} {:answer/id #uuid "8a3a0ce2-8a79-54fa-8343-e971d2422d99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{\frac{14}{15}}" :db/id 17592186364637} {:answer/id #uuid "f4455b8e-f267-51f3-aa7d-3fbe77f9d1e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14}{15}" :db/id 17592186364638} {:answer/id #uuid "2e5bbc39-c4f1-5323-92f9-76aa49514b50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{56}{15}" :db/id 17592186364639} {:answer/id #uuid "17e0d913-1b89-5074-8bb7-aa0e2c7fe8e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{\frac{14}{15}}" :db/id 17592186364640}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364640} :answer-field/id #uuid "9e415229-8430-5c71-8b3d-4d06654a0d86" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364635}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c2ec86a9-5d87-5c18-b457-bd17da5e552f" :question/math-academy-id "q-97713" :question/problem "Let $V=C[-1,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-1,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)={t}^{2}+1.$" :question/worked-solution "The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{2}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+t)|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{3}+1)-(-\frac{1}{5}-\frac{2}{3}-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{3}+2 \\  & =\frac{56}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{\frac{56}{15}}=2\sqrt{\frac{14}{15}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364749 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "544ecd2d-bde7-5531-b6ed-1f7d10a3f9e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\pi " :db/id 17592186364751} {:answer/id #uuid "cab4f01d-178a-546b-bd23-3fe90d910fbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186364752} {:answer/id #uuid "71a1d39e-5367-5159-b5e6-12901992c3c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\sqrt{3}\pi " :db/id 17592186364753} {:answer/id #uuid "dc508202-a859-5fdd-a4a8-38f77d73654b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186364754} {:answer/id #uuid "b7d064ef-4a9d-55d2-9e65-78879a8a071e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15\pi \sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186364755}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364754} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf4dec28-6ad5-5a64-90ef-6978e1019e65" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364750}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4b0f3d46-2a1f-5dae-8237-79287f94cce2" :question/math-academy-id "q-109331" :question/problem "Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{y-3}$ that lies between the lines $y=3$ and $y=\frac{15}{4}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y-3})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y-3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}=\frac{1}{4(y-3)}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{4y-11}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=4y-11.$ Then, $\text{d}y=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$y$** | $3$ | $\frac{15}{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\sqrt{{4}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364763 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fcb5da96-fdf6-506d-a347-ba03ad8b8327" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}" :db/id 17592186364765} {:answer/id #uuid "d6e63ff4-6c91-5fa1-a20c-db6b29dba942" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}{x}_{1}+\frac{5}{6}{x}_{2}" :db/id 17592186364766} {:answer/id #uuid "93457fc2-9a25-539e-8bd0-7b28a3e4e43f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}" :db/id 17592186364767} {:answer/id #uuid "5322b9ce-bec7-588c-b91b-d0d6087a93d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{6}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}" :db/id 17592186364768} {:answer/id #uuid "7077e8a0-56bb-5adb-95a3-7b2345f829a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}" :db/id 17592186364769}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364769} :answer-field/id #uuid "3daba52f-8b3a-5463-9b29-a5456ae64429" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364764}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1d2e9b0a-6339-50e4-8938-2c9567f7a9d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-109637" :question/problem "The second-order initial value problem

$$
12{y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}-2y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2},\, && {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &=f(t),\, && {x}_{2}(1)=q\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{6}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2},\, && {x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},\, && {x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, $$
\displaystyle p=1,q=-2,f(t)=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},
$$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(1-(-2))(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =3(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364852 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a2016816-28e8-5d51-9785-1496f42addb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186364854} {:answer/id #uuid "a1103bae-8319-57e0-97ad-c5f4b71339b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186364855} {:answer/id #uuid "58d4f932-503e-5417-a6ef-0f99b77003fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186364856} {:answer/id #uuid "7872df49-3602-579a-81a7-9757623ee8c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186364857} {:answer/id #uuid "51e49929-146d-5950-b7fb-a559e7e56524" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186364858}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364858} :answer-field/id #uuid "6c3b44ec-e362-5848-b757-e1a30a3bc178" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364853}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ee16459a-bf12-529f-aa3b-cc89f5e9cb99" :question/math-academy-id "q-113501" :question/problem "The domain of the function $f(x)=\frac{4x+3}{5x+2k}$ is $$
\displaystyle (-\infty ,\frac{2}{5})\cup (\frac{2}{5},\infty ).
$$ What is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "A reciprocal function is defined for all values of $x$ except for those that make the denominator zero. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2k & =0 \\ 5x & =-2k \\ x & =-\frac{2k}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point that must be excluded from the domain is $x=-\frac{2k}{5}.$ 

On the other hand, we can see that $x=\frac{2}{5}$ is excluded from the domain. Equating this to $-\frac{2k}{5},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2k}{5} & =\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{k}{5} & =-\frac{1}{5} \\ k & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364927 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b8109b0a-084e-505e-9677-6cf31816c39a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt{2}\,\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186364929} {:answer/id #uuid "dc3b6592-41e1-5b53-94ef-adc717ecca52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}\,\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186364930} {:answer/id #uuid "867fe616-bbda-594a-bfee-71689e98ac0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}\,\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186364931} {:answer/id #uuid "b7cb1890-ceb3-525c-9a55-9c6ad9e148bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{28\sqrt{2}\,\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186364932} {:answer/id #uuid "0c7ca7ae-4d0c-52bf-ab6d-6e2d8df75e36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186364933}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364932} :answer-field/id #uuid "14229d88-ad4c-5463-b8a3-92a65fb233c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364928}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c6bfdd4b-1abf-5cab-8f44-31d764fee083" :question/math-academy-id "q-126730" :question/problem "Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{1-2y}$ that lies between the lines $y=-3$ and $y=0.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{1-2y}) \\  & =\frac{-2}{2\sqrt{1-2y}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}=\frac{1}{1-2y}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-2y}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-2y}\sqrt{\frac{2-2y}{1-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {[-\frac{2}{3}(1-y)^{3/2}]}_{-3}^{0} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi (-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{28\sqrt{2}\,\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364934 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7d8e2098-e0ef-5cf9-96dd-acd02787309d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,\frac{2}{7},-2⟩" :db/id 17592186364936} {:answer/id #uuid "1a0852f3-752e-59a5-b8ff-cfa1a2a782fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{7},\frac{3}{7},2⟩" :db/id 17592186364937} {:answer/id #uuid "f79463e1-06ab-536c-b4c3-abce5c52faa2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{3}{7},\frac{6}{7},-\frac{2}{7}⟩" :db/id 17592186364938} {:answer/id #uuid "6eed8b1f-82a4-5ee7-8d20-7e61cb4cb70c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,1,\frac{6}{7}⟩" :db/id 17592186364939} {:answer/id #uuid "18c7d5c6-2e72-53b6-a3aa-1b32001b22b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{2}{7},\frac{3}{7},\frac{6}{7}⟩" :db/id 17592186364940}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364940} :answer-field/id #uuid "f0cecf4f-0a8b-57fb-8125-c6782ff53ff7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364935}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0ec6ccbf-4d58-58ab-b1bd-0cceb820f4a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-127220" :question/problem "What is the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨8t,\,3{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{3}⟩$ at the point $P(16,12,16)?$" :question/worked-solution "For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(16,12,16)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨16,12,16⟩ \\ ⟨8t,\,3{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨16,12,16⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}8t &=16 \\ 3{t}^{2} &=12 \\ 2{t}^{3} &=16.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equality, $t=2.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(16,12,16)$ is at the tip of $r(2).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,6t,\,6{t}^{2}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(2) & =⟨8,\,6(2),\,6(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,12,24⟩ \\  & =4⟨2,3,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(2)‖ & =4\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{4+9+36} \\  & =4\sqrt{49} \\  & =28\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(2)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at $P(16,12,16):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(2)}{‖{r}^{′}(2)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{28}\cdot 4⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{7},\frac{3}{7},\frac{6}{7}⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "7d8e2098-e0ef-5cf9-96dd-acd02787309d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,\frac{2}{7},-2⟩" :db/id 17592186364936} {:answer/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-127298" :question/problem "Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,p(t)$ at the point corresponding to $t=0$, given that  $p(0)=2\,i+j-k\,$ and $\,{p}^{′}(0)=i-2\,j-2\,k.$" :question/worked-solution "For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j+z(t)k$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$

$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,p(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\right)\cdot p(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p(t)) \\  & =-\frac{2t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,p(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,{p}^{′}(t) \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{2(0)}{{({0}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,p(0)+\frac{1}{{0}^{2}+1}\,{p}^{′}(0) \\  & =0(2\,i+j-k)+(\,i-2\,j-2k) \\  & =\,i-2\,j-2k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(0):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}‖r(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=0
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-2x,-6y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x &=4\lambda x \\ -6y &=2\lambda (y-1)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(1+2\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(\lambda +3) &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-2y & =0\,⇒\,y=0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,0),(0,2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-\frac{1}{2}+3)=-\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,y=-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}=-\frac{11}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a contradiction.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,0),\,(0,2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(0,2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-11$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at the point $(0,0)$ and its maximum value is $1.$"} {:db/id 17592186365226 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c067ceed-329e-51d4-8634-a1d0a81bb476" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186365228} {:answer/id #uuid "e75d0918-e0c0-5785-afab-223f2739e64f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186365229} {:answer/id #uuid "d89c552a-fc32-5beb-8d5d-4662a900a5fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186365230} {:answer/id #uuid "3d19bfcb-0c7d-52e7-9dba-653ffcc18e58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186365231} {:answer/id #uuid "27d0d7f6-36e2-5084-93d4-3a3fe65c5a47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186365232}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365230} :answer-field/id #uuid "3bd3adff-ea86-59fd-bc52-90fe39fade8a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365227}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c6ff3f5a-d486-56fd-99cb-379dcba19a45" :question/math-academy-id "q-162792" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ on the paraboloid ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-y=0.$

*Hint: You may assume that the global maximum of $f(x,y,z)$ exists on the surface.*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of $f$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-y=0.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}={0}^{2}+{z}^{2}\,⇒\,z=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

| $\,(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,(0,0,0)\,$ | $$

When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $kx\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=20\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $10\,m,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/cd/cd42eb74e5bba02951118c349a1b25f7193c39aa53f6504403918dfa984eb2c2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=20\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$

$$

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4-x & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=4\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=4\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (4-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =4(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+18 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-{x}^{2}+36 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(4)=\sqrt{-(4)^{2}+8(4)+36}=2\sqrt{13}\,m/s
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365260 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9676d1bd-b5f6-576b-af89-b417c0b3f836" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365262} {:answer/id #uuid "acd5375e-9e97-53b6-9073-a053c886f8bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365263} {:answer/id #uuid "a553426d-f0bb-5e6d-a4fa-349049cf240a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{6}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365264} {:answer/id #uuid "6aa4d97d-b040-5b59-a4e2-7990a8d14150" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365265} {:answer/id #uuid "af4992d7-4f53-5694-ab5f-c15156f271e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365266}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365264} :answer-field/id #uuid "de8be0bb-c786-552b-8444-d92b5d0e42e6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365261}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6e8a8914-09f4-5fec-89f5-6922293a4aaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-163549" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(10-2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle." :question/worked-solution "![](images/33/33b95a6985a53b76eb7f74771825c18f21d1e59b2245325e14690a365a2a8bb0.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(10-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=10-2x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10-2x & =0 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=5\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,5)$ | $5$ | $(5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $4$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=5\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=10-2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (10-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=10x-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =10(0)-(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =20x-2{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(5)=\sqrt{-2(5)^{2}+20(5)+4}=3\sqrt{6}\,m/s
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365267 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6dde8744-6fdc-5e2d-b736-074a3c935944" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186365269} {:answer/id #uuid "2e60c10f-bfb0-5906-b010-ebfe71f74caa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186365270} {:answer/id #uuid "e931fb28-3c65-5cdd-bd58-88282355e37a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186365271} {:answer/id #uuid "dd1e58b1-199d-5fb2-88e7-6318356fb651" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186365272} {:answer/id #uuid "59060e22-55d4-5810-9281-aa0ce058e469" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186365273}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365270} :answer-field/id #uuid "a4d2807e-e4a2-58a8-bf6a-268785e8822d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365268}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "850e5b75-4192-55dd-95c1-60411426a4e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163550" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $kx\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $3\sqrt{2}\,m,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/cd/cd42eb74e5bba02951118c349a1b25f7193c39aa53f6504403918dfa984eb2c2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=3\sqrt{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}(3\sqrt{2})^{2} \\ 18-9k & =0 \\ 9k & =18 \\ k & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365274 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6838b8cf-fec7-51b2-8373-943cee569878" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186365276} {:answer/id #uuid "8205c3ac-78de-533c-ae96-ff65f5828af8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "28" :db/id 17592186365277} {:answer/id #uuid "c11907f7-3548-559e-a061-4bcaf9c1b34e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186365278} {:answer/id #uuid "a7869954-b653-5a50-9765-f8085d861bd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186365279} {:answer/id #uuid "2bec3e13-4258-5707-beaf-f4fdea05190d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186365280}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365280} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3028a6b-dad4-502a-85ce-856d7efdc2e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365275}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "346646b9-04ff-58cb-a1cc-6c9b42073112" :question/math-academy-id "q-163551" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m$ and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\pi \,m,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/b3/b396b80995e34fe348b3d059737b1eec3d4ce5a9d2e9138a8e7d4ed5c0945dc0.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=\pi \,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ 32 & =8+k \\ k & =24.\end{aligned}

$$"} {:db/id 17592186365288 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "75f9bb39-d662-5b7f-b26c-4c6a27fffc10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{14}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365290} {:answer/id #uuid "40369435-8306-5137-8429-a26ad39afe91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\sqrt{2}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365291} {:answer/id #uuid "b0ede10b-ba4c-5e79-b731-b8038347c020" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365292} {:answer/id #uuid "5a09cbc5-7125-5f56-932d-0251a7308a75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365293} {:answer/id #uuid "07428674-2986-5965-9daa-705a8555f7a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{7}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186365294}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365290} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e05aabc-648f-50bd-bc69-595d4091baa3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186365289}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ecee2124-1bd8-5650-8e8b-4c51642487c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163553" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(6-6x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle." :question/worked-solution "![](images/61/61388466bb2d97b5080707e769ae862e633bfb0fe1d2b5f16c75daa14da76e53.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(6-6x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=9{x}^{2}.

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3{x}^{3}+C.

$$

$$

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=\sqrt[3]{7}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt[3]{7})^{3}+C \\ C & =2-\frac{7}{3} \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{{x}^{3}-1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$"} {:db/id 17592186365571 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bce27b2-5df3-5a8e-869e-d080b7d5082b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11+\frac{30m}{n}" :db/id 17592186365573}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365573} :answer-field/id #uuid "07649995-d867-534f-9e43-6b83134b223f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365572}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ac716160-cd13-516f-8618-dcec93b16168" :question/math-academy-id "q-315831" :question/problem "What is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{2}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1)\,\text{d}x
$$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $m$ and $n.$*

$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{2}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(
$$
{{field-1}}$)\cdot \frac{6}{n}]$" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}f({x}_{m})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{m}=a+mΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1),$ the lower bound is $a=2$ and the upper bound is $b=8.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{8-2}{n}=\frac{6}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1)\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}f({x}_{m})\cdot Δx \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[f(2+m\cdot \frac{6}{n})\cdot \frac{6}{n}] \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[f(2+\frac{6m}{n})\cdot \frac{6}{n}] \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(5(2+\frac{6m}{n})+1)\cdot \frac{6}{n}] \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{m=1}^{n}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(11+\frac{30m}{n})\cdot \frac{6}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365650 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "517eede4-99bb-52d2-97e3-f8374df62d2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{6}" :db/id 17592186365652} {:answer/id #uuid "c6f3f9b6-b53a-53c7-bf9f-e0faf4b67757" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186365653} {:answer/id #uuid "91c0de02-4938-5944-8322-3c82815d39c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13}{9}" :db/id 17592186365654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365654} :answer-field/id #uuid "38ef1f7e-5939-5a29-9243-3eb86db8bf23" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186365651} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "216b48ff-3aab-5bae-8ba5-6310b65d6803" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186365656} {:answer/id #uuid "4ec31888-ebfc-581c-bcb5-559f7ddb3ca3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186365657} {:answer/id #uuid "47ab90d3-7782-57db-9f99-399fd7664ec1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186365658}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365658} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b65a05f-c72c-5ce6-b833-fab58379b7f4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186365655}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0869ab2e-660c-52ea-8198-a9faff4849b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-333999" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
3{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-{x}^{2}=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0
$$

Use Euler's Method with two steps to approximate $y(3)$ and ${y}^{′}(3).$

$$
y(3)≈{{field-1}},\,{y}^{′}(3)≈{{field-2}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{y}^{″} & ={x}^{2}-2{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2{y}^{′}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=2, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3},\, && z(1)=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=3.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=3$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{3-1}{2}=1.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=2$ and $z(1)=0.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}=\frac{{1}^{2}-2\cdot 0}{3}=\frac{1}{3} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0\cdot 1=0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 1=\frac{1}{3} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+0=2 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $2$ |  |  | $\frac{1}{3}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=\frac{1}{3} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}=\frac{({2}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{3})}{3}=\frac{10}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 1=\frac{1}{3} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{10}{9}\cdot 1=\frac{10}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=2+1=3 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{7}{3} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{10}{9}=\frac{13}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $2$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{10}{9}$ | $\frac{10}{9}$ |
| $3$ | $\frac{7}{3}$ |  |  | $\frac{13}{9}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(3)≈\frac{7}{3}$
and
${y}^{′}(3)=z(3)≈\frac{13}{9}.$"} {:db/id 17592186365668 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9cd42562-09cd-51eb-b4a2-b584bedeb569" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186365670} {:answer/id #uuid "9e6ed429-cb7b-5097-aa61-71d601e00811" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{5t}+e^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186442520}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442520} :answer-field/id #uuid "e0c533ef-5493-5cd1-a424-830212f48ffc" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365669} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e04a12ae-abe9-59a0-b308-9184898a8572" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186365672} {:answer/id #uuid "90a5ac54-ed2a-5377-933c-378e5c24686e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{5t}+e^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186442516}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442516} :answer-field/id #uuid "df0b6879-e091-50fa-802c-bc06c1af37d2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365671}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "162963ac-9899-549d-9b3f-b09605170db6" :question/math-academy-id "q-334389" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-5t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-5t) &={e}^{-5t} \\ r(5t) &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-5t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-10t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10t}({e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-5t}+{e}^{5t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot (-\frac{1}{10t}({e}^{-5t}-{e}^{5t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t} & {e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t} \\ {e}^{5t}-{e}^{-5t} & {e}^{5t}+{e}^{-5t}\end{bmatrix}.

 $r(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t},\,t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩$ at an arbitrary point where $t\in (0,\infty )?$" :question/worked-solution "For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),\,y(t),\,z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\sqrt{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)}^{2}+(1)^{2}+{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}+1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1+{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{(1+{t}^{2})^{2}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1+{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{1+{t}^{2}}⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}⟨-1,\,{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{2}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "4725da3c-09bc-5907-8640-bf7c25de282c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{1+t}⟨-1,\,{t}^{2},\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}t⟩" :db/id 17592186365726} {:answer/id #uuid "101c1f8f-90f7-5afb-9a2a-9d9d07341ab6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}},0,\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}⟩" :db/id 17592186365787} {:answer/id #uuid "e7153d39-ff14-5c43-a90f-c9463613ccd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{2}{9},\frac{8}{9},\frac{4}{9}⟩" :db/id 17592186365788} {:answer/id #uuid "7b4893f4-d976-5d25-b643-929e8ba9edcb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{69}},\frac{8}{\sqrt{69}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{69}}⟩" :db/id 17592186365789} {:answer/id #uuid "d9f9c136-39ba-5393-9857-3e448e41c70a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{9},\frac{8}{9},\frac{4}{9}⟩" :db/id 17592186365790} {:answer/id #uuid "ca08ec85-b4ca-5869-bc18-73f064ee828a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{9},-\frac{8}{9},\frac{4}{9}⟩" :db/id 17592186365791} {:db/id 17592186365808 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ca5fb1c3-f4d9-5a37-a9bd-6708fe402752" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4t+2" :db/id 17592186365810}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365810} :answer-field/id #uuid "2af25afe-e912-5735-b096-591cb5639115" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365809}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9269cd51-19e6-5e98-96ab-0e051bb84772" :question/math-academy-id "q-337290" :question/problem "$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

| $$
\displaystyle x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+\,\,
$$ |  | $-2t-3$ |  | . |

|  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-(-{e}^{t})\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=\frac{4}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4}{3}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-\frac{8}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{8}{3}t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot (-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}-\frac{8}{3}\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}+\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ \frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}(2t-1)-8(t+1) \\ 2(2t-1)+8(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2t-3 \\ 4t+2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365845 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66469292-e41e-5a67-99ec-df0aaf68e52e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$1$ only" :question/math-academy-id "q-338833" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-20\lambda {y}^{′}+100{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+{y}^{′}\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0,\,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2},\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $$
\displaystyle y\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+{y}^{′}\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0
$$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-20\lambda m+100{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-10\lambda )(m-10\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=10\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{10\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{10\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{10\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{10\lambda x}+10B\lambda x{e}^{10\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $$
\displaystyle y\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+{y}^{′}\,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0
$$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ \frac{3}{2}B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{5\lambda }+\frac{10}{3}B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{5\lambda }(1+\frac{10}{3}\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{5\lambda }>0,$ we must have

$$
\lambda =-\frac{3}{10}.
$$

Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{10\lambda x} \\  & =Bx{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "e9883a8c-7a90-5bdd-a094-5cb18a2dfc22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$Bx{e}^{-x}$ and $C{e}^{x/2}(x+\frac{3}{2})$" :db/id 17592186365867} {:db/id 17592186365942 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "97309906-dff0-599d-b092-0740a0732b6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-4x}" :db/id 17592186365944} {:answer/id #uuid "833af303-c46f-5b0d-8a79-139d161c6a97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{-4x}" :db/id 17592186455139}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455139} :answer-field/id #uuid "f5699544-5216-55d0-b396-9487609e9ee4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365943}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "593a3349-a7fc-5c8f-8d89-90616a43f4a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-343757" :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

$$

$$

where $f(x)$ is a $3$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$  
{{field-1}} 
$$
\displaystyle +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x))
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+4y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+4y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{-4x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=1.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{-4(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 1 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-4x}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼{e}^{-4x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365945 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21b93f35-5863-505d-95aa-0b03a081a02c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{e}^{5x-15}" :db/id 17592186365947} {:answer/id #uuid "373fbf8e-f9c5-58a2-82ab-389c0f096a7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2e^{5x-15}" :db/id 17592186454989}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186454989} :answer-field/id #uuid "2f550799-2c78-5c0d-95ef-a64651fc88f0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365946}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3a5b1020-667d-5b46-950b-9e388e936e0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-343942" :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}-5y=f(x),\,y(3)=-2
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $4$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

The solution is

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}-5y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}-5y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{5x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(3)=-2.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =A{e}^{5(3)}+{y}_{p}(3) \\ -2 & =A{e}^{15}+0 \\ A & =-2{e}^{-15}.\end{aligned}

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$

Therefore, the solution is

{y}^{″}+3y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-5
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4\pi $-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{n}{2}x).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+3=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-5.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=-5$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & =B\sqrt{3}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B\sqrt{3} & =-5-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "a7a87f86-90b0-5b7d-9095-19d6fbf68ef5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{3}})" :db/id 17592186365950} {:answer/id #uuid "59abbacc-a27b-5a19-ac83-400c63f14c79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{3}})" :db/id 17592186365951} {:answer/id #uuid "6f06faa6-96dc-5bf0-bb0f-d24428537c3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}})" :db/id 17592186365952} {:db/id 17592186365984 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "81fb9a2a-e974-5e21-a24c-b83847d0670c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186365986}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365986} :answer-field/id #uuid "991e8bfb-d216-5777-8b02-41d6beedd873" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365985} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "65696180-4576-5e92-bc35-eb4097717b74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186365988}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365988} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d560f3e-45c6-5297-9dbb-a7f86861cc41" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365987}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "77799534-8c26-5a8c-81b1-59219a3dda8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-354994" :question/problem "A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=5-\frac{1}{2}t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=3\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

The maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=$

$\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached at $t=$
{{field-2}}$\text{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 5-\frac{1}{2}t & =0 \\ t & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme values using the second derivative test. The second derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-\frac{1}{2}t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(10)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (5-\frac{1}{2}t)\text{d}t \\  & =5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(4)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5(4)-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{2}+C & =3 \\ 20-4+C & =3\,⟹\,C=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity is given by $v(t)=5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}-13.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(10)=5(10)-\frac{1}{4}(10)^{2}-13=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached at $t=10\,\text{s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186366059 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid
