:question/id #uuid "07bd3910-da00-5269-ba42-c4e894fc0a77" :question/math-academy-id "q-38305" :question/problem "If the linear transformation $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $5y=6x$ then, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. 

- Statement $⟨\frac{6}{5},1⟩\in \text{Im}(T)$ is false.
Notice that the point $(\frac{6}{5},1)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $5y=6x$ since $5\cdot 1\ne \frac{6}{5}\cdot 6.$ Therefore, 
$⟨\frac{6}{5},1⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).$

- Statement $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$ is true.
Since $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line passing through the origin, we have that the standard matrix $T$ is singular. So, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement “$\text{nullity}(T)=0$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$” is false.
Since  statement $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$ is true we have that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim(Ker}(T))\ne 0.$"} {:db/id 17592186366104 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29f0dba1-7067-5d87-99e6-9cf227b19ccd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186366106} {:answer/id #uuid "6fbc4e23-72cd-5330-af02-7585346a0eaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186366107} {:answer/id #uuid "c4eb1a09-3f4d-5544-bbe3-aa4a4488f180" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}" :db/id 17592186366108} {:answer/id #uuid "e6af34c5-cd3c-5f65-9633-120d1ff65e02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186366109} {:answer/id #uuid "e115b02c-9eb3-5e9c-9adc-f461206a1807" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}" :db/id 17592186366110}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366109} :answer-field/id #uuid "b10f82d7-23d8-5faa-bd60-f6f74f7c290a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366105}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5a318f0c-c590-5820-90e1-5e9d0a54a78b" :question/math-academy-id "q-39411" :question/problem "![](images/48/48d76f34becfba9f58658c3c38ba2df0e76ad6ff20b83ffc836e213c4eea4565.png)

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx.
$$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[6]{\pi },\,\,{y}^{3}\le z\le \sqrt{\pi }}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](images/86/86af6e58f4f13e79bb9672cef329572f006e5f4875178ede7908bddbd0dec404.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/83/83041605fcd79db34f249664b12311a4e5d797c331bcaf1279f03b5b68891b23.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{z}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/b5/b5a3fc034b713ce5fca98fbd0cca3c454d18e42e0e73eecc7ec18c51a8e7ebb5.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the bottom curve given by $z=\sqrt[3]{0}=0.$

![](images/54/54fa3b1c3a15391e0a87c15017b07594c4f2cca7fb741cd7480909a64e3d39db.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2}){[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\frac{1}{3}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})]}_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186366158 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e8cd826f-58a3-53f3-aa32-8e8009f34e9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x)=(x+2)^{3}$ and $b=7$" :db/id 17592186366160} {:answer/id #uuid "26c00d20-c2c8-5017-8c58-bc84d579333c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x)={x}^{3}$ and $b=7$" :db/id 17592186366161} {:answer/id #uuid "b6c5b7c0-3606-57cf-9d02-1f791c707185" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x)=(x+2)^{3}$ and $b=5$" :db/id 17592186366162} {:answer/id #uuid "ea23c9c8-b65c-5145-b50c-dfc710522478" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x)={x}^{3}$ and $b=5$" :db/id 17592186366163} {:answer/id #uuid "6974f7c5-1d82-5469-9ed1-c0be7a7e6618" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x)=(x+4)^{3}$ and $b=9$" :db/id 17592186366164}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366161} :answer-field/id #uuid "24cfe0c6-efb9-5afc-b56a-61a0caf09182" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366159}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eeeb41dd-6f6c-5a62-9ecb-abbdad0e75d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-49236" :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{4}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(4+\frac{3i}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=4.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{3}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{3}{n}=\frac{b-4}{n}\,⟹\,b=7.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{i}=4+\frac{3i}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})={x}_{i}^{3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{4}^{7}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(4+\frac{3i}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].
$$

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x-4,\,x>0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\underbrace{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{\text{chain rule}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+2y=t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{t}+B{e}^{2t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta $ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0-3\alpha +2(\alpha t+\beta )=t-4
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
2\alpha t+(-3\alpha +2\beta )=t-4.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2\alpha &=1\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ -3\alpha +2\beta &=-4\, && (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Hence, $\alpha =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\beta =-\frac{5}{4},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{2}t-\frac{5}{4}=\frac{2t-5}{4}.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5}{4}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186366413 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c4230ad4-7cfc-5d03-bab5-c470ed638956" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{\text{max}}=3\,\text{m}/\text{s},\,t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366415} {:answer/id #uuid "b65c9efc-7c3f-5bfb-817c-61630ff08b12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s},\,t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366416} {:answer/id #uuid "63061252-851d-512f-947d-df9b1f834d52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{\text{max}}=1\,\text{m}/\text{s},\,t=\frac{\pi }{3}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366417} {:answer/id #uuid "cefa53ae-b66e-5476-a63b-cd4860f7c92b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{\text{max}}=3\,\text{m}/\text{s},\,t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366418} {:answer/id #uuid "58b00c9b-e358-5249-91e6-9a3e85bd720d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s},\,t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366419} :answer-field/id #uuid "ca8329e9-7ccd-5315-91fb-dae2ef3df42f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2bf4373d-fd90-5472-8b82-87ff2c920c93" :question/math-academy-id "q-82049" :question/problem "A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity." :question/worked-solution "The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. 

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =-12\cdot 1 \\  & =-12<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C & =1 \\ 0+C & =1\,⟹\,C=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186366469 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23945947-fedd-5c9d-86b1-0b85abeb69d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=\frac{\sqrt[3]{3}}{2}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366471} {:answer/id #uuid "c3668db4-3cd6-5102-95d2-aa1b2d810918" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=\frac{\sqrt[3]{9}}{4}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366472} {:answer/id #uuid "31af86cd-c5b1-5034-926a-bb2e740bcb70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=\frac{64}{27}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366473} {:answer/id #uuid "8fa594f0-0758-5b21-a86c-503d1a8ec844" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=\frac{13}{9}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366474} {:answer/id #uuid "3154bc9c-5cac-52ee-a2c8-aae7ac271761" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=\frac{16}{3}\,\text{s}" :db/id 17592186366475}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366473} :answer-field/id #uuid "97e11da6-4568-5fe4-a411-496c1c7d2886" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366470}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a54d954d-f678-50a4-85cb-fbb21be9de6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-84225" :question/problem "A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)={t}^{1/3}-1,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=8\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary." :question/worked-solution "The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\underbrace{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{\text{chain rule}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-10y=5t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=40.
$$

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,\underbrace{14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}}_{Q(x)}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=40
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly: 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2} & =40 \\ 15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}(-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2})+3\sqrt{10}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2}) & =40 \\ 15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2}+10{y}_{2} & =40 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2} & =8 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+({y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2}+1) & =8+1 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}+1)}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}+1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$

$$

$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}-12\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+6\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}-12\sqrt{5}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})+6\sqrt{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})+12 & =0 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}+30{y}_{1}+12 & =0\end{aligned}

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}+30{y}_{1}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1})-7{y}_{2}^{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1}+25-25)-7{y}_{2}^{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1}+25)-75-7{y}_{2}^{2}+12 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}+5)^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2}-63 & =0 \\ 3({y}_{1}+5)^{2}-7{y}_{2}^{2} & =63\end{aligned}

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}+5, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.

we get the following:

$$

$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$

 

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{1}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{1}-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1})-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}+1-1)-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}+1)^{2}-2\cdot 1-4{y}_{2} & =4 \\ 2({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & =4{y}_{2}+6 \\ 2({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & =4({y}_{2}+\frac{3}{2})\end{aligned}

Find the area bounded between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x+1},$ the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x+1} \\ {y}^{3} & =x+1 \\ x & ={y}^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-0)-(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-1 \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{3}{4}|=\frac{3}{4}.$"} {:db/id 17592186366815 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "193c9497-7ea6-5a1d-b9f5-a009ce93ca23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6x-y+12z-24=0" :db/id 17592186366817} {:answer/id #uuid "f29eacee-8051-57cb-aee4-51b137c18ee1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6x-y+z+12=0" :db/id 17592186366818} {:answer/id #uuid "710265a2-6141-5b27-8548-bda3797d8905" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-2y-5z+11=0" :db/id 17592186366819} {:answer/id #uuid "d24d01c2-6eb5-5662-b203-5deae9c0dd73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6x-3y-4z+24=0" :db/id 17592186366820} {:answer/id #uuid "8c31a377-21c2-5c10-92eb-4e6439b5d5dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4z+13=0" :db/id 17592186366821}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366817} :answer-field/id #uuid "ac4c269d-3ccc-505a-8b3b-1f9e614487fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "baefe5d5-6705-561e-af37-627a61278732" :question/math-academy-id "q-102704" :question/problem "Given the function $f(x,y,z)=6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes  through the point where $(x,y,z)=(\frac{1}{2},3,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{1}{2},3,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},3,2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨6,-1,12⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 6(x-\frac{1}{2})-(y-3)+12(z-2) & =0 \\ 6x-y+12z-24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186366836 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8fd57de8-9613-5a2d-b250-1256e758fcdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\,k" :db/id 17592186366838} {:answer/id #uuid "c7c75d6b-cf75-544e-b91d-ce8ce69634d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i-3\,j" :db/id 17592186366839} {:answer/id #uuid "9676ca3b-a8bf-5169-b714-9f4c43df824b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,j+k" :db/id 17592186366840} {:answer/id #uuid "7b2c6bbe-a185-592a-8dbf-f13ee1a9cd63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\,i+2\,j" :db/id 17592186366841} {:answer/id #uuid "90f8d1f8-016d-523f-b081-bc76f0d11212" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,j" :db/id 17592186366842}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366839} :answer-field/id #uuid "bc4e76b2-9e53-585b-b42d-cd7facc74bf5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366837}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7f694a45-bb80-5fc5-bc87-30958ae2f792" :question/math-academy-id "q-105711" :question/problem "Calculate $∇\times (F-G)$ at the point $(0,2,1)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,i+xy\,k,\,(∇\times G)(x,y,z)=-i+2z\,j-x\,k.
$$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-G) & =∇\times F-∇\times G.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & 0 & xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(0)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡z)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(0)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡z)]k \\  & =(x-0)i-(y-\frac{1}{z})j+(0-0)k \\  & =x\,i+(\frac{1}{z}-y)j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-G) & =∇\times F-∇\times G \\  & =x\,i+(\frac{1}{z}-y)j-[-i+2z\,j-x\,k] \\  & =x\,i+(\frac{1}{z}-y)j+i-2z\,j+x\,k \\  & =(x+1)\,i+(\frac{1}{z}-y-2z)j+x\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(0,2,1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F-G))(0,2,1) & =(0+1)\,i+(\frac{1}{1}-2-2(1))j+0\,k \\  & =i-3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186366843 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3df17644-84e9-5490-9a46-e21ae8d3b3cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-j-k" :db/id 17592186366845} {:answer/id #uuid "2734c944-dc51-5802-8c7b-f65c2498e403" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,i-3\,j" :db/id 17592186366846} {:answer/id #uuid "17483ec0-7c0a-540e-92d1-d728c39f27ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-j" :db/id 17592186366847} {:answer/id #uuid "4a934b73-4c26-5600-b8f6-04d31b2de547" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\,i+4\,k" :db/id 17592186366848} {:answer/id #uuid "6640ab9d-dc7f-5c52-867f-9e77c070d6b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,k" :db/id 17592186366849}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366846} :answer-field/id #uuid "7ef56c19-5bdd-55b2-961c-455e339ce25d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366844}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8c99c802-9c0a-555e-905b-2fc17880a001" :question/math-academy-id "q-105713" :question/problem "Calculate $∇\times (F+G)$ at the point $(4,3,-1)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=-3\,i+z\,j+8\sqrt{x}\,\text{k},\,(∇\times G)(x,y,z)=-i-j.
$$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ -3 & z & 8\sqrt{x}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(8\sqrt{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(z)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(8\sqrt{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(-3)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(z)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3)]k \\  & =(0-1)i-(\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}-0)j+(0-0)k \\  & =-i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F+G) & =∇\times F+∇\times G \\  & =-i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}\,j+[-i-j] \\  & =-i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}\,j-i-j \\  & =-2\,i-(\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}+1)j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(4,3,-1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F+G))(4,3,-1) & =-2\,i-(\frac{4}{\sqrt{4}}+1)j \\  & =-2\,i-3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367156 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e72e8ea-222c-5696-85a6-15e06bc5d8f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.2" :db/id 17592186367158} {:answer/id #uuid "c801f412-cd90-57a4-9f70-22aa8c930e72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.6" :db/id 17592186367159} {:answer/id #uuid "1b09400a-7fbd-53f2-9bcc-0bab7833a681" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.1" :db/id 17592186367160} {:answer/id #uuid "0ce4fc24-159a-5d8f-9c20-59c1ebc960ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.4" :db/id 17592186367161} {:answer/id #uuid "b3a04eeb-327b-5191-bf82-b02968049bf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6.4" :db/id 17592186367162}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367159} :answer-field/id #uuid "0478d695-2aab-54a7-b4c5-059cc27c474d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367157}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3c3da72b-c9a5-5658-bb6d-d3a4b0f842f2" :question/math-academy-id "q-111328" :question/problem "The random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution.

$$" :question/worked-solution "We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186367170 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a10c819-f962-517a-bd28-778bb054c660" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186367172} {:answer/id #uuid "f8bd6f3a-a1b1-5284-b572-c14440792d05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186367173} {:answer/id #uuid "bbdd6d29-1b1d-5faa-967d-b7e4790b2d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186367174} {:answer/id #uuid "a86ebf85-357d-5b1f-a8a6-d8391e75ebd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186367175} {:answer/id #uuid "bdb1fcf1-a588-5a87-b4b4-50ba24deaed7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186367176}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367174} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7de7570-8cd8-57af-9496-2dce3e12f896" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367171}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cc544fb2-b29c-5843-ace8-c118d11d787f" :question/math-academy-id "q-115947" :question/problem "Consider the section of the hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1$ that lies in the second quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4$ on the hyperbola at the point where $x=-3,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point." :question/worked-solution "Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\right)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\right)-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \left(\frac{2x}{3}\right)-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4$ and $x=-3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (-2)-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0 \\ -8-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=-3$ into the equation of the hyperbola.

At the point where $x=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(-3)^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ 3-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the second quadrant.

 Finally, substituting $y=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367177 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ae467fb3-f63f-54bc-88d8-32c99fe9e08d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186367179} {:answer/id #uuid "bd67acba-1d7d-5904-9fd2-988231e488fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186367180} {:answer/id #uuid "b1b4a166-30db-52fa-98df-8a94aafd5f98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186367181} {:answer/id #uuid "3d267227-97a9-5d1c-9990-ea64e0fab1ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186367182} {:answer/id #uuid "6edc32ff-1826-5302-8b38-a4e5f595c725" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186367183}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367180} :answer-field/id #uuid "933d59db-68a6-5d20-bc41-310ebed025cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367178}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "04fc9383-ba9d-51b2-b7ff-6b5bffaa64a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-115950" :question/problem "Consider the curve $\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)=2.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2$ on the curve at the point where $x=\frac{1}{2},$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point." :question/worked-solution "Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\right)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{y}\right) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2$ and $x=\frac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}}\right)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{y}\right) & =0 \\ -8+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{y}\right) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=\frac{1}{2}$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=\frac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ 2+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}-8+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (1) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367184 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bc6f8c3f-8a6b-59cf-bc0b-fd0db0d474a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=6" :db/id 17592186367186} {:answer/id #uuid "424214f9-9d50-5467-95e0-cf55272efa8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=10" :db/id 17592186367187} {:answer/id #uuid "4aae2e57-321d-5434-85a8-2486b5ffa4bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=4" :db/id 17592186367188} {:answer/id #uuid "e1dba1cc-5a3a-58e2-8afb-f17a55ff188a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t=8" :db/id 17592186367189} {:answer/id #uuid "3056aeb4-4139-510a-a7c5-74326f7efd1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No stationary points" :db/id 17592186367190}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367186} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf9d4ba5-fd55-5850-904b-986ef258a618" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367185}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "76fd517a-05e5-5caa-be51-ae532ba4527b" :question/math-academy-id "q-122099" :question/problem "The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}⟩,\,t>2.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨15,1⟩$ when $t=11,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary." :question/worked-solution "The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+{C}_{1},\sqrt{t-2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(11)=⟨15,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=11,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(11) & =⟨3(11)+{C}_{1},\sqrt{11-2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨15,1⟩ & =⟨33+{C}_{1},3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-18$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3t-18,\sqrt{t-2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3t-18,\sqrt{t-2}-2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3t-18=3(t-6) & =0\,⇒\,t=6, \\ \sqrt{t-2}-2 & =0\,⇒\,t=6.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=6,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary."} {:db/id 17592186367191 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "753bc59c-7939-56cc-879b-3cec122d331b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}" :db/id 17592186367193} {:answer/id #uuid "f24d7098-d939-5aa6-950f-fd14eb017097" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{v}^{2})=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}" :db/id 17592186367194} {:answer/id #uuid "9bbc9175-4c96-5988-aa07-bd9572c01406" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}" :db/id 17592186367195} {:answer/id #uuid "2d505332-cf6c-5ec5-915e-4c36344f470f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}" :db/id 17592186367196} {:answer/id #uuid "eb2c040f-5718-5092-9cb7-71a8d668b302" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4}{v}^{2})=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}" :db/id 17592186367197}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367193} :answer-field/id #uuid "6a99db37-d18c-5eb8-8ecd-26a2b8b0ca2b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367192}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "176edb15-1bd9-590d-8107-8cb1c8611e83" :question/math-academy-id "q-122317" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?" :question/worked-solution "![](images/30/30e0e58a17f1683f1c6ca58ea8e4d3df97d7edb76676b0ed6d1a75f62d0c0803.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{2}+2}.

$$
\lim_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨\lim_{s\to 2}{e}^{s-2},\,\lim_{s\to 2}\sqrt{6-s},\,\lim_{s\to 2}\frac{3}{s+2}⟩.
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 2}{e}^{s-2} & ={e}^{2-2} \\  & ={e}^{0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 2}\sqrt{6-s} & =\sqrt{6-2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 2}\frac{3}{s+2} & =\frac{3}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lim_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨1,2,\frac{3}{4}⟩.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 2}‖f(s)‖ & =‖\lim_{s\to 2}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖⟨1,2,\frac{3}{4}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4+\frac{9}{16}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{89}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{89}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367282 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ceda09b-42f8-501d-a383-08efd0867b0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{43}" :db/id 17592186367284} {:answer/id #uuid "da2e911c-55ed-5fd6-866a-fe5e7e2cf6ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{7}" :db/id 17592186367285} {:answer/id #uuid "32ef5bef-ea92-5876-bf4e-23d487bb23cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186367286} {:answer/id #uuid "0f5ef615-4108-595c-9baf-0410f3446bfd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{41}" :db/id 17592186367287} {:answer/id #uuid "b70edbfb-5c4e-5a16-8623-9544c5290403" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186367288}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367284} :answer-field/id #uuid "e8a52fda-2eeb-5ae8-9dd3-08dcd0def12c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367283}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "34bb4860-846c-55de-a294-5c24aba89120" :question/math-academy-id "q-130220" :question/problem "Calculate $\lim_{s\to 2}||f(s)||,$ if $f(s)=⟨\frac{5}{{e}^{s-2}},\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s),\,{s}^{3}-5⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that

$$

$$

$$

$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s) & =3\lim_{s\to 2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s) \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2(0)) \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}

$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "375c4e5c-7d67-56ef-85e2-f7a3cf1d5df9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨3,0,\frac{17}{4}⟩" :db/id 17592186367292} {:answer/id #uuid "705b9303-8d0d-5413-b351-1fa47be9f916" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-7,4,\frac{7}{4}⟩" :db/id 17592186367294} {:answer/id #uuid "c3b3744e-0fee-5753-859b-edbb8569e30b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2,-2,\frac{1}{4}⟩" :db/id 17592186367295} {:db/id 17592186367296 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f051480a-75e8-5c87-bf6f-99de5d0719ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-14\,i-20\,j" :db/id 17592186367298} {:answer/id #uuid "d2068f35-4c95-59b4-95a2-2096dc5afaf8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7\,i+32\,k" :db/id 17592186367299} {:answer/id #uuid "70a9cf8f-48a6-55ae-ae57-cb4008436102" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\,j+4\,k" :db/id 17592186367300} {:answer/id #uuid "778b0044-8b6b-501b-8660-010f97c1c94b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10\,i-4\,j" :db/id 17592186367301} {:answer/id #uuid "0474b124-6bdb-52eb-86e8-ccbb0fd4bbeb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10\,i-24\,j" :db/id 17592186367302}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367302} :answer-field/id #uuid "821e2d8c-9de0-5908-b816-e15dd8600250" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367297}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7575dd83-1f8c-533f-90bd-c13c49b96abe" :question/math-academy-id "q-130303" :question/problem "Find $\lim_{t\to \,-1}[4f(t)-7g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={t}^{3}\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+2)\,k \\ g(t) & =\frac{2}{t}\,i+(3-t)\,j-({t}^{2}-1)k\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{t\to \,-1}f(t) & =(\lim_{t\to \,-1}{t}^{3})i+(\lim_{t\to \,-1}{t}^{2})j+(\lim_{t\to \,-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+2))k \\  & =(-1)^{3}\,i+(-1)^{2}\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1+2)\,k \\  & =-i+j \\ \lim_{t\to \,-1}g(t) & =(\lim_{t\to \,-1}\frac{2}{t})i+(\lim_{t\to \,-1}(3-t))j-(\lim_{t\to \,-1}({t}^{2}-1))k \\  & =\frac{2}{(-1)}\,i+(3-(-1))\,j-((-1)^{2}-1)k \\  & =-2\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{t\to \,-1}[4f(t)-7g(t)] & =\lim_{t\to \,-1}4f(t)-\lim_{t\to \,-1}7g(t) \\  & =4\lim_{t\to \,-1}f(t)-7\lim_{t\to \,-1}g(t) \\  & =4(-i+j)-7(-2\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-4\,i+4\,j+14\,i-28\,j \\  & =10\,i-24\,j\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367366 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "81140528-55a2-55ee-a446-c4ecc4c389dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x{y}^{2}+2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186367368} {:answer/id #uuid "4d99e938-b77d-5e49-9ef0-2b8dd93510e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186367369} {:answer/id #uuid "eaf7538b-e8be-53f6-845e-acbc84a6dd44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-y\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186367370} {:answer/id #uuid "a76b0d37-e266-5f23-bb84-9c2088fc0784" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy+3y\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186367371} {:answer/id #uuid "50aebbec-bc0b-570c-b51a-a4d30ffaac7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x{y}^{3}-y\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186367372}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367372} :answer-field/id #uuid "f51dbd77-8136-52af-a21a-6a5b89bd8649" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367367}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8e4f4f05-cab9-5b00-b80d-9d3be44e8ac8" :question/math-academy-id "q-131245" :question/problem "Calculate $∇\cdot (\frac{1}{2}F+4G)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F={x}^{2}{y}^{3}\,i+{y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,j,\,∇\cdot G=-\frac{1}{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x).
$$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following  linearity properties for divergence:

- $∇\cdot (kF)=k∇\cdot F$

- $∇\cdot (F+G)=∇\cdot F+∇\cdot G.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot (\frac{1}{2}F+4G) & =∇\cdot (\frac{1}{2}F)+∇\cdot (4G) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}∇\cdot F+4∇\cdot G.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\cdot F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =2x{y}^{3}+2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot (\frac{1}{2}F+2G) & =\frac{1}{2}∇\cdot F+4∇\cdot G \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2x{y}^{3}+2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+4\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =x{y}^{3}+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =x{y}^{3}-y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367394 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08de6403-2d52-5dd0-9c3b-bab664422477" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\,j-4\,k" :db/id 17592186367396} {:answer/id #uuid "c7a6a601-5e44-5d4b-94df-9d7577be2469" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\,i-\,j-\,k" :db/id 17592186367397} {:answer/id #uuid "0b4ffcf0-3a28-5bc9-a8c2-b21966504cde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\,i-2\,j-\,k" :db/id 17592186367398} {:answer/id #uuid "53d72b2a-2368-5e35-99e7-9decb1de1bc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\,i-3\,k" :db/id 17592186367399} {:answer/id #uuid "1c8b6117-ec3a-598e-98e3-464fe7089ab4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,i-\,j+\,k" :db/id 17592186367400}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367397} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d516dd2-3a3f-57cb-81e8-97240a83bf25" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367395}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a228f632-61ee-5c03-aaca-8c928152bf6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-131469" :question/problem "Calculate $∇\times (2F+G)$ at the point $(-1,1,4)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=2\sqrt{y}\,i+z\,j+yz\,k,\,(∇\times G)(x,y,z)=x\,i-y\,j+\,k.
$$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (2F+G) & =∇\times (2G)+∇\times G \\  & =2∇\times F+∇\times G\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 2\sqrt{y} & z & yz\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(z)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\sqrt{y})]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(z)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{y})]k \\  & =(z-1)i-(0-0)j+(0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}})k \\  & =(z-1)\,i-\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (2F+G) & =2∇\times F+∇\times G \\  & =2[(z-1)\,i-\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,k]+x\,i-y\,j+\,k \\  & =(x+2z-2)\,i-y\,j+(1-\frac{2}{\sqrt{y}})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(-1,1,4),$ we get

$$
(∇\times (2F+G))(-1,1,4)=5\,i-\,j-\,k
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367415 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9ac561cd-4afb-5983-a6f4-d4eb2282622a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}}{2}" :db/id 17592186367417} {:answer/id #uuid "b95dc5bf-88d3-59aa-a735-241d3ae8562e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{t}" :db/id 17592186367418} {:answer/id #uuid "535f3c6d-b465-549e-91ca-4a2b92cf64a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}" :db/id 17592186367419} {:answer/id #uuid "c5b17d89-40ae-5fe4-8c66-1be5d8fdc9dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}" :db/id 17592186367420} {:answer/id #uuid "6d0a6633-8e0c-5c5e-964b-530af5aa51ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186367421}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367417} :answer-field/id #uuid "286f4b92-5146-53e6-94b4-5d0de177995b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367416}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "637c470e-0d8c-59d9-a6f9-8a2dca1476a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-132053" :question/problem "Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & ={e}^{-t}\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-t}\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t+{\cos }^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{-t}\sqrt{2({\cos }^{2}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =({e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩)\times (2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩) \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}\,\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}\,\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}({\cos }^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t)k \\  & =2{e}^{-2t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=2{e}^{-2t}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-2t}}{{(\sqrt{2}{e}^{-t})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-2t}}{2\sqrt{2}{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367470 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7bfc3282-f67f-5c37-ac20-e055804cec92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186367472} {:answer/id #uuid "5da30080-28c4-5744-8ac6-43e6e2a96e89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4)\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186367473} {:answer/id #uuid "936e31ff-aad2-5671-b08c-0fa686997e21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4t)\sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+1}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186367474} {:answer/id #uuid "7d95b191-aa8b-5d93-9bb0-e81b8a9878a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{{t}^{2}+2t+2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186367475} {:answer/id #uuid "a4eba06b-dd48-5f6b-83d8-0809f2454d04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4)^{2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186367476}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367472} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f020de9-ae3e-53bd-98e8-98a1724485d9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367471}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "48e4ffbf-2c4f-5623-a301-c10de09f0525" :question/math-academy-id "q-139028" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3-{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{2}+4t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-{t}^{2})=-2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+4t)=2t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{{(-2t)}^{2}+{(2t+4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+16t+16}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+16t+16}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{16(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\cdot 4\cdot \sqrt{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(3-{t}^{2})\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367484 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3f3602d4-7774-5286-bdb0-42626915479b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨3,\,2⟩" :db/id 17592186367486} {:answer/id #uuid "a86646f6-0aea-5838-9281-711fc0aaab24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨6,\,4⟩" :db/id 17592186367487} {:answer/id #uuid "d16f8a6b-65f3-5d35-965b-7c8661d15a52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,\,0⟩" :db/id 17592186367488} {:answer/id #uuid "ed2cc10f-e116-5a70-8e54-83885a24828a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨6,\,0⟩" :db/id 17592186367489} {:answer/id #uuid "a0aedead-4663-537d-a1e2-ed4fd155d953" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,\,4⟩" :db/id 17592186367490}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367488} :answer-field/id #uuid "b7670fb6-77b3-5fc1-8438-31c45735ec36" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367485}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6c400062-b704-53b2-a5d1-f71fc8c9b881" :question/math-academy-id "q-139103" :question/problem "A particle $P$ of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is subject to the external forces 

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨2,\,4{\sin }^{3}⁡t⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{\cos }^{2}⁡t⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in Newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨2,\,4{\sin }^{3}⁡t⟩+⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{\cos }^{2}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨2+8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4{\sin }^{3}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{\cos }^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t({\sin }^{2}⁡t+{\cos }^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot ⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩+C \\ ⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨-1,\,-1⟩+C \\ C & =⟨1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally  the velocity at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367491 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bc1c5cf-dc00-565a-b5de-2aecc673a9c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,\text{m/s}" :db/id 17592186367493} {:answer/id #uuid "f18c3353-7bd9-553a-8189-af5d9ebc05d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+1)\,\text{m/s}" :db/id 17592186367494} {:answer/id #uuid "963e84d8-033d-5eb5-b676-05760356d3fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\,\text{m/s}" :db/id 17592186367495} {:answer/id #uuid "e69a533f-6590-56bb-878f-944cce976492" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{4(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}+1}\,\text{m/s}" :db/id 17592186367496} {:answer/id #uuid "20c5b775-7962-5062-98fe-596bd75c4a41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\operatorname{ln}⁡2+1)\,\text{m/s}" :db/id 17592186367497}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367493} :answer-field/id #uuid "90ce23db-20f0-51ed-8d0e-5662917a63a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367492}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "fb76b3d3-7747-5184-8deb-72097c45f2c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-139104" :question/problem "A particle $P$ of mass $5\,\text{kg}$ is subject to the external forces 

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨\frac{3t-7}{{t}^{2}-1},\,5t⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨\frac{7t-3}{{t}^{2}-1},\,5t⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in Newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=1\,\text{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨\frac{3t-7}{{t}^{2}-1},\,5t⟩+⟨\frac{7t-3}{{t}^{2}-1},\,5t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10t-10}{(t+1)(t-1)},\,10t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10(t-1)}{(t+1)(t-1)},\,10t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10}{t+1},\,10t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot ⟨\frac{10}{t+1},\,10t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{t+1},\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{2}{t+1},\,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{2}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1),\,{0}^{2}⟩+C \\ ⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨0,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}⟩+⟨0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=1,$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1),\,{1}^{2}-1⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=1$ equals the magnitude of $v(1).$ Therefore,

$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$

$$

The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=x$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-xy,\,Q=-z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-xy)\cdot (-2x)-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4)\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2{x}^{2}y+2{x}^{2}y+2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)=1 \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-xy,\,Q=-z=-x,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-(-xy)\cdot 1-(-x)\cdot 0+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y-xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367839 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5e0e4dc6-cc83-5e7f-b79b-720783cf7352" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5M}{3}" :db/id 17592186367841} {:answer/id #uuid "a0587d1f-391c-5f9b-b8d8-5028a4784a60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "M" :db/id 17592186367842} {:answer/id #uuid "4546c8b6-bbbc-54a2-93a7-576b3f98f83a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5M" :db/id 17592186367843} {:answer/id #uuid "5adb24a3-dc97-532e-a764-ed7f738bd46a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M" :db/id 17592186367844} {:answer/id #uuid "ca913f2f-94bb-5779-968a-0f4050cccdc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{5}" :db/id 17592186367845}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367841} :answer-field/id #uuid "836bf381-5e9c-5e6d-b2b3-b979431c05d9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "277b81af-ece5-57d8-a083-94f5105fa453" :question/math-academy-id "q-163181" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$
The mass density at each point is proportional to the sum of its distance from the 
$x$-axis and its distance from the $y$-axis. Find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(|x|+|y|)=k(x+y),
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}k(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}2+2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{[2y+{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =k(4+4) \\  & =8k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{M}{8}$ and hence,

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(x+y)=\frac{M}{8}(x+y).
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot (x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{8}(\frac{16}{3}+8) \\  & =\frac{5M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367846 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7d7207b7-4fda-5f9d-a776-fb1f6b0bb92c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14M}{15}" :db/id 17592186367848} {:answer/id #uuid "1e842a0a-61ed-5c50-bb33-fa3671a32175" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7M}{12}" :db/id 17592186367849} {:answer/id #uuid "9efac7e2-97f9-57f2-8dea-ec632a1aa019" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{28M}{5}" :db/id 17592186367850} {:answer/id #uuid "c8bfe486-709a-5ba4-9d2d-497eabbffd3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{18}" :db/id 17592186367851} {:answer/id #uuid "2750671c-4e31-5c69-bc02-fa6f4189ee66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{25M}{16}" :db/id 17592186367852}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367850} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7a3feb3-84c3-54d4-90e6-341ec4dd20f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b38b3077-133c-52ce-8205-890ef0b0a1a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163184" :question/problem "![](images/6f/6fc8ecc2fe5ee32ec165c2624d21f85794fc53c5d74d255987ad7120e5926516.png)

The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $y$-axis. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 2x},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/3c/3cd38c4eca16f60ac918a6867e858ae3c1d4589a3a02d04f7b34f5cf7e24ac62.png)

From the description, the mass density function can be written as 

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k|x|=kx,
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}kx\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2x}x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}[xy]_{y=0}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{16k}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3M}{16}$ and hence,

$$
\lambda (x,y)=kx=\frac{3M}{16}x.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2x}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{3}x{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}(2x)+\frac{1}{3}x(2x)^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{14}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7M}{8}{[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7M}{8}\cdot \frac{32}{5} \\  & =\frac{28M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367853 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08398c3d-3e03-5d83-8397-2ca807e951ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6M" :db/id 17592186367855} {:answer/id #uuid "e8bb5c5e-4771-5a0d-8b21-0e4447b56a1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7M}{2}" :db/id 17592186367856} {:answer/id #uuid "0a55a3fe-9a71-5c66-b7d5-042ecf4ed23a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4M}{3}" :db/id 17592186367857} {:answer/id #uuid "c032f735-7507-5c6b-a3f6-5a28802ae331" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14M}{3}" :db/id 17592186367858} {:answer/id #uuid "291ed787-40cd-51ad-a736-6c41c7b22191" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3M" :db/id 17592186367859}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367858} :answer-field/id #uuid "65b269d1-bfcb-5c77-a4a9-ff25c88ac590" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367854}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a7f0c8ba-8052-5102-b6bb-8f55d8855ad2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163215" :question/problem "![](images/f2/f2882faa5326248c0a8376a8b05ce5e8008ed2c545b4ea212611334723a57185.png)
