This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\underbrace{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{\text{chain rule}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+2y=t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{t}+B{e}^{2t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta $ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0-3\alpha +2(\alpha t+\beta )=t-4
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
2\alpha t+(-3\alpha +2\beta )=t-4.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2\alpha &=1\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ -3\alpha +2\beta &=-4\, && (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Hence, $\alpha =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\beta =-\frac{5}{4},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{2}t-\frac{5}{4}=\frac{2t-5}{4}.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5}{4}.
$$

The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. 

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =-12\cdot 1 \\  & =-12<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t-2}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+{C}_{1},\sqrt{t-2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(11)=⟨15,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=11,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(11) & =⟨3(11)+{C}_{1},\sqrt{11-2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨15,1⟩ & =⟨33+{C}_{1},3+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-18$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3t-18,\sqrt{t-2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3t-18,\sqrt{t-2}-2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3t-18=3(t-6) & =0\,⇒\,t=6, \\ \sqrt{t-2}-2 & =0\,⇒\,t=6.\end{aligned}

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=6,$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=x$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-xy,\,Q=-z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-xy)\cdot (-2x)-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4)\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2{x}^{2}y+2{x}^{2}y+2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)=1 \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-xy,\,Q=-z=-x,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-(-xy)\cdot 1-(-x)\cdot 0+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y-xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(|x|+|y|)=k(x+y),
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}k(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}2+2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{[2y+{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =k(4+4) \\  & =8k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{M}{8}$ and hence,

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(x+y)=\frac{M}{8}(x+y).
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot (x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{8}(\frac{16}{3}+8) \\  & =\frac{5M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{x}{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨0,2,-2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨0,2,-2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}c\operatorname{ln}⁡y &=0 \\ \frac{cx}{y}+2cy &=2 \\ -c &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0\,⟹\,y=1.

And substituting $c=2$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =(-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{1}^{2} \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-1,1,1).$" "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

Using the additive property of the definite integral, we write

$$

The 1st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,3].$ The corresponding region is a semi-cirle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi \cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}+2.\end{aligned}

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
{x}^{2}-2x-8=(x+2)(x-4).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8} & =\frac{3x-6}{(x+2)(x-4)}=\frac{A}{x+2}+\frac{B}{x-4},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
3x-6=A(x-4)+B(x+2).
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(4)-6 & =A(4-4)+B(4+2) \\ 6 & =6B \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-2)-6 & =A(-2-4)+B(-2+2) \\ -12 & =-6A \\ A & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}=\frac{2}{x+2}+\frac{1}{x-4}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{x+2}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}(x-4)|+C\end{aligned}
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-2t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t).
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is a linear polynomial. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a linear polynomial, i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha +\beta t,
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =2,$ $\beta =-2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2-2t,

and the general solution is

$$
y={e}^{-2t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)+2-2t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at $y=2\,\text{m}$ with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=2$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-3$ and the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-3}{\text{factor of }2}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm \frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{3}{2},\pm 1,\pm 3.
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(0,\frac{3}{2}),$ are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $1$ | $3$ |
|  | $2$ | $2$ | $6$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-\frac{1}{2})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-\frac{1}{2})(2{x}^{2}+2x+6).
$$

Now we must see if the polynomial $g(x)=2{x}^{2}+2x+6$ has real roots. For this, we must find the value of its discriminant $D.$ Note that

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(2)^{2}-4(2)(6) \\  & =4-48 \\  & =-44.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D<0,$ the polynomial $g(x)$ doesn't have real roots.

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Notice that the augmented matrix $M$ is already in its row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-1 & 4 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{5}{4}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get 

$$

$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ \frac{5}{4}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.

$$
y =\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.
$$

As we determined previously, the coefficients of this series satisfy the recurrence relation

$$
a_{n+1} =\dfrac{a_n }{n+1  }, \qquad n= 0,1,2, \ldots
$$

Since we are looking for the general solution of the differential equation, we can set the first term of its power series solution to an arbitrary number. So, we can set $a_0=C,$ where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Now, using the recurrence relation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{{a}_{0}}{0+1}=\frac{C}{1}, \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1+1}=\frac{C}{1\cdot 2}, \\ {a}_{3} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{2+1}=\frac{C}{1\cdot 2\cdot 3}, \\  & \,\,⋮ \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{C}{n!}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =C+\frac{C}{1}\,x+\frac{C}{1\cdot 2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{C}{1\cdot 2\cdot 3}\,{x}^{3}+⋯+\frac{C}{n!}\,{x}^{n}+⋯ \\  & =C(1+x+\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+⋯+\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}+⋯) \\  & =C({\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}).\end{aligned}
$$

Recall the definition of the standard Maclaurin series of the exponential function:

$$
e^{x} = 1+x+\frac{1}{2!}x^2+\cdots + \dfrac{x^n}{n!} + \cdots = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{x^n}{n!}
$$

So, finally, we can write the general solution of our differential equation as 

$$
y = C e^x.
$$

The solution of a differential equation is not always a recognizable standard series. But if we are able to find the recurrence relation for the coefficients, we can always present the solution as a general power series." Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region.

First, the phrase **enclosed by the $xy$-plane** tells us that the bottom of the solid is
$$
z=0.
$$

The plane
$$
z = 4 - x - y
$$
is the top of the solid.

Also, the planes
$$
x = 0 ,  x = 2 ,  y = 0 ,  y = 1
$$
describe the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. So the base region is the rectangle
$$
D = \{  ( x , y ) : 0 \le  x \le  2 , \text{ } 0 \le  y \le  1 \}  .
$$

Therefore, for each point $(x,y)$ in this rectangle, the variable $z$ runs from the bottom surface to the top surface:
$$
0 \le  z \le  4 - x - y .
$$

So the volume is
$$
V = {\iiint }_{R} \text{d} V = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{4 - x - y} \text{d} z  \text{d} y  \text{d} x .
$$

Now we evaluate:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}V &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} {[ z ]}_{z = 0}^{z = 4 - x - y} \text{d} y  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} ( 4 - x - y )  \text{d} y  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {[ ( 4 - x ) y - \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} ]}_{y = 0}^{y = 1} \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} ( 4 - x - \frac{1}{2} ) \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} ( \frac{7}{2} - x ) \text{d} x \\  &  = {[ \frac{7}{2} x - \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} ]}_{0}^{2} \\  &  = 7 - 2 \\  &  = 5.\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the solid is $5.$

In problems like this, the planes involving only $x$ and $y$ usually describe the base region in the $xy$-plane, while the $xy$-plane and the surface or plane involving $z$ describe the lower and upper bounds for $z$." $$
r=3,\,(\theta ,z)\in C,
$$

where
$C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

Hence, the cost to manufacture its mesh is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A
$$

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{C}\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A.
$$

The function under the first integral is constant, so we have

$$
{∬}_{C}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(C)=2\pi \cdot 3=6\pi .
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $z.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A & =\frac{(3-0)}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }\cdot {[{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }((2\pi )^{2}-0) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $\theta .$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A & =(2\pi -0){\int }_{0}^{3}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\pi ({3}^{2}-0) \\  & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2\pi }(6\pi +6\pi +18\pi )=15.
$$

Therefore, the cost to manufacture the mesh of the cylindrical heater is $\$15.$" "We found that the surface of the heater can be described in cylindrical polar coordinates as

$$
\mathbf{f}(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}\theta ,z⟩\hspace{2em}(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $\mathbf{r}(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
\mathbf{r}(\theta )=\mathbf{f}(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $\mathbf{r}(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
\mathbf{r}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf{r}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{'}(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we normalize the vector found in Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=20\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(20)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =200\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=200-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=10\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =200-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =200-\frac{k}{2}(10)^{2} \\ 50k & =200 \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{y}^{″} & ={x}^{2}-2{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2{y}^{′}}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=2, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3},\, && z(1)=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=3.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=3$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{3-1}{2}=1.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=2$ and $z(1)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}=\frac{{1}^{2}-2\cdot 0}{3}=\frac{1}{3} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0\cdot 1=0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 1=\frac{1}{3} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+0=2 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, we conclude that

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-5t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-5t) &={e}^{-5t} \\ r(5t) &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-5t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 5-\frac{1}{2}t & =0 \\ t & =10.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(|x|+|y|)=k(x+y),
$$

$$

$$

$$

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+6}{{x}^{2}-4} & =\frac{2x+6}{(x-2)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{(x+2)}+\frac{B}{(x-2)},\end{aligned}

which gives

$$

$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2)+6 & =A(2-2)+B(2+2) \\ 10 & =4B \\ B & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-2)+6 & =A(-2-2)+B(-2+2) \\ 2 & =-4A \\ A & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{2x+6}{{x}^{2}-4}=-\frac{1}{2(x+2)}+\frac{5}{2(x-2)}.

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$

$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+6}{{x}^{2}-4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-2)^{5}|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{(x-2)^{5}}{x+2}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-7,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$

Finally, the definite integral is

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

So, we get the following result:

3{x}_{i-1}+{y}_{j-1}-1\le \frac{3}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-1\le 3{x}_{i}+{y}_{j}-1.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\left[\frac{3}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})+\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-1\right]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le \frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,+\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{3}{2}({4}^{2}-{1}^{2})(4-2)=45 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})(4-1)=18 \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =(4-1)(4-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 45+18-6\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 57\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=57.
$$"] [17592186341884 :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

which simplifies to

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$

$$"] [17592186348305 :question/worked-solution "The substitution $z={x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$

$$

where $C=0.08{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the package is released from rest. So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0)=0,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =\frac{25}{2}\operatorname{tanh}⁡\left(\frac{2}{25}g\cdot 0+C\right) \\ 0 & =\frac{25}{2}\operatorname{tanh}⁡(C) \\ \operatorname{tanh}⁡(C) & =0 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at the point $(0,0)$ and its maximum value is $1.$"] [17592186365226 :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of $f$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-y=0.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186365845 :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions.

={\left[\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}(2\theta )+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}\theta \right]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -0)+\frac{1}{4}(0-0)+\frac{4}{3}(0-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186367715 :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/6f/6fe710e758ccda9a826d79f8219dc82b25f8cc39f65d92f02a6c28594c428a96.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{2}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=6-2x=6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta ,z)\hspace{0.167em}:\hspace{0.167em}0\le r\le \sqrt{2},\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta <\pi ,\hspace{0.222em}0\le z\le 6-2r\operatorname{cos}\theta \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}4\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}4\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{0}^{6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }4r\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}4r[z]_{z=0}^{z=6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}4r(6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}24r-8{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\left[12{r}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \right]}_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }12(\sqrt{2})^{2}-\frac{8}{3}(\sqrt{2})^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }24-\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\left[24\theta -\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \right]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi } \\  & =24(\pi -0)-\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3}(0-0) \\  & =24\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186367736 :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=x$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-xy,\,Q=-z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\left(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R\right)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-xy)\cdot (-2x)-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4)\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2{x}^{2}y+2{x}^{2}y+2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)=1 \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-xy,\,Q=-z=-x,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}\left(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R\right)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-(-xy)\cdot 1-(-x)\cdot 0+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{y}^{3}-8y-xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186367839 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(|x|+|y|)=k(x+y),
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}k(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{\left[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+xy\right]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}2+2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{[2y+{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =k(4+4) \\  & =8k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{M}{8}$ and hence,

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(x+y)=\frac{M}{8}(x+y).
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot (x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\left[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x{y}^{3}\right]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{8}{\left[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}\right]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{8}\left(\frac{16}{3}+8\right) \\  & =\frac{5M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186367846 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 2x},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/3c/3cd38c4eca16f60ac918a6867e858ae3c1d4589a3a02d04f7b34f5cf7e24ac62.png)

From the description, the mass density function can be written as 

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k|x|=kx,
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}kx\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2x}x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}[xy]_{y=0}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\left[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}\right]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{16k}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3M}{16}$ and hence,

$$
\lambda (x,y)=kx=\frac{3M}{16}x.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2x}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\left[{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{3}x{y}^{3}\right]}_{y=0}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}(2x)+\frac{1}{3}x(2x)^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{14}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7M}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7M}{8}{\left[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}\right]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7M}{8}\cdot \frac{32}{5} \\  & =\frac{28M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186367853 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

as shown below.

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\left[{x}^{2}y+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\right]}_{y=0}^{y=2x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{3}+\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{14}{3}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\left[\frac{7}{6}{x}^{4}\right]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7M}{24}(16-0) \\  & =\frac{14M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186367860 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

as shown below.

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$

$$"]] "retractions" [[17592186332715 :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (y+11)^{5/3}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Now, we let $u=y+11.$ Then differentiating with respect to $y$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}y=\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (y+11)^{5/3}\,\text{d}y & =\int {u}^{5/3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{8/3}}{8/3}+C \\  & =\frac{3}{8}(y+11)^{8/3}+C \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\frac{3}{8}\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}] & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[(y+11)^{8/3}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{3}(y+11)^{5/3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y+11)+0 \\  & =(y+11)^{5/3}\cdot 1 \\  & =\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{5}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186332719 :question/worked-solution "First, let $u=2-3x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u$, solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2-3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-3x|+C\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186332722 :question/worked-solution "We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrrr} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 3 & 3 & -9 & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & 9 & 0 & 3 \\ \hline  & 3 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{3{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+x-1}{x-3}=3{x}^{2}+1+\frac{2}{x-3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+x-1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}+1+\frac{2}{x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}+x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186332723 :question/worked-solution "We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrr} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -5 & 1 & 7 & 10 \\  & ↓ & -5 & -10 \\ \hline  & 1 & 2 & 0\end{array}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+7x+10}{x+5}=x+2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{2}+7x+10}{x+5}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+2)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{1}+2x{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}]+2[1-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+2 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186332725 :question/worked-solution "First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+2}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x+2}{2(x-\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x+2}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{3}{2} & 1 & 2 \\  & ↓ & \frac{3}{2} \\ \hline  & 1 & \frac{7}{2}\end{array}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+2}{(x-\frac{3}{2})} & =1+\frac{\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)}{(x-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =1+\frac{7}{2(x-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =1+\frac{7}{2x-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+2}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1+\frac{7}{2x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\int \text{d}x+7\int \frac{1}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x+\frac{7}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-3|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}+\frac{7}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186332726 :question/worked-solution "First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+1}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x+1}{3(x+\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{x+1}{(x+\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{2}{3} & 1 & 1 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \hline  & 1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{array}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+1}{(x+\frac{2}{3})} & =1+\frac{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}{(x+\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{3(x+\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{3x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+1}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1+\frac{1}{3x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\int \text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[x+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+2|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{3}+\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186332729 :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{4|x|\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|4x|\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\operatorname{arcsec} ,$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec} (u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $4x.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$

$$"] [17592186348300 :question/problem "Estimate $\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0).$"] [17592186348300 :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the differential:

$$

At the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0),$ the differential is

$$"] [17592186348305 :question/worked-solution "The substitution $z={x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

with

We then compute an integrating factor:

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{2x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2z) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 6 \\ {e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2{e}^{2x}z & =6{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{2x}z) & =6{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}

where we used that $x>0$ and $y>0.$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186348314 :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x/2}.$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$"] [17592186348424 :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$

\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-3}{\text{factor of }2}.

$$

$$

$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

Since $y\le 0,$ we obtain

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9\,⟹\,y\ge -\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

$$
y =\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n.

As we determined previously, the coefficients of this series satisfy the recurrence relation

$$
a_{n+1} =\dfrac{a_n }{n+1  }, \qquad n= 0,1,2, \ldots
$$

Since we are looking for the general solution of the differential equation, we can set the first term of its power series solution to an arbitrary number. So, we can set $a_0=C,$ where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Now, using the recurrence relation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{{a}_{0}}{0+1}=\frac{C}{1}, \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1+1}=\frac{C}{1\cdot 2}, \\ {a}_{3} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{2+1}=\frac{C}{1\cdot 2\cdot 3}, \\  & \,\,⋮ \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{C}{n!}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =C+\frac{C}{1}\,x+\frac{C}{1\cdot 2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{C}{1\cdot 2\cdot 3}\,{x}^{3}+⋯+\frac{C}{n!}\,{x}^{n}+⋯ \\  & =C(1+x+\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+⋯+\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}+⋯) \\  & =C({\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{n!}).\end{aligned}
$$

Recall the definition of the standard Maclaurin series of the exponential function:

$$

So, finally, we can write the general solution of our differential equation as 

$$

$$

Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf{r}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{'}(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{n} & =\frac{\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}}{||\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{y}{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+0\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186362496 :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $E$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $E$ is given by

$$"] [17592186362505 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$

$$

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$

$$

Therefore, by applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2y-(-4y))\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2y\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186362527 :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $G$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $G$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}G\cdot \,\text{d}S={∬}_{S}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $G=⟨0,0,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $G$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides.

![](images/9e/9e894018baf5f651e2d43cb48a324a5470c9061e6da10f666978519b3bff4c7f.png)

Let's consider the flux of $G$ through these two sides.

* Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}G\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-32⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =-xy-32.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $G$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot \text{d}{S}_{1} & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}(-xy-32)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(xy+32)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(xy+32)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y+32x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+64)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}+64y]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =-132.\end{aligned}
$$

* Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}G\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy-2{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $G$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}G\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}G\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-132+4 \\  & =-128.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186362539 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{y}^{″} & ={x}^{2}-2{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2{y}^{′}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=2, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3},\, && z(1)=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=3.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=3$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{3-1}{2}=1.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=2$ and $z(1)=0.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186367839 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

$$

$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(|x|+|y|)=k(x+y),
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}k(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}2+2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =k{[2y+{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =k(4+4) \\  & =8k\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k(x+y)=\frac{M}{8}(x+y).

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}kx\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2x}x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}[xy]_{y=0}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =k{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{16k}{3}\end{aligned}
